Gondatti  states  that  the  ancient\nVogul  heroes  ate  the  hearts  and  livers  of  their  slain  enemies\n“  that  their  strength  might  be  transferred  to  their  own  bodies\nand  that  the  foe  might  never  again  be  able  to  rise  from  the\ndead.”  8  Beliefs  regarding  the  potencies  hidden  in  the  heart\nrecur  in  a  Chronicle  of  889,  which  states  that  the  Hungarians\ncut  the  captives’  hearts  in  pieces  and  ate  them  as  some  sort\nof  remedy  j  and  to  this  day  the  sacrificial  priest  of  the  Cheremiss  prays  God  to  protect  men  against  “  those  who  cut  out\nthe  heart  and  the  liver.”  The  same  belief  was  doubtless  held\nby  the  forefathers  of  the  Finns,  for  among  their  Esthonian\nkinsmen  it  was  still  flourishing  in  the  thirteenth  century,  since\nthe  Sakkala  peasants  are  said  to  have  torn  the  heart  from  the\nbreast  of  a  living  Danish  Crusader,  and  after  roasting  it,  to\nhave  divided  it  among  themselves  and  eaten  it  “  in  order  to\nbe  brave  against  the  Christians.”  By  drinking  another  man’s\nblood  the  Voguls  and  others  believe  that  soul-powers  pass\nfrom  one  body  into  another.9  Even  in  such  insignificant  parts\nof  the  body  as  the  hair,  nails,  and  teeth  a  soul  (or  soul-power)\nis  believed  to  lie  concealed.  How  else  could  the  means  of\nguarding  the  soul  against  falling  into  evil  hands  be  explained?\nNovitskiy  expressly  relates  that  a  Vogul  sacrificial  priest\nwarned  his  people  against  the  Russian  missionaries  in  the  fol¬\nlowing  words:  “Take  care,  my  friends  .  .  .  when  they  start\nto  cut  your  hair,  they  cut  off  your  souls.”  In  this  connection,\nit  may  be  mentioned  that  the  Ostiaks  believed  that  by  scalping\nan  enemy  they  could  prevent  his  ghost  from  walking.10  Even\nthose  objects  which  have  been  in  contact  with  a  man  sustain  a\ncertain  relation  to  the  soul.  Among  causes  of  illness  the  Lapps\nrecognize  the  power  of  a  dweller  in  the  underworld  to  take\nto  himself  some  article  of  attire  which  has  been  in  contact\nwith  the  sick,  such  as  cap,  gloves,  or  boots ;  11  and  from  this\nis  deduced  the  magical  theory  of  pars  pro  toto  which  finds\napplication  likewise  in  rites  of  sacrifice.\n\nIn  close  relation  to  the  remains  of  the  deceased  stands  his\n\nshape,  or  shadow,  which  can  occasionally  free  itself  from  the\nbody  even  during  life.  Of  a  man  who  is  unconscious  the\nCheremiss  says  that  his  “  shape  ”  or  “  shadow  ”  (ort)  has  left\nhim;  and  in  like  manner,  if  any  one  gives  him  a  severe  fright,\nhe  declares:  “  Thou  drivest  mine  ort  away.”  If  a  Cheremiss\ndreams  of  a  city,  he  is  convinced  that  his  ort  has  wandered\nthither  by  night ;  otherwise,  he  argues,  he  could  not  have  seen\nthe  city  exactly  as  it  is.  Dreaming  is  also  called  “  the  drtys\nwandering”;  and  when  the  man  awakes,  his  ort  returns  to  his\nbody.12\n\nThe  ort  of  the  Cheremiss  corresponds  to  the  urt  of  the\nVotiaks.  If  the  urt  does  not  succeed  in  coming  back  to  its\nabode  before  the  man  wakes,  he  falls  ill,  is  pale,  and  begins\nto  pine  away,  so  that  a  sleeper  must  not  be  aroused  suddenly.13\nIn  general  the  disappearance  of  the  soul  is  regarded  as  a  cause\nof  grave  illness,  and  in  such  a  contingency  it  is  advisable  to\nhave  recourse  to  a  magician  or  shaman  in  order  that  he  may\nseek  the  lost  soul  and  bring  it  back  to  the  body.  Sometimes\nit  happens  that  the  “  soul  ”  of  the  dying  goes  to  the  nether\nworld,  but  returns  after  a  while ;  and  then  the  man  recovers.\nThus  an  Ostiak  song  tells  of  a  hero  who,  in  battle,  received\na  sword-stroke  on  his  head  and  lost  consciousness.  For  a  time\nhis  “  shadow  ”  ascended  to  heaven,  only  to  return  when  his\ndead  brother’s  “  shadow  ”  informed  him  that  his  hour  was\nnot  yet  come.14  A  very  wide-spread  belief  holds  that  the\nshaman’s  “  shadow  ”  can  go  to  the  underworld  to  seek  aid\nthere.\n\nThe  closeness  of  the  connexion  between  a  man’s  body  and\nhis  u  shadow  ”  is  shown  by  an  account  of  Lapp  shamanism\nwhich  dates  from  the  thirteenth  century.  This  states,  among\nother  matters,  that  during  a  shaman’s  journey  in  the  nether\nworld  a  hostile  “  shadow  ”  struck  out  the  stomach  of  his\nu  shadow,”  the  mishap  being  clearly  visible  in  the  magician’s\nreal  body,  which  was  lying  in  the  tent;  15  and  several  similar\ninstances  will  be  cited  in  a  subsequent  chapter  on  the  shamans."

Its  exterior\nis  parti-coloured,  and  its  wings  resemble  those  of  a  bat.”\nShamans  can  always  see  it  near  them.  Should  any  one  hear\nits  call,  he  turns  to  it  with  the  words:  “  If  one  of  my  kins¬\nfolk  is  to  die,  draw  thou  nigh  to  me.”  If  some  relative  is\nactually  the  person  in  question,  the  urt  approaches  the  inquirer;\nbut  otherwise  it  withdraws  from  him.  According  to  Friis,\nthe  Norse  Lapps  called  such  a  bird,  heard  by  night  lamenting\nwith  a  human  voice,  a  Suoje-lodde  (“  Suoj e-bird  ”),  the\nword  Sueje  being  used  in  the  Swedish  Lapmark  to  denote\nthe  shaman’s  “  tutelary  genius,”  the  appellation  having\napparently  meant  primarily  “  shadow.”  The  spectres  of\nshamans  are  especially  liable  to  metamorphosis.22\n\nThe  tutelary  genius  of  a  man  is  called  Haltia  (“  Ruler  ”)\nby  the  Finns;  and  each  individual  has  his  own,  which  pre¬\ncedes  him. A  man’s  Varjohaltia  (“  Shadow-ruler  ”)\ncould  inform  him  beforehand  of  coming  events,  as,  e.g.,\nwhether  he  would  reap  a  good  or  a  bad  harvest.  It  was  be¬\nlieved  in  some  districts  that  a  child  made  its  own  Haltia  when\nit  was  three  days  old;  before  the  expiration  of  that  time  it\nwas  dangerous  to  leave  the  infant  alone,  for  a  changeling\nmight  be  substituted  in  its  stead.  That  the  Haltia  manifested\nitself  in  the  form  of  the  culprit  is  obvious  from  such  phrases\nas  u  it  was  not  he,  but  his  Haltia,”  or  “  the  dead  themselves\ndo  not  walk,  it  is  their  Haltias  which  appear  as  ghosts.”\n\nThe  Saattaja  (“  guide  ”)  —  an  expression  which  is  com¬\nparatively  rare  —  and  the  Onni  (“  fortune  ”)  seem  to  denote\nprecisely  the  same  being  as  the  Haltia;  and  a  man’s  a  fortune,”\nwhich  might  be  propitious  or  the  reverse,  never  left  him  till\ndeath. The\nChuvash  act  in  the  same  way,  saying:  “  If  the  dead  over  there\nask  of  thee  if  there  are  others  to  come  after  thee,  answer\nthem:  c  My  ears  heard  none,  my  eyes  saw  nothing,  my  nostrils\nknew  no  scent.’  ” 11  Missionaries  relate  that  when  the  Lapps\ncovered  up  their  dead  in  shrouds,  they  were  very  careful  to\ncover  up  the  body  completely.12  This  was  most  likely  done\nfor  fear  that  the  soul  of  the  deceased,  which  was  supposed  to\ndwell  in  the  body  even  after  death,  would  otherwise  leave  its\ndwelling-place  and  come  to  frighten  those  left  at  home.\n\nThe  Cheremiss  are  so  cautious  that  as  soon  as  signs  of  im¬\nminent  death  are  forthcoming,  they  remove  the  sick  from\ntheir  beds  to  a  litter  of  straw.  According  to  the  Hill-\nCheremiss  the  person  dying  on  a  bolster  of  down  must  reckon\nup  the  number  of  feathers  in  the  coming  life,  and  similarly,\nthose  dying  on  hair-mats  must  count  the  hairs  of  the  same.13\nObviously,  the  removal  of  the  sick  to  the  litter  of  straw  has\nits  origin  in  the  fear  that  death  contaminated  a  bed.\n\nAs  a  means  of  protection  articles  made  of  metal  have  been\nused  widely.  The  Finns  cast  a  copper  coin  in  the  water  in\nwhich  the  corpse  is  washed.  It  was  believed  in  some  places,\nthat  unless  one  gave  a  copper  coin  to  the  person  who  washed\nthe  corpse,  his  hand  would  become  diseased.14  Among  the\nScandinavian  Lapps,  the  one  washing  and  covering  up  the\ndead  had  to  bear,  on  his  right  arm,  a  ring  of  brass,  given  to\nhim  by  some  relative  of  the  deceased  “  so  that  no  evil  could\nbefall  him.”  15  In  Russian  Lapmark  the  coffin  and  the  grave\nof  the  deceased  are  prepared  by  such  men  whose  womenfolk\n\nare  not  pregnant,  or  have  ceased  to  suckle  their  children;\notherwise,  the  child  might  be  smitten  with  a  mortal  illness.16\nA  further  very  widely  spread  custom  was  that  no  one,  often\nnot  even  the  neighbours,  might  go  about  his  ordinary  occupa¬\ntions  while  the  corpse  was  still  in  the  village,  but  that  every¬\none  had  to  be  prepared,  if  necessary,  to  serve  the  dead.\nAccording  to  the  Samoyedic  idea,  it  is  extremely  reprehen¬\nsible  to  go  hunting  or  fishing  during  a  similar  period;  they\nforbid  even  the  crossing  of  a  stream.17  Among  the  Esto¬\nnians  it  is  strictly  forbidden  to  chop  wood,  to  heat  the  bathhouse,  to  wash  clothes,  to  sweep  the  floor,  and  to  comb\none’s  hair  while  the  body  is  in  the  house.  Neither  is  it  suit¬\nable  to  visit  friends  or  to  receive  visitors. This\nbuilding  would  seem  to  have  little  actual  meaning  for  the\ndead,  since  these  are  buried  in  the  earth,  and  it  must  there¬\nfore  be  connected  with  the  old  method  of  disposing  of  the\ndead.  Perfectly  clear  examples  show  how  the  method  of\nburial  has  gradually  passed  from  the  erection  over  the  ground\nto  burial  within  it  3  an  intermediate  form  being  the  low  grave\nwhich  is  not  filled  in  again,  but  only  covered  with  boards  and\nbirch-bark.64\n\nThe  development  of  the  dwelling-place  of  the  dead  to  the\ncoffin  is  shown  also  by  the  old  burial  customs  of  the  Finns.\nIn  his  work  on  the  Iron  Age  in  Karelia,  Schwindt  mentions\nregarding  the  ancient  burial-places  examined  by  him,  that  an\nerection  resembling  a  house  over  the  ground,  joined  together\nwith  wood,  with  jutting-out  corners,  was  lowered  into  the\ngrave;  it  was  at  times  even  fitted  with  a  floor  of  boards,  over\nwhich  skins  were  spread.  The  dead  were  laid  in  this  building\nclad  in  festive  costume,  covered  most  often  with  birch-bark\nand  supplied  with  all  kinds  of  necessary  articles.  The  build¬\ning  was  covered  with  a  roof  of  boards.  A  grave  of  this\ndescription  was  filled  in  and  covered  with  one  or  two  layers\nof  stones.65  Noteworthy  also  is  the  Volga  Finns’  custom,\nmentioned  earlier,  of  furnishing  their  coffins  with  a  win¬\ndow.\n\nOf  early  origin  would  seem  to  be  a  custom,  preserved\namong  the  Ugrians  and  the  Karelian  Finns,  of  burying  their\ndead  bedded  in  a  boat  or  punt.  Even  at  the  present  time  the\ncoffin  is  called  the  “  punt  ”  ( ruuhi )  in  some  parts  of  Karelia.\nMunkacsi  has  assumed,  that  the  Ugrian  custom  of  using  an\noaken  punt  as  a  coffin,  is  a  direct  outcome  of  the  belief  which\nthey  held  regarding  the  world  of  the  dead,  and  especially  of"

Graveyard  in  Russian  Karelia\nAccording-  to  Blomstedt\n\nIn  the  same  way  as  the  Ugrians  buried  their  dead  in  boats,\nLapp  sleighs  were  used  by  the  Lapps  as  coffins. Most  of  the  dead  were  buried  between\ntwo  hollowed  logs,  of  which  the  lower  formed  the  coffin  and\nthe  upper  one  the  lid.69  Among  the  Siberians  such  a  coffin  is\nerected  over  the  ground  upon  two  or  four  pillars.\n\nThe  oldest  method  of  burial  of  the  Finno-Ugrians  is  also\nmade  clear  by  a  word,  meaning  in  Samoyed  “  corpse  ”  ( halmer ,\nkameloy  etc.),  in  Mordvin  “grave”  ( kalmo ,  kalma ),  and  in\nFinnish  “  grave  ”  {kalma)  and  also  “  death  ”  and  “  the  scent\nof  death.”  In  an  explanation  of  this  word  Setala  says:  “  On\nthe  grounds  of  the  meaning  of  the  word  both  in  Finnish  and\nin  Samoyed,  we  can  assume  that  its  original  meaning  was\n‘  corpse,’  ‘  the  dead  one.’  The  oldest  method  of  burial  un¬\ndoubtedly  consisted  merely  in  the  laying-out  of  a  body,  a\nhabit  prevalent,  and  followed  even  now,  among  many  peoples,\nwhich  habit  would  explain  why  the  same  word  can  have  the\ntwo  meanings  c  corpse  ’  and  ‘  grave.’  ”  70\n\nReliable  reports  on  the  burning  of  bodies  are  to  be  found\nsolely  among  the  Baltic  Finns.  In  certain  ancient  remains  in\nFinland,  burnt  bones  have  been  found  in  graves.  Henry  the\nLett  relates  in  his  Chronicle  how  the  Esthonians,  when  they\nreturned  to  their  old  beliefs  during  the  unsettled  period  of\nthe  Crusades,  “  took  back  their  wives,  whom  they  had  forsaken\nduring  the  time  they  stood  under  the  influence  of  Christianity,\nexhumed  their  dead,  whom  they  had  buried  in  cemeteries,  and\nburned  them  in  their  old  heathen  way.”  The  other  Finno-\nUgric  peoples  seem  to  have  burned  bodies  only  when  the\ndead  were  supposed  to  be  dangerous  to  those  surviving.   "passage_text": "DEATH  AND  BURIAL\n\namong  the  Finno-Ugric  stocks,  except  in  those  branches,  which\ncontinuously,  and  for  the  longest  period,  have  been  under\nGermanic  influence,  we  may  conclude  that  the  burning  of\nthe  dead  did  not  originally  form  part  of  the  burial-customs\nof  the  Finno-Ugrians,  and,  where  it  may  occasionally  be  found\namong  them,  is  merely  in  the  nature  of  a  temporary  loan  from\nother  peoples.”  71\n\nThe  Finno-Ugric  peoples  bury  their  dead  in  certain  burialareas,  which,  among  the  agricultural  tribes,  are  often  fenced\nin.  Every  village  has  its  own  cemetery,  or  several  villages\nlying  closely  together  may  have  a  common  one.  This  comes\nfrom  the  fact  that  from  the  original  mother-village,  newer\nones  have  been  formed  in  the  course  of  time,  the  inhabitants\nof  which  continue  to  use  the  burial-area  of  the  original  village.\nIn  the  same  way  as  the  old  villages  were  family-villages,  the\nold  cemeteries  were  family-cemeteries.  That  it  was  not  the\ncustom  to  bury  strangers  in  them  is  shown,  among  other  proofs,\nby  the  custom  of  the  Votiaks,  who  besides  their  villagecemetery,  sometimes  have  a  special  one,  often  situated  by  the\nmain  road,  for  the  burial  of  wandering  strangers,  stricken  by\ndeath  during  their  sojourn  in  the  village.72\n\nUsually,  the  cemetery  is  a  consecrated  thicket  or  wood,\nwhere  possible,  of  firs  (Finnish,  kuusikko ),  where  the  Votiaks\nand  the  Cheremiss  hang  up  on  the  trees  all  kinds  of  garments,\ncloths,  kerchiefs,  etc.,  presented  to  the  dead,  “  so  that  they\nshould  not,  lying  on  the  ground,  be  turned  to  earth.”  At\ntimes,  even  the  solitary  graves  are  ringed  round.  According\nto  Rytschkov  this  was  done  “  so  that  the  dead  should  not\nleave  their  dwelling-place  and  trample  down  the  surrounding\nfields.”  73  The  Eastern  Cheremiss  have,  further,  a  custom  of\nplacing  on  their  graves  a  cuckoo  made  of  wood,  and  fastened\nto  the  end  of  a  long  pole.74  What  the  meaning  attached  to\nthis  bird  may  originally  have  been,  the  present  generation  no\nlonger  knows.  Some  say  the  cuckoo  sounds  its  note  for  the\nedification  of  the  dead.  Certain  Siberian  tribes  have  also  a\n\ncustom  of  setting  up  figures  of  birds  on  the  graves  of  their\ndead.\n\nWhether  the  use  of  special  cemeteries  had  its  origin  already\nin  Finno-Ugric  times  is  doubtful.  According  to  tradition,  the\nLapps,  in  their  earlier  periods,  did  not  possess  special  burialplaces,  because  their  dead  were  buried  at  any  spot.  In  the\nsummer,  when  it  is  extremely  difficult,  and  even,  at  times,\nimpossible,  to  transport  the  corpses  to  the  remote  burialplaces,  the  Lapps  have  to  our  day  buried  their  dead  in  the\nforests  and  on  the  uplands,  wherever  they  happened  to  be\ndwelling,  and  then  with  the  arrival  of  winter  removed  them\nto  the  churchyard.75"

CHAPTER  III

MEMORIAL  FEASTS  FOR  A  PARTICULAR

DEAD  PERSON

THE  duties  of  the  living  with  regard  to  the  dead  do  not

with  all  honours.  The  dead  continue  to  need  the  help  and  care
of  the  living.  If  a  dead  man  is  not  given  his  rights,  he  may
resent  it  and,  coming  back,  disturb  the  peace  of  his  survivors.
Such  of  the  dead  as  haunt  their  old  homes  are  called  by  the
Esthonians  “home-visitors”  (Kodukaiat).  Generally,  they
are  masters  and  mistresses  who  in  their  life-time  were  par¬
ticularly  order-loving,  economical  and  strict.  They  are,  of
course,  seldom  seen,  but  every  now  and  then  they  are  heard
making  noises  to  remind  their  family  of  their  duties,  or  they
may  even  attack  their  children  if  these  have  not  arranged  the
memorial-feast  due  to  them.1

Memorial  feasts  may  be  either  general  ones,  celebrated  in
memory  of  all  deceased  relations,  or  special,  in  which  case  a
certain  deceased  relative  is  the  object  of  remembrance.  Of
these,  the  latter  seem  to  be  of  older  origin.

The  first  memorial  feast  celebrated  in  remembrance  of  a
member  of  the  family,  takes  place  on  the  actual  burial-day,
so  that  this  first  feast  is  at  the  same  time  a  burial  feast.

Lundius,  the  missionary,  relates  of  the  Swedish  Lapps,  that
when  their  dead  were  buried,  they  drank  “  funeral  beer.”
When  the  liquor  was  handed  round,  the  Lapps  first  dipped
their  fingers  into  it  and  smeared  their  faces.  Having  become
intoxicated,  they  began  to  praise  the  dead  man,  saying  that  he
was  shrewd  and  strong,  that  he  was  an  able  forester,  that  he

understood  well  his  wife  and  children,  that  he  was  a  mighty
shaman,  etc.2  This  wetting  of  the  fingers  and  smearing  of
the  face  can  be  traced  to  a  corresponding  custom  among  the
Norwegian  Lapps  of  whom  Randulf,  the  missionary,  relates,
that  before  going  to  the  Lord’s  Supper,  they  used  to  take  a
glass  of  beer  or  gin,  if  they  had  any,  and  dipping  three  fingers
into  the  drink,  make  the  sign  of  the  cross  on  their  foreheads.
At  other  times  they  made,  with  fingers  dipped  into  the  drink,
three  dots  on  the  breast,  one  with  each  finger.  This  was  done
by  the  Lapps  in  order  to  get  their  dead  relations  to  protect
them.3  The  memorial  drink,  as  well  as  the  three  finger¬
marks,  is  with  the  Lapps  a  later  Scandinavian  custom.

The  custom,  however,  of  killing  the  reindeer  that  dragged
the  dead  man  to  his  grave,  seems  to  be  an  original  Lapponian
usage.  This  sacrifice  performance  is  described  by  Rheen,  the
missionary,  in  the  following  way:  —  “Three  days  after  the
funeral  of  the  dead  man,  the  Lapps  take  the  reindeer  which
conveyed  him  to  the  cemetery,  kill  it  in  his  honour,  and  con¬
sume  it  in  company  with  their  relations  and  dependants.
They  collect  all  the  bones,  and  having  made  a  chest,  put  them
into  it,  burying  the  chest  in  the  earth.  They  then  make  an
image  of  wood  which  is  placed  on  the  chest,  the  image  being
large  or  small,  according  to  the  size  of  the  dead  man.”  4  Ac¬
cording  to  Graan,  three  rods  besmeared  with  blood,  on  which
were  placed  pieces  of  the  heart  and  lungs  of  the  reindeer,  were
also  buried  with  the  bones.5

Even  after  the  funeral  feast,  the  deceased  was  remembered
by  taking  some  tobacco,  or  anything  else  he  may  have  been
fond  of,  to  his  grave.  Rheen  mentions  that  if  the  deceased
was  a  rich  man,  reindeer  were  killed  in  his  honour  one,  two  or
even  three  years  after  his  death.  Here  also  the  slaughtered
animal’s  bones  had  to  be  hidden  in  the  earth.  A  black  piece
of  thread  had  to  be  sewn  into  the  ear  of  the  reindeer  chosen
for  the  sacrifice.6

Near  the  grave  the\nfuneral  meal  is  cooked,  and  when  they  have  eaten  enough,\nthe  burial  guests  take  the  rest  home.13  According  to  later\ncustom  the  best-beloved  reindeer  of  the  deceased  is  killed,  the\nmeat  being  eaten,  and  the  bones  and  horns,  together  with  the\nsleigh  and  harness,  are  placed  on  the  grave.14\n\nThe  funeral  feast  of  the  North  Voguls  is  described  by  Gondatti. The  bottom  of  the  pan  is  knocked  out,  after  which\nit  is  left  by  the  grave.  If  the  deceased  has  been  conveyed  by\nreindeer,  the  latter  are  strangled  by  the  grave,  the  meat  being\nboiled  and  eaten  on  the  spot,  the  hide  buried,  and  the  bones\nplaced  by  the  dead  man.15\n\nLike  the  Lapps,  the  Ugrians  frequently  remember  their\ndead,  especially  during  the  first  period  of  their  life  in  Hades.\nIn  most  districts,  however,  they  have  no  fixed  memorial  days,\nbut  settle  these  according  to  agreement  with  relations. The  ceremonies  are  very  simple:  —  they\ncook  some  food,  and,  having  kept  it  at  the  grave  for  a  while,\nthey  eat  it  at  home. On\nthe  ground  tea,  gravy,  gin,  and,  finally,  some  cold  water  are\npoured,  whence  the  term  “  water-pouring  ”  is  derived.16\nAccording  to  Munkacsi,  the  Northern  Voguls  celebrate\nmemorial  feasts  on  the  third  day  after  death,  then,  at  the  end\nof  “  the  holy  week,”  and,  after  that  time,  thrice  a  year. With  the  Southern  Ugrians,  such  days\nare  the  ninth,  the  sixteenth,  and  thirty-sixth,  and  a  half-year\nor  a  whole  year  after  death.18\n\nA  strange  custom  among  the  Northern  Ugrians  is  the\nmaking  of  a  memorial  doll  of  the  deceased,  of  which  Novit¬\nskiy  says:  “  A  curious  irrational  and  shameless  custom  is  that\nwhich  is  observed  by  their  women  after  the  death  of  their\nhusbands.  The  widow  carves  a  wooden  doll,  resembling  a\nhuman  being,  to  represent  her  dead  husband,  takes  some  of\nher  husband’s  clothes,  dresses  the  doll  in  them  and  provides\nit  with  ornaments  worn  by  the  deceased,  and  putting  it  in  the\nplace  where  her  husband  used  to  sit,  cooks  for  this  lifeless\nblock  of  wood  all  the  dishes  that  used  to  please  the  deceased.\nWhen  they  sit  down  in  the  place  of  honour  to  eat,  she  places\nthe  image  beside  her,  embracing  and  kissing  the  doll  as  if  it\nwere  a  living  being,  fully  believing  that  the  deceased  sees  all\nthis  and  that  his  soul  enters  this  image  at  times.  She  keeps\nthe  doll  for  some  time,  going  on  with  this  nonsense  for  a\nyear  or  even  longer,  and  then  buries  it  with  its  clothes  on  in\nthe  earth,  exhibiting  her  sorrow  by  weeping  and  wailing.”  19\n\nCastren  and  Pallas  relate  that  memorial  dolls  of  this  descrip-\n\ntion  were  made  to  represent  persons  who  had  been  in  some\nway  important.  The  image  was  kept  in  the  tent  of  the  de¬\nceased  and  was  shown  the  same  honours  as  its  precursor.  It\nwas  fed  at  every  meal,  dressed  in  the  morning  and  undressed\nin  the  evening,  and  a  widow,  who  had  loved  her  husband,\neven  went  so  far  as  to  place  it  beside  her  in  bed.  According\nto  Castren  the  image  was  worshipped  in  this  way  for  three\nyears,  after  which  it  was  buried.  They  supposed  that  the\nbody  of  the  deceased  had  disintegrated  during  these  three\nyears.20  In  some  places  the  image  was  kept  for  five  years,  if\nthe  deceased  was  a  man,  and  for  four,  if  a  woman.  In  our\ndays  the  image  is  burned  after  the  course  of  the  said  time.\nYet  the  old  idea  also  remains  that  the  doll  should  be  buried  in\nthe  grave  of  the  deceased.  Where  they  are  in  the  habit  of\nbuilding  the  so-called  grave-houses,  the  doll  is  placed  in  these.\nDuring  the  time  when  Finsch  was  travelling  among  the\nUgrians,  he  saw,  among  the  most  Northern,  small  buildings\non  their  graves  of  the  size  of  kennels,  provided  with  a  door,\nand  within  them  a  doll,  dressed  in  Ugrian  garments.  These\ndolls  noticed  by  Finsch  were  plainly  such  as  had  been  taken\nto  the  graveyard  at  the  end  of  the  memorial-time  and  placed\nin  the  grave-house.21\n\nThe  memorial  doll  is  also  to  be  found  among  some  Samoyed  tribes,  though  the  custom  of  making  images  of  shamans\nseems  here  to  be  more  widely  spread.  According  to  Lehtisalo,\nthe  Yuraks  make  a  wooden  image  of  the  “shadow”  of  the\nshaman,  which  resembles  a  reindeer-bull.   "passage_text": "MEMORIAL  FEASTS\n\nhabit  of  taking  an  ox  to  the  clergyman  after  the  death  of  the\nhost,  and  a  cow  after  that  of  the  hostess.  Sometimes  the\nclergyman  was  expected  to  prepare  a  meal  of  these  for  the  fu¬\nneral  guests.  In  North  Karelia  the  people  were  in  the  habit\nof  tying  the  cow  due  to  the  clergyman  to  a  tree  in  the  grave¬\nyard  for  some  time,  the  clergyman  having  to  take  it  from\nthere.\"4\n\nThe  different  memorial  days  are  celebrated  by  the  Volga\nFinns  in  varying  ways,  some  of  them  being  more  solemn  than\nothers.  Thus,  Georgi  relates  of  the  Votiaks,  that  at  the  first\nmemorial  feast,  which  is  celebrated  on  the  third  day,  the\nfriends  of  the  house  of  mourning  are  assembled  only  to  eat\npancakes  and  drink  beer,  some  of  which  is  also  poured  out  in\nthe  yard  for  the  dead,  but  on  the  seventh  day  a  sheep  is  killed,\nand  on  the  fortieth,  a  cow  or  a  horse.35\n\nThe  memorial  feast  of  the  third  day  among  the  Siryans\n(District  of  Orlov)  is  described  by  Dobrotvorskiy.  When  the\nguests  have  arrived,  wax-tapers  are  lighted  in  the  window\nand  on  either  side  of  the  threshold.  The  door  is  opened  for\na  while,  when  the  guests  are  sitting  down  at  table,  to  invite\nthe  soul  (lot)  of  the  deceased  to  the  feast.  In  the  farther¬\nmost  corner,  a  hat  or  a  kerchief  is  placed,  depending  on  the  sex\nof  the  deceased.  On  the  place  where  the  hat  has  been  set\ndown,  no  one  seats  himself.  On  the  table  beside  it,  they\nplace  a  bowl  filled  with  pancakes,  porridge,  milk  and  gin.\nEvery  guest  considers  it  his  duty  to  put  into  the  bowl  of  the\ndeceased  some  of  the  food  displayed  on  the  table.36\n\nThe  memorial  feast  of  the  seventh  day  is,  in  most  places,\nlike  that  of  the  third  day.  Some  one  of  the  relatives  of  the\ndeceased  goes  to  the  grave  to  remember  him.  At  home,  they\nlight  a  candle  on  the  brim  of  the  vessel  of  food  offered  to  the\ndeceased.  When  the  first  pieces  of  food  are  dropped  into  this\nvessel,  everyone  utters  a  few  words  of  remembrance,  pointing\nout  that  it  is  now  the  seventh  day  of  the  memorial  feast.  In\nother  places  the  seventh  day  is  kept  almost  as  solemnly  as\n\nthe  fortieth.  The  participants  in  the  ceremony  go  to  the  grave\nwith  two  horses  to  invite  the  deceased ;  they  kill  a  hen  for\nhim,  sometimes  even  a  sheep ;  in  the  evening  they  go  to  the\nbath-house  with  him  5  all  night  he  is  regaled  5  and  not  until\ndawn  is  he  taken  back  to  his  new  home.37\n\nAccording  to  a  general  idea  of  the  Volga  Finns  and  of  many\nother  East  European  peoples,  the  deceased  remains  during  the\ncourse  of  forty  days  in  a  very  near  relationship  to  his  old  home.\nThe  Votiaks  say  that  the  “  soul  ”  of  the  dead  lives  at  home\nfor  forty  days  after  death.  It  is  therefore  the  duty  of  his\npeople  to  show  kindness  and  hospitality  to  the  deceased,  par¬\nticularly  during  that  time.  In  some  places,  it  is  customary,\nduring  these  forty  days,  to  put  down  a  bowl  for  the  deceased\nevery  time  the  family  and  servants  sit  down  to  take  a  meal.3*\n\nThe  Siryans  believe  that  after  the  funeral,  the  deceased\nreturns  with  the  funeral  guests  to  his  old  home  and  remains\nthere  for  the  above-named  time.  For  that  time,  therefore,\nit  has  been  customary  to  hang  up  a  towel  in  some  fixed  place\nin  the  hut,  so  that  the  deceased  may  wipe  his  face  every  time\nhe  washes  himself.  No  living  soul  may  touch  it,  as  death\nmight  be  the  immediate  consequence.39\n\nThe  Mordvins  say  that  the  deceased  passes  over  to  the\nrealm  of  the  dead  forty  days  or  six  weeks  after  his  death.40\nThe  same  idea  is  found  also  among  the  Baltic  Finns  who  have\nbeen  under  Russian  influence.  According  to  Groundstroem\nthe  Votes  dared  not  speak  ill  of  the  dead  for  six  weeks,  for\nthey  believed  that  the  soul  of  the  deceased  stayed  for  that  time\nin  his  home,  mostly  under  the  table.  They  were  careful  also\nnot  to  stretch  their  legs  under  the  table,  as  they  might  easily\ntrample  on  the  deceased.41  Like  the  Siryans,  the  Karelians  in\nthe  Government  of  Tver  were  in  the  habit  of  hanging  a  towel\nfor  six  weeks  on  the  back  wall  of  the  hut,  so  that  the  deceased\nwhen  coming  home,  might  wipe  himself.42  A  similar  custom\nis  found  among  the  Russians,  from  whom  the  Finnish  tribes\nseem  to  have  borrowed  it."
}

MEMORIAL  FEASTS

According  to  one  report  the  Votiaks  believe  that  if  they  do
not  celebrate  a  memorial  feast  then,  the  dead  will  not  give  the
new-comer  a  place  in  their  community,  but  will  make  him
continue  to  wander  about  the  village,  as  the  deceased  had  done
in  the  course  of  the  year.51

The  anniversary  is  celebrated  by  the  Eastern  Cheremiss,
in  the  District  of  Birsk,  in  such  a  manner  that  all  the  clothes
of  the  deceased  are  hung  upon  his  favourite  horse,  which  is
then  taken  to  the  grave  and  led  three  times  round  it.  They
light  a  three-branched  candle  on  the  grave,  saying  at  the  same
time  to  the  dead  man  that  the  anniversary  has  arrived  and
promising  to  kill  the  horse  in  his  honour.  Having  arrived  at
the  homestead,  the  horse  is  killed  at  once  and  a  memorial
meal  prepared  of  its  flesh.  While  sacrificing,  the  relations
say  to  the  deceased:  “  Eat  what  we  have  prepared  for  thee;
we  have  not  harnessed  thy  horse,  we  have  not  used  it,  now
take  it  with  thee.”  At  the  end  of  the  feast,  the  bones  of  the
horse  are  taken  to  the  graveyard,  where  they  are  hung  in  a
tree,  but  the  hide  is  sold  for  the  benefit  of  the  poor  and  the
fatherless.52

In  honour  of  particular  persons  the  Votiaks  further  cele~
brate  a  remarkable  memorial  feast,  which,  however,  does  not
take  place  at  a  specially  fixed  time,  but  sometimes  a  year  or
several  years  after  death.

This  festivity,  which  is  generally  celebrated  late  in  autumn,
is  called  by  the  Votiaks  a  “  horse-wedding  ”  or  “  the  wedding
of  the  dead,”  these  names  being  derived  from  the  fact  that
it  is,  above  all,  a  cheerful  feast  with  wedding-songs  and  wed¬
ding-presents.  The  sacrificial  animal,  which  is  generally
killed  in  the  yard,  must  be  a  horse,  if  the  deceased  in  question
is  a  man,  but  a  cow,  if  a  woman.  In  some  places  where  the
memorial  feast  is  celebrated  the  first  year  after  death,  the
animal  which  the  deceased  liked  best  and  which  he  used  in  his
lifetime,  is  generally  sacrificed  to  him.  All  his  relations  are
invited,  these  alone  partaking  of  the  sacrificial  meal,  as  it  is

against  custom  to  invite  strangers.  The  most  important  per¬
formance  consists  of  the  taking  of  the  animal’s  bones  in  the
evening,  by  candle-light,  with  music  and  singing,  to  the  grave¬
yard,  where  they  are  hung  upon  a  tree.53

A  curious  custom  among  the  Mordvins  is  the  “  harvest  of
the  dead.”  Already  when  sowing  in  spring  they  pray  to  the
Lord  to  let  the  corn  grow  for  the  welfare  of  the  living  and
the  dead.  During  the  harvest-festival  the  relatives  of  the
deceased  also  reap  the  portion  of  the  dead  man,  each  of  them
cutting  only  a  few  straws.  The  chief  part  is  played  by  the
widow,  who  all  day  wears  a  belt  of  straw  made  by  herself.
Cattle  are  slaughtered  for  this  feast.54  Among  the  Siryans,
traces  of  a  memorial  feast  in  the  harvest-field  have  also  been
found.55

Besides  feasts  decided  on  beforehand,  particular  memorial
feasts  are  occasionally  celebrated  for  some  special  reason.  Ac¬
cording  to  a  general  idea,  the  dead  may  remind  the  living  in
in  a  dream,  or  by  all  kinds  of  signs,  of  their  wishes.  Memorial
feasts  are  chiefly  celebrated  in  such  cases  of  illness  as  have
been  declared  by  a  wise  man  to  originate  from  some  one  among
the  dead.  Among  the  Mordvins,  the  patient  must  then  creep
on  all  fours  to  the  grave  of  the  deceased  to  ask  his  forgive¬
ness.56  Should  an  animal — a  horse  or  a  cow  —  disappear
from  the  pasture-land,  or  go  astray  in  the  forest,  one  of  the

adversities,  such  as  a  failure  in  distilling  brandy,  or  the  loosen¬
ing  of  a  wheel  on  a  journey,  the  restlessness  of  a  baby,  etc.,
may  become  reasons  for  preparing  a  memorial  feast.57  A
widow,  at  least,  must  always  be  on  the  lookout.  If  the
Cheremiss  woman’s  back  aches,  she  believes  that  her  deceased

By  Kekri  other  spirits  also  were  meant,  for\nwhom  all  sorts  of  eatables  and  drinkables  were  prepared  on\nthe  evening  before  the  feast  day,  some  in  the  cow-house  for\nthe  welfare  of  the  cattle,  others  in  the  stable  for  luck  with\nhorses,  others  under  big  trees  and  by  huge  stones  in  the  fields\nor  in  the  forest,  and  yet  others  in  all  these  places  at  once.\nAccording  to  the  Catholic  way,  the  host  received  the  saints\noutside  in  the  yard,  in  the  darkness  of  the  evening  before  the\nfeast,  taking  them  to  the  bath-house,  which  had  been  particu¬\nlarly  cleaned  and  heated  for  their  use  and  provided  with  cold\nand  hot  water  and  “  bath-brooms.”  A  table  with  meat  and\ndrink  had  also  been  placed  there. Masks\nfor  the  face  were  made  of  birch-bark,  paper,  etc.  People,\nmasked  in  this  way,  were  called  Kekritar. Or,  on  the\nnight  before  Kekri,  they  walked  under  the  windows  to  listen\nto  what  was  being  talked  about  in  the  hut,  and,  from  the  con¬\nversation  going  on  there,  to  infer  what  would  happen  during\nthe  following  year.  Further,  in  the  evening,  they  would\ncount  the  sticks  in  the  oven,  and  if  they  were  all  there  in  the\nmorning,  no  one  needed  to  trouble  himself  about  possible\ndeaths  in  the  following  year,  but  otherwise  there  would  be  as\nmany  deaths  at  the  house  as  the  number  of  the  absent  sticks\nindicated.  When  making  bread  they  took  from  the  straw\nas  many  ears  of  corn  (rye)  as  there  were  members  in  the\nfamily  and  pressed  them  into  the  bread. If  the  piece  happened  to  fall  with  the\n\ncrust  downwards,  life  would  go  well  during  the  year;  other¬\nwise  some  disaster  was  to  be  expected.  In  some  neighbour¬\nhoods  it  was,  moreover,  customary,  on  the  evening  before  All\nSaints’  Day,  to  place  on  the  window-sill  one  grain  of  salt  for\neach  member  of  the  family.  He  whose  grain  of  salt  melted\nduring  the  night,  was  to  die.  It  was  also  customary  to  burn\nKekri-fires,  most  probably  for  the  purpose  of  driving  away\nspirits.  The  fire  was  burnt  on  some  hill  and  was  made  of\noakum  mixed  with  straw.7\n\nA  corresponding  feast  is  known  also  among  the  Esthonians\nand  seems  to  be  common  among  the  Baltic  Finns,  though  the\nwandering-time  of  the  dead  has  later  been  influenced  by  the\nCatholics,  who,  since  835,  have  celebrated  the  first  of  Novem¬\nber  as  All  Saints’  Day  and,  since  998,  the  second  of  November\nas  All  Souls’  Day. In  a  song  from  the\nIrtysh  it  is  told  how  the  soul  of  a  hero  who,  in  the  clash  of\nbattle,  has  received  a  blow  on  the  head  rendering  him  un¬\nconscious,  leaves  the  body  to  climb  by  a  narrow  stairway  to\nheaven,  and  how  he  is  met  by  three  red-legged  squirrels  who\nsay  to  him:  “  This  is  our  word:  we  eat  our  food  in  the  midst\nof  human  blood,  we  drink  our  drink  in  the  midst  of  human\nblood,  go  back!”  When  the  soul  of  the  hero  returned,  con¬\nsciousness  returned  also  to  him. The  most  general  methods  of  purification,\nused  both  for  people  and  for  the  implements  of  the  hunter\nor  fisher,  were  smoking  over  a  fire,  jumping  over  fire,  washing\nin  water,  or  being  besprinkled  with  water. The  players  are  masked  in  order  to  prevent  the

At  sunrise  after  the  last  feast  night  the  skin  is  borne  out
through  the  window  to  the  warehouse-shed  where  the  dish
first  placed  on  the  table  before  it  in  the  house  is  placed  in
front  of  it.  After  two  or  three  days  the  hunters  gather  together
again  in  the  house  and  then  go  into  the  shed,  where  each  takes
a  morsel  of  food  from  the  dish  and  eats  it  “  for  luck.”  35

From  the  prayers  and  wishes  made  by  the  Ostiaks  to  the
dead  bear,  it  appears  plainly  that  in  doing  honour  to  it  they
wish  to  honour  the  whole  race  of  bears.  As  an  example  of
this  the  words  of  the  Ostiak  woman  as  she  places  a  ring  in
the  bear’s  claw  may  be  cited:  “When  I  go  to  gather  berries,
go  thou  round  one  tree,  round  two  trees.”  When  they  set
food  before  the  bear-skin  they  say:  “  Do  not  touch  my  horse
or  my  cow,  I  placed  the  dish  before  thee.”  36

The  Finns  called  the  bear  feast  “  the  wedding.”  The
house  had  to  be  cleaned  and  everyone  clad  in  his  or  her  best.
A  young  man  was  arrayed  as  a  bridegroom  and  a  young  girl
as  a  bride,  or  one  only  of  these  was  chosen:  a  bridegroom  if
the  bear  was  a  female,  and  a  bride  if  a  male.  The  head  of
the  bear  was  placed  highest  on  the  table  and  the  rest  of  the
meat  in  its  natural  order.  In  the  place  of  honour  sat  the
bridegroom  and  bride.  The  singing  of  runes  in  honour  of
the  bear  was  customary  among  the  Finns,  certain  of  these  be¬
ing  sung  while  the  bear  was  carried  to  the  house.  In  these  the
hunters  endeavoured  to  show  themselves  innocent  of  the  kill¬
ing  of  the  bear,  declaring  that  the  bear  had  wounded  itself
or  that  they  had  taken  its  life  by  accident.  Arrived  at  the
house-door  the  hunters  asked  singing  whether  the  floor  had
been  scrubbed  and  the  room  cleaned,  or  also  singing  urged
the  womenfolk  to  get  out  of  the  way  and  to  beware  of  the
holy  bear.37

That  the  object  of  the  ceremonies  with  the  Finns  was  to
ensure  good  bear-luck  in  hunting,  appears  from  the  oldest
account  of  their  bear  feast  ceremonies.  Bishop  Rothovius,  in
his  speech  at  the  inauguration  of  the  University  of  Abo  in

1640,  relates  the  following  concerning  the  customs  of  the
Finns:  “  When  they  capture  a  bear,  they  must  hold  a  feast  in
the  dark,  drinking  the  health  of  the  bear  from  its  skull,  act¬
ing  and  growling  like  the  bear,  procuring  in  this  way  further
success.”  *

The  skull  of  the  bear  had  to  be  left  overnight  on  the  table
and  taken  the  following  morning,  ceremoniously  as  at  a  wed¬
ding,  to  a  certain  tree.  First  went  the  “  bridegroom  ”  and
“  bride  ”  side  by  side,  after  these  a  man  carrying  beer  in  a
vessel,  after  him  a  singer,  then  the  one  who  carried  the  skull,
and  lastly  the  rest  of  the  people.

The  Samoyeds,  who  like  the  Finns  specially  preserve  the
skull,  hang  it  up  in  a  tree  or  place  it  on  the  end  of  a  long  pole,
generally  near  a  road.38

Like  the  bear,  other  wild  animals  had  also  to  be  treated
with  honour.  More  particularly  the  wild  reindeer  and  other
scarce  and  valuable  animals  had  to  be  received  with  special
ceremonies.  The  Ostiaks,  when  they  kill  a  stag  or  an  otter,
often  cut  pictures  of  these  in  a  pine  near  the  village  as  they
do  with  the  bear.39

Lapps’  method  of  carefully  preserving  all  the  bones  of  beasts
of  prey.  That  this  care  was  not  only  expended  on  the  bones

dry  sand-hillocks  or  clefts  between  rocks  where  neither  dog
nor  other  prowling  animal  can  reach  them.  This  is  because
these  animals  lived  on  dry  land;  the  bones  of  those  living  in
in  the  water  are  hidden  in  springs.”  40  Even  today  the  Lapps

the  stone,  the  nature  of  the  offering  being  inquired  after  also
in  the  above-mentioned  manner.4

sible  when  the  Seide  was  a  great  rock  or  a  stone  embedded  in
the  earth.  Consulting  these,  the  Lapp  laid  his  hand  on  the
rock  and  began  his  questions  in  the  unshakable  belief  that
his  hand  would  stick  to  it  and  not  be  loosened  until  he  chanced
to  hit  on  the  exact  event  that  would  happen  to  him.5

The  place  where  the  Seide  stood  and  its  nearest  surround¬
ings  were  “  holy  ”  ( 'passe )  to  the  Lapps.  The  mountain  on
which  the  stone  gods  were  placed,  was  called  in  general  “  the

these  are  met  with  in  Lapmark  even  today.

One  of  the  best  known  holy  mountains  in  Finnish  Lapmark
is  the  Rastekaise  in  Utsjoki,  on  the  top  of  which  there  are  two
large  stones,  and  which  even  today  is  regarded  by  the  super¬

  "passage_text": "THE  SEIDES  OF  THE  LAPPS\n\nworship  the  stone  gods  when  in  the  neighbourhood  of  these,\nbut  otherwise  gods  of  wood.”  32  It  would  appear,  therefore,\nthat  the  wooden  pillars  were  set  up  only  as  occasion  arose,\nperhaps  to  represent  some  spirit  dwelling  in  a  more  distant\nplace.  The  stone  Seides  were  regarded  by  the  Lapps,  accord¬\ning  to  Hogstrom,  as  being  much  more  holy  than  those  of\nwood.33  These  wooden  Seides  are  not,  however,  to  be  con¬\nfounded  with  the  wooden  images  fashioned  to  represent\nNature  gods.\n\nSacrifices  to  the  Seides  were  naturally  not  offered  up  in  pre¬\ncisely  the  same  manner  over  the  whole  of  the  wide  Lapland\narea,  but  one  may  observe  general  main  forms  of  an  archaic\nkind  among  them.\n\nOne  of  the  very  best  accounts  of  a  sacrifice,  which  has  been\npreserved  for  posterity,  dates  from  the  seventeenth  century\nand  is  from  the  Lule  Lapps.  When  these  had  decided  to\nmake  an  offering,  they  bound  fast  the  sacrificial  animal  behind\nthe  tent,  thrust  a  knife  into  its  heart  and  carefully  gathered  its\nheart’s  blood.  The  horns  and  the  bones  from  the  head  and\nneck,  together  with  the  hoofs,  were  carried  to  the  holy  place\nin  which  their  Seide  stood.  When  the  Lapp  had  come  to  the\nSeide,  he  took  off  his  hat,  bowed  low  to  the  idol  and  smeared\nit  with  blood  and  fat  from  the  sacrifice.  The  horns,  were\npiled  in  a  great  pyramid  behind  the  stone,  the  pile  being  called\nthe  “  horn-yard  ”  and  containing  sometimes  as  many  as  a\nthousand  horns.  Of  the  meat  of  the  sacrifice  which  was  eaten\nby  those  making  the  offering  themselves,  a  small  piece  was\ncut  from  every  quarter,  threaded  on  to  a  switch  of  birch  and\nhung  on  to  the  front  of  the  horns.  At  times  the  slaughtering\nmight  take  place  at  the  holy  place,  the  meat  being  then  pre¬\npared  and  eaten  there.  Besides  the  bones,  the  hide  of  the\nreindeer  was  also  left  on  the  holy  mountain  5  the  head  was\nhung  on  a  tree,  where  such  were  to  be  found  in  the  vicinity\nof  the  idol.34\n\nThe  Kemi  Lapps  had  a  custom  of  cutting  down  a  tree  near\n\n1 10\n\nthe  Seide  stone,  calling  it  the  luete-muor  (“sacrifice  tree”).\nBefore  the  sacrifice  the  god  was  asked,  by  lifting  him,  what\nhe  wished  in  return  for  giving  assistance  in  some  matter  or\nother.  The  animal  chosen  for  the  offering  was  bound  fast  to\nthe  tree  and  slaughtered  “  after  a  long  speech.”  Both  the\nstone  and  the  tree  were  besmeared  with  blood,  and  when  the\nmeat  was  prepared,  small  strips  were  cut  out  of  it,  threaded\non  to  a  ring  made  of  young  pliable  branches  and  hung  up  in\nthe  sacrifice  tree.  After  which,  the  sacrificial  meal  was  begun.\nShould  anything  be  left  over,  it  could  not  be  taken  home  but\nmust  be  left  at  the  place  together  with  the  animal’s  hide  and\nhorns.35\n\nThe  Norwegian  Lapps,  before  the  slaughtering,  cut  a  small\npiece  out  of  each  ear  and  the  tail  of  the  animal  and  placed\nthem  before  the  god  as  a  preliminary  taste.  The  sacrificial\nanimal  was  killed  by  stabbing,  and  flayed  in  such  a  manner\nthat  the  horns  and  the  hoofs  remained  fast  to  the  hide.  There¬\nafter,  several  small  sticks  were  prepared,  lines  and  figures\nbeing  cut  in  them.  The  sticks  were  called  “  the  sacrifice  tree  ”\nand  were  placed  smeared  with  blood  near  the  god  3  their  func¬\ntion  was  to  represent  “  wax  candles.”  We  see  from  this  that\nthe  Lapps  at  that  time  tried  to  ape  Scandinavian  customs.  When\nthe  meat  was  carved,  a  piece  from  every  quarter  was  cut  out\nfor  the  idol.  The  fire  was  made  in  a  fixed  spot,  near  which\nthere  had  to  be,  where  possible,  a  spring  or  brook  3  the  whole\nof  the  flesh  of  the  sacrifice  was  cooked  at  once.  With  the  fat\nthat  rose  in  the  cauldron  and  with  the  blood,  the  sacrificial\npriest  smeared  certain  curiously-shaped  stones,  placing  them\nafterwards  near  the  god.  Then,  with  his  followers,  he  finished\noff  the  whole  of  the  carcase,  taking  due  care  not  to  spread  the\nbones  about,  but  to  leave  all  on  the  place  of  offering,  where\nthe  hide  also  was  left.   "passage_text": "THE  SEIDES  OF  THE  LAPPS\n\nhi\n\ncustom  of  the  Russian  Lapps,  as  described  by  Genetz.  Cer¬\ntain  features  of  the  performance  seem  to  point  to  a  sacrifice\nin  honour  of  Nature  gods.  The  sacrifice  had  to  be  begun\nearly  in  the  morning  and  the  gods  prayed  to  with  the  face\nturned  towards  the  east.  After  the  flesh  had  been  devoured,\nthe  hide  with  horns  and  hoofs  attached  was  built  up  with\nbranches  of  birch  and  fixed  to  a  pole  in  a  position  resembling\nthat  of  a  live  reindeer.37  Up  to  a  few  score  years  ago  these\nLapps  sacrificed  as  many  as  twenty-four  reindeer  at  a  time.\nA  great  sacrificial  feast  of  this  description  was  not,  however,\ncelebrated  every  year,  nor  were  the  reindeer  killed  all  at  once,\nbut  during  the  space  of  several  days,  a  few  at  a  time.  All\nthe  participants  in  the  feast  had  to  cleanse  themselves  and\nput  on  clean  garments.  The  sacrificial  food  was  regarded  as\nbeing  so  holy,  that  one  might  not  spill  any  even  on  one’s\ngarments.  During  the  ceremony  the  shaman  stood  alone,  at\none  side,  with  his  face  turned  to  the  east.  The  reindeer  hides\nthat  were  stuffed  with  birch-twigs  were  also  placed  with  their\nheads  to  the  east.  After  the  ceremonies  the  priests  had  to\ncleanse  themselves  again.38\n\nBesides  reindeer,  the  proper  time  for  sacrificing  which  was\nin  the  autumn,  the  Lapps  also  slaughtered  other  animals  in\nhonour  of  their  Seides,  such  as  birds  and  other  game,  occa¬\nsionally  also  strange  domestic  animals  procured  from  their\nneighbours.  Sometimes  a  dog  might  be  offered  up  entire  to\nthe  Seide,  or  living  animals,  which  were  imprisoned  in  chasms\nin  the  mountain  or  grottoes,  or  were  left  alive  on  some  solitary\nisland  as  a  gift  to  the  gods.  There  are  even  reports  of  chil¬\ndren  being  sacrificed.39\n\nIn  like  manner  as  the  Mountain  Lapps  sacrificed  their  rein¬\ndeer,  the  Fisher  Lapps  fed  their  Seides  on  fish.  When  a\nfisherman  went  out  to  fish,  he  generally  went  first  to  the  stone,\nkissed  it  three  times  and  said:  a  If  I  now  succeed  in  catching\nfish  in  the  sea  or  the  river,  I  promise  thee  their  intestines  and\nlivers.”  After  making  a  catch,  the  promise  was  fulfilled.\n\n1 1 2\n\nEven  as  late  as  the  middle  of  the  last  century,  the  Norwegian\nLapps  are  said  to  have  sometimes  smeared  their  stones  in  secret.\nAs  sacrifices  to  the  Seides  in  later  periods,  there  are  reports\nof  money  being  offered  up,  both  in  Finnish  and  Russian  Lapmark  $  also  rings  of  brass,  tobacco,  etc.,  all  of  which  objects\nwere  placed  in  small  hollows  in  the  stones.40\n\nIf  we  follow  the  development  of  religious  beliefs  and  cus¬\ntoms  among  other  related  peoples,  we  can  observe  that  the\nSeides  worshipped  by  the  Lapps  under  the  naked  sky,  contain\ntwo  different  classes  of  spirits,  of  which  the  one,  the  so-called\nhouse  or  family  gods,  little  by  little,  are  generally  moved  into\nthe  dwelling-house  of  the  worshipper  3  while  to  the  other,  to\nwhom  might  be  given  the  Greek  name  “  heroes,”  many  people\nbegan  to  build  special  small  bothies."

these  with  the  chip  to  the  newly  founded  kuaia  of  his  new

A  curious  statement  is  that  he  who  carries  the  Vorsud  must
not  put  his  foot  on  the  bare  ground,  but  must  walk  all  the  time
on  planks  laid  on  the  ground.

Many  circumstances  in  the  above  descriptions  recall  the
customs  followed  at  a  Votiak  wedding.  The  very  tunes
played  on  this  occasion  are  wedding  tunes.  In  some  places,
it  is  further  customary  to  distribute  presents  at  the  kuaia
feast,  as  at  a  wedding.  In  the  District  of  Mamadysh  a  custom
recalling  a  wedding  is  connected  with  the  above  mentioned
ceremonies,  namely,  that  the  Vorsud  is  taken  to  the  new  home
like  a  bride  in  a  sleigh  with  two  horses  and  tinkling  bells,  the
women  being  dressed  in  wedding  costume.  That  the  Votiaks
themselves  consider  the  Vorsud  feast  to  be  a  wedding  festivity
is  seen  from  the  name  of  this  feast,  mudor  suan  (“  mudor
wedding  ”).  Among  the  Votiaks,  certain  ceremonies  recalling
those  of  the  mudor  wedding  are  now  observed  at  the  inaugura¬

this  festivity  cc  hut  wedding  ”  ( korka  suan),  on  which  occasion
as  at  a  wedding  a  “  host  ”  (toro)  officiates.  As  the  Indo-Euro¬

Volga  Finns  acquired  theirs  through  a  foreign  culture.  The
fact,  however,  that  the  above  named  ceremonies  refer  to  a
time  when  the  Votiaks  were  still  living  in  the  old  kuaia ,  in¬

prays  to  the  son  of  the  family  spirit  to  accompany  him  to  the

of  such  great  importance  to  the  son  that  if  for  one  reason  or
another  the  father  quarrels  with  his  son  and  refuses  to  give
him  a  Vorsud,  the  son  must  procure  it  by  robbery.  If  the  son
who  is  angry  with  his  father  says,  when  taking  the  Vorsud:
u  I  leave  the  smaller,  I  take  the  greater,”  the  consequence,
according  to  the  interpretation  of  the  magicians,  is  that  the
son  gets  the  older  Vorsud,  and,  in  a  religious  sense,  stands
higher  than  his  father.  If,  after  this,  any  of  his  younger
brothers  is  in  want  of  a  Vorsud,  he  must  apply  to  his  brother
with  his  request  and  not  to  his  father.12

After  the  mudor  wedding,  the  kuala,  is  a  sanctuary ;  the
Vorsud  lives  in  it,  and  from  that  day,  worship  is  carried  out
there.  To  keep  up  this  is  the  sacred  duty  not  only  of  that
generation,  but  also  of  the  following,  for  according  to  the
beliefs  of  the  Votiaks,  the  sacrifices  in  a  building  consecrated
as  a  sanctuary  must  never  be  interrupted.  He  who  does  not
observe  this  rule,  will  meet  with  some  great  accident.  The
people  tell  with  terror  how  such  persons  have  lost  their  prop¬
erty,  have  gone  mad,  etc.  If,  for  instance  at  the  change  of
guardians,  the  kuala  should  be  removed  from  one  place  to
another,  the  building  is  pulled  down,  and  the  timber  of  the
walls  is  placed  in  the  same  order  when  built  anew.  The
ashes  of  the  hearth,  the  stones,  and  the  Vorsud  case  are  taken
with  ceremony  to  the  new  place,  together  with  the  timber.
Besides  being  removed  when  changing  a  guardian,  the  kuala
may  also  be  taken  away  for  some  other  reason.  Thus,  for  in¬
stance,  it  once  happened  that  a  sacrificial  bull,  when  about  to
be  killed,  broke  loose  and  ran  away  from  a  u  great  kuala”
the  sacrifices,  in  the  midst  of  their  devotions,  having  to  leave
off  and  pursue  it.  The  place  where  the  animal  was  at  last
caught,  was  considered  to  be  so  pleasing  to  the  kuala  spirit
that  the  whole  building  was  removed  there.13  If,  from  any
cause,  people  are  obliged  to  destroy  a  kualay  the  sacrifice  case
and  the  stones  of  the  hearth  may  not  on  any  account  be  lost.
As  an  instance  of  the  superstition  of  the  Votiaks  the  following

legend  is  mentioned:  A  man  destroyed  his  kuala  and  built  in
its  stead  a  barn,  leaving  the  sacrifice  case  and  the  stones  under
the  hearth.  Once,  some  young  men  who  had  gone  there  to
sleep  were  awakened  suddenly  by  groans  from  under  the  barn,
like  the  wailing  of  a  sick  man.  The  next  night  the  same  wail¬
ing  was  heard.  At  last,  the  master  himself  went  to  sleep  there,
and  found  that  it  was  none  other  than  the  Vorsud  who  was
moaning.  He  then  promised  to  remove  the  stones  and  the
case  into  a  new  kuala ,  which  he  did,  and  thenceforward  there
was  silence  in  the  barn.14

Considering  that  the  name  of  Vorsud,  at  the  sacrifice  meet¬
ings  of  the  Votiaks,  is  generally  used  in  the  singular,  most
frequently  in  connection  with  the  kuala  family’s  name,  as
“  mozga  Vorsud,”  “  utsa  Vorsud,”  etc.,  it  would  seem  as  if
every  Votiak  kuala  had  possessed  only  one  family  spirit.  This
was,  however,  not  so  in  olden  times,  as  is  proved  by  the  cir¬
cumstance  that  the  Votiaks  consider  themselves  able  to  dis¬
tribute  them  among  their  descendants.  In  one  prayer  the
name  of  Vorsud  is  also  used  in  the  plural.15  The  idea  of
several  spirits  in  one  kuala  appears,  moreover,  in  the  follow¬
ing  legend:  A  certain  Votiak  became  a  Christian  and  re¬
nounced  the  ancient  customs  of  sacrifice,  but  did  not  destroy
his  kuala .  After  some  time  the  spirits  began  annoying  him;
when  lying  in  bed,  he  seemed  to  feel  a  heavy  stone  pressing
on  his  breast ;  when  he  went  to  the  barn  to  sleep,  the  spirits
came  there,  too,  to  annoy  him.  At  last,  the  man  made  up  his
mind  to  shoot  them,  and  one  night  he  walked  about,  gun  in
hand,  waiting  for  them.  At  midnight  three  persons  in  white
came  out  of  the  kuala ,  the  first  a  beardless  youth,  the  second
also  young  but  with  the  beginnings  of  a  beard,  the  third,  a
woman.  The  man  fired,  and  the  vision  vanished  at  once.
After  that  they  did  not  show  themselves  any  more,  but  re¬
moved  to  another  place,  sending  the  man  a  severe  illness  as  a
punishment.16

FAMILY  GODS

there  were  several  family  spirits,  points  also  to  their  human
origin.  According  to  the  belief  of  the  Votiaks,  the  kuala
spirits  generally  appear  as  human  beings.  At  times,  however,
though  rarely,  the  Vorsud  may  reveal  itself  in  some  other
form.  In  a  story  of  the  Votiaks  in  the  District  of  Glazov,  a
kuala  sanctuary  is  mentioned  as  having  been  on  the  site  where
the  present  town  of  Vyatka  is  situated.  It  is  related  that
when  the  Russian  settlers,  after  having  driven  out  the  Votiaks
from  their  then  dwelling-places,  began  pulling  down  the  kuala ,
a  bird  flew  out  of  the  sanctuary,  meeting  its  death  beside  the
church  just  erected,  as  if  stricken  by  an  invisible  power.17

The  Votiak,  having  founded  for  himself  a  kuala  of  his
own,  still  visits  the  old  kualay  and  sometimes  even  the  still
older  mother  kuala .  The  first,  in  comparison  with  the  second,
is  a  “  little  kuala  ”  likewise  the  second  in  comparison  with  the
third,  while  the  second,  compared  with  the  first,  is  a  “  great
kuala”  and  in  the  same  way,  the  third  in  comparison  with
the  second.  According  to  their  kuala  worship  the  Votiaks  are
commonly  divided  into  two  groups,  to  both  of  which  the  same
person  may  belong  —  the  family  of  the  “  great  kuala yy  and
the  family  of  the  “ little  kuala”  To  illustrate  the  present
kuala  cult  of  the  Votiaks  and  the  relations  of  the  different
family  groups  with  each  other,  it  may  be  mentioned  that  the
same  Votiak  in  the  village  of  Ostorma-Yumya  in  the  District
of  Mamadysh,  besides  visiting  the  “little  kuala”  which  is
situated  in  his  own  yard  and  in  whose  sacrifices,  besides  himself,
the  families  of  his  three  younger  brothers  take  part,  also  fre¬
quents  the  “  great  kuala”  situated  in  the  same  village  and
visited  by  seventy-three  families  in  all.  The  other  families  in
the  village,  belonging  to  other  clans,  go  each  their  own  way  to
sacrifice.  The  above  mentioned  seventy-three  families  visit
also  the  kuala  in  the  neighbouring  village  or  Staraya-Yumya,
from  which  Ostorma-Yumya  and  certain  other  villages  were
originally  formed.  The  “  great  kuala  ”  of  Staraya-Yumya  is
visited,  not  only  by  its  own  villages,  but  by  the  seventy-three

families  of  Ostorma-Yumya,  and,  also,  by  all  the  persons  liv¬
ing  in  the  neighbouring  villages  who  belong  to  the  same  tribe.
In  later  days,  however,  people  have  more  and  more  ceased
coming  from  strange  villages  with  their  offerings  to  the  “  great
kuala  ”  of  the  mother  village.

The  relationships  among  the  family  groups  are,  of  course,
not  the  same  in  every  Votiak  village.  Sometimes  a  u  little
kuala  ”  may  be  visited  by  quite  a  number  of  families,  up  to
several  score,  this  depending  wholly  on  the  zeal  of  the  Votiak
families  in  founding  new  kuala  sanctuaries  for  themselves.

Those  Votiaks,  who  have  removed  as  settlers,  and  even
those  who  now  remove  far  from  their  native  place,  and  who,
therefore,  cannot  take  part  in  the  sacrifices  of  their  native
village,  remember,  however,  the  kuala  of  their  ancestors  in
their  own  kualas.  Thus  for  instance,  a  Votiak  family  living
in  the  village  of  Mozga  in  the  District  of  Birsk,  remembers  the
“  great  kuala  ”  in  the  native  village  of  the  same  name  in  the
district  of  Yelabuga,  because  their  ancestors  had  removed
thence,  bringing  with  them  mudor.  A  remarkable  feature  of
the  kuala  cult  of  the  Eastern  Votiaks  is,  further,  the  circum¬
stance  that  the  so-called  “  little  kualas  ”  have  come  to  be
neglected  j  relatives  perform  their  sacrifices  only  in  the  mutual
family  sanctuary,  several  of  which  may  be  found  in  one
village,  depending  on  the  number  of  different  families.  Un¬
der  such  circumstances,  mudor  weddings  take  place  only  when
Votiaks  remove  as  settlers  from  the  old  village  to  a  new
one.

Reverence  for  the  old  home  has  been  best  preserved  in  the
oldest  native  districts  of  the  Votiaks,  where,  in  certain  neigh¬
bourhoods  at  present  uninhabited,  we  may  see  remains  of
crumbling  huts,  which  are  sometimes  visited  at  the  command
of  the  sorcerer,  for  the  purpose  of  sacrificing  in  cases  of  severe
illnesses.  A  hut  of  this  nature,  which  is  called  “  the  utter¬
most  kuala”  is  most  probably  the  oldest  home  of  the  family
that  has  been  retained  in  memory."

  "passage_text": "FAMILY  GODS

General,  regular  kuala  sacrifices  are  performed  by  the
Votiaks  at  somewhat  different  times  in  different  places,  but,
according  to  the  most  widespread  custom,  three  times  a  year
—  in  the  spring,  in  summer,  and  in  autumn.  Later,  it  has
become  customary  to  sacrifice  much  oftener  in  the  family  kuala ,
in  some  places  on  every  Christian  holy  day.

On  regular  holy  days,  the  Votiaks  sacrifice  in  the  “  little  ”
as  well  as  in  the  “  great  ”  kualay  representatives  being  some¬
times  sent  also  to  the  greater  sanctuary  of  the  mother  village.
The  sacrificial  ceremonies  in  the  different  sanctuaries  resemble
each  other  very  much,  with  the  exception  of  unimportant  de¬
viations.  On  the  other  hand,  the  times  and  order  of  sacrificing
in  the  kualas  of  different  rank  vary,  sacrifices  being  sometimes
carried  out  first  in  the  “  little  kuala  ”  and  then  in  the  u  great
kuala ”  and  vice  versa.  In  some  places  the  sacrificial  cere¬
monies  are  held  late  in  the  evening,  in  others  in  the  daytime.
At  times  the  festivity  lasts  for  two  or  three  days.

The  oldest  account  of  a  kuala  sacrifice  originates  from  the
province  of  Ufa  and  was  published  by  Ryckov  in  the  eight¬
eenth  century.  The  author  relates  that  the  Votiaks  sacrifice,
“  near  certain  branches  of  fir  regarded  by  them  as  representing
the  family  god,”  a  young  calf,  whose  ears  they  then  place  on
the  shelf  on  which  the  fir  branches  lie.  The  sacrificial  animal
they  kill  in  the  sanctuary  itself.18

Of  the  same  period  is  the  description  by  Georgi,  who  gives
a  more  detailed  account  of  the  sacrifice  performed  at  Easter.
The  author  states  that  both  men  and  women  partake  in  the
ceremony,  having  cleansed  themselves  first  by  taking  a  bath
in  the  bathhouse.  Each  one  brings  with  him  to  the  kuala
guardian  the  objects  necessary  for  the  sacrifice.  When  the
meat  is  cooked,  the  officiating  priest  places  a  portion  from
every  dish  and  also  some  beer  on  a  table  opposite  the  door.
On  the  shelf  above  the  table  some  fir-twigs  are  laid,  and  on
these  he  puts  a  dish  with  morsels  from  the  sacrifice.  These
he  takes  after  a  while,  together  with  the  drinking  vessel,  in

his  hand,  asking  from  the  Vorsud  happiness,  health,  children,
cattle,  bread,  honey,  etc.19

saying  good-bye  or  asking  his  neighbour  to  come  and  see  him.
Also  among  the  Hill  Cheremiss,  amongst  whom  one  very  rarely
comes  across  a  kudo>  the  belief  has  been  preserved  that  the
kudo-\ odyz  continues  to  live  in  the  place  of  the  former  kudo ,
and  that  he  who  quarrels  in  the  said  place  or  besmirches  it,  will
undoubtedly  fall  ill.26

After  marriage,  the  Cheremiss  woman  still  goes  at  first  for
some  time  to  the  kudo  of  her  old  home  to  sacrifice,  should  she
meet  with  illness  or  any  other  misfortune  declared  by  the  sor¬
cerer  to  have  been  caused  by  the  spirits  of  the  “  old  place.”
Similarly  the  scattered  younger  families  turn  when  necessary  to
the  spirits  of  older  kudo.  Thus,  the  “  little  family  ”  remains
always  dependent  on  the  “  great  family  ”  in  some  way  or
other.27

Georgi  speaks  also  about  a  material  image  of  the  family  god,
stating  that  “  in  many  houses,  perhaps  in  every  house,  there  is
in  a  corner  in  a  case,  a  coarse  little  doll  of  wood,  dressed  in
male  attire.”  When  describing  the  wedding  ceremonies  of  the
Cheremiss,  he  further  relates  that  “  when  everything  is  ready
in  the  wedding  house,  the  family  god  is  placed  on  the  table
and  the  sacrificing  priest  {kart)  of  the  village  prays  in  front
of  it.”  Considering  that  the  Cheremiss  have  not  been  in  the
habit  of  keeping  the  sacrifice  case  in  the  dwelling-house,  there
is  reason  to  suppose  that  the  family  god  mentioned  by  Georgi
is  the  kudo-\ odyz.28

A  similar  family  cult  doubtless  existed  among  the  Mordvins,
and  even  among  the  Baltic  Finns.  Among  the  Esthonians,
remains  of  it  seem  to  have  been  preserved,  through  alien  in¬
fluence,  until  modern  times.  The  Vorsud  case  of  the  Votiaks
corresponds,  with  them,  to  the  “  Tonni  vakk  ”  {vakk  =
“case”).  On  Tonni  or  Antony Js-day  (January  seventeenth)
one  must  brew  beer  or  slaughter  some  animal  —  the  latter
being  generally  a  sheep,  though  a  bull  is  sometimes  mentioned.
At  nightfall,  the  Tonni  vakk  was  taken  from  its  recess,  candles
were  lighted  on  the  rims  of  the  case,  and  it  was  carried  all

round  the  dwelling  house,  the  cattle  sheds,  and  the  yard.
From  each  part  of  the  carcase  of  the  sacrificial  animal  a  piece
of  meat  was  cut  as  a  sacrifice  to  Tonni,  and  of  the  gravy  a  little
was  also  sprinkled  on  the  nearest  paths.  Lastly  the  people
sat  down  to  eat.

Tonni’s  case,  which  had  to  be  made  by  the  sorcerer,  was  kept
in  a  place  known  only  by  the  master,  generally  in  the  attic  of
the  storehouse.  In  this  were  placed  all  the  year  round,  for  one
reason  or  another,  various  offerings:  —  when  the  corn  was
threshed,  when  beer  was  brewed,  when  milking  a  cow  that  had
lately  calved,  when  shearing  the  sheep,  and  when  spinning  yarn
or  weaving  cloth.  When  slaughtering,  they  sacrificed  meat,
blood  or  fat.  The  case  had  to  be  particularly  remembered  on
the  occasion  of  illness  among  either  human  beings  or  animals.
Falling  ill  was  considered  to  be  a  consequence  of  the  case  hav¬
ing  been  damaged  or  of  some  one,  when  passing,  having  made
a  noise,  or  because  the  people  had  forgotten  to  sacrifice  to  it.
There  is  a  report  even,  that  the  case  used  to  contain  a  doll-like
image.  That  the  Esthonians  also  had  known  both  a  lesser
family  spirit  and  a  greater  one,  is  shown  by  a  tradition,  accord¬
ing  to  which  not  only  every  family  but  also  every  village  had  its
common  sacrifice  case.29

There  are  no  reliable  statements  regarding  the  corresponding
family  worship  of  the  Finns.  Yet,  in  the  social  life  of  the
Karelians  there  are  indications  that  these  belonged  to  two  dif¬
ferent  families,  a  smaller  and  a  larger  one,  the  chieftainship
of  the  last  named  —  where  its  head  was  not  chosen  by  election
—  descending  from  a  father  to  the  eldest  son  of  the  eldest
branch  of  the  family.  A  result  of  the  worship  of  the  fore¬
fathers  of  the  family  was  most  likely  the  alien  position  of  the
wife  in  her  husband’s  home,  for,  as  with  the  Votiaks,  the  women
in  Finnish  Karelia  kept  their  own  family  name  even  after
their  marriage.30"

THERE  is  every  reason  to  believe  that  those  Lapp  Seides,
which  were  worshipped  by  a  larger  following,  were  dedi¬
cated  to  the  spirit  of  some  more  famous  man,  the  founder  of  a
family,  a  shaman,  etc.  Such  people  were  worshipped  also
among  other  Finno-Ugric  peoples  and  the  Samoyeds.  Ven¬
iamin  relates  of  the  Yuraks  that  certain  of  their  stone  or
wooden  gods,  the  latter  having  a  head  coming  to  a  point,  were
worshipped  by  a  great  tribe,  spread  over  a  wide  area,  others
again  by  only  a  very  scant  congregation.  The  former  are
generally  situated  in  the  neighbourhood  of  such  places  as  the
Yuraks  are  accustomed  to  gather  at,  to  hunt  or  fish  or  to  seek
food  for  their  reindeer.  He  mentions  two  such  ancient  sacred
places,  visited  by  great  numbers,  of  which  one  was  situated
on  the  holy  island  Vajgats.  At  these  meetings  the  Samoyeds
sacrifice  reindeer  and  dogs  to  their  tutelary  spirits,  besmearing
the  mouths  of  the  idols  with  the  blood  and  fat  of  the  sacrifice,
and  having  eaten  the  flesh,  hanging  up  the  head,  and  even
at  times,  the  hide,  on  a  holy  tree.1  Of  later  origin  is  possibly
a  custom  of  the  Eastern  Samoyeds  of  throwing  pieces  of  the
flesh  of  the  sacrifice  into  the  fire.  Bloodless  sacrifices  are  per¬
formed  among  the  Ostiak  Samoyeds.  These  sometimes  do
not  slaughter  the  sacrificial  deer,  but  content  themselves  with
cutting  out  the  face  of  the  god  or  other  strange  figures  on  its
back.  After  a  ceremony  of  this  description  the  animal  is  re¬
garded  as  holy,  and  may  not  be  used  for  any  purpose  or
eaten.2

The  “  sacred  places”  of  the  Yuraks  are  not  fenced  in,
neither  are  buildings  to  be  found  on  them,  the  idols  standing  al-

ways  under  the  open  sky.3  On  the  other  hand,  special  buildings
for  their  idols  are  met  with  among  the  Ostiak  Samoyeds.  A
building  of  this  kind,  hidden  away  in  the  forest,  is  described
by  Donner  in  the  following  words:  “  As  the  dwelling-place
of  the  gods  they  use  here  a  building  standing  on  four  high
supports,  resembling  greatly  the  average  barns  by  the  River
Ob.  In  the  fore-wall  there  was  a  little  opening  and  against
the  back  wall  stood  the  god,  made  of  wood  and  resembling
a  human  being,  together  with  his  marital  partner.  The  face
was  very  clumsily  carved,  the  eyes  formed  of  two  large  blue
glass-pearls,  imparting  a  very  quaint  expression  to  the  old
man.  The  images  were  dressed  in  fine  furs  and  had  around
them  a  number  of  weapons  made  of  pewter  with  which  to
protect  themselves  j  and,  fashioned  of  the  same  material,
swans,  geese,  snakes,  reindeer  and  other  animals,  by  the  help
of  which  they  were  supposed  to  be  able  to  flee  on  the  approach
of  an  unconquerable  enemy.  Near  the  door  was  posted  a
little  man  dressed  as  a  Russian  policeman,  holding  a  wooden
sabre  in  one  hand,  while  in  the  other  he  swung  a  great  sword.
The  dwelling-place  of  the  gods  was  furnished  with  gaudy
cloths  and  expensive  furs,  and  before  the  image  of  the  ancestor
the  most  varying  objects  lay  on  the  floor,  among  other  things
a  great  deal  of  money,  of  which  many  coins  were  a  couple  of
hundred  years  old.  In  the  branches  of  the  holy  trees  sur¬
rounding  the  building  garments,  horns  of  animals,  hides,  etc.,
were  hung.”  4

Similar  spirits,  bound  to  certain  fixed  places,  are  also  pos¬
sessed  by  the  Ostiaks  and  Voguls  in  great  numbers.  The
mightiest  of  these  are  honoured  by  a  great  circle  extended
over  a  wide  area,  others  again  only  by  a  small  one,  or  merely
by  the  population  of  a  single  village.  “  All  places  dedicated
to  idols,”  says  Pallas,  “  the  boundaries  of  which  are  exactly
defined  by  rivers,  brooks,  or  other  marks,  are  spared  by  the
Ostiaks,  who  neither  cut  down  trees  nor  mow  grass,  neither
hunt  nor  fish,  abstaining  even  from  drinking  the  water  within

their  boundaries,  for  fear  of  offending  the  gods.  Should  they
be  obliged  to  traverse  these  waters  by  boat,  they  are  careful
not  to  approach  too  closely  to  the  shores  or  to  touch  them
with  their  oars,  and  if  the  way  through  them  is  very  long,
they  supply  themselves  with  water  before  reaching  the  holy
place,  as  they  would  sooner  suffer  the  worst  tortures  from
thirst  than  drink  of  the  holy  water.”  5  These  holy  places,
however,  have  not  definite  boundaries,  still  less  are  they  fenced
in,  but  especially  in  the  southern  districts  there  is  a  little  build¬
ing  resembling  a  storehouse,  intended  for  the  preservation  of
offerings  and  the  images.  Like  their  house  gods,  the  spirits
living  at  fixed  holy  places  of  the  Ostiaks  and  Voguls  have  all
been  materialised  into  images.  Most  often  they  have  been
shaped  as  wooden  figures  resembling  human  beings,  at  times
as  rag-dolls  made  out  of  stuffed  sacks  or  natural  stones  3  fur¬
ther,  they  have  also  been  formed  of  bronze,  copper,  lead,  or
even  of  bones.  As  assistants  these  have  often  images  resem¬
bling  various  animals.  The  storehouses  for  offerings  are  gen¬
erally  under  the  care  of  a  special  person,  who  then  also
carries  out  the  sacrificial  ceremonies  and  receives  the  offerings,
money,  skins,  etc.  Very  often  this  occupation  is  hereditary  in
the  same  family.6

That  these  powerful  and  dreaded  spirits,  regarded  as  being
able  to  visit  people  with  sickness,  were  originally  human,
has  not  been  forgotten  by  the  people.  A  part  of  them  are  said
to  have  been  former  rulers  or  heroes,  whose  mighty  deeds
are  extolled  in  songs,  others  are  expressly  said  to  be  the
founders  of  the  clans.  Those  again  that  are  furnished  with
images  of  animals  were  probably  famous  shamans.  An  example
of  how  a  powerful  spirit  is  believed  to  develop  out  of  a  man
of  mark  after  death  is  given  by  an  Ostiak  folk-poem,  in
which  a  Vasyugan  hero  displays  an  uncommon  nobility  of
character  by  burying  the  body  of  a  dead  enemy-hero,  erecting
his  sword  on  the  grave,  and  consoling  him  by  saying:  “  In
the  times  of  coming  daughters,  in  the  times  of  coming  sons,

thou  shalt  be  called  to  life,  and  thou  shalt  become  an  offeringspirit  accepting  offerings.” 7

At  times  one  may  see  many  images  in  the  same  offeringhouse.  Two  hundred  years  ago,  Novitskiy  visited  a  “  great  ”
god-house,  containing  five  wooden  images  resembling  human
beings  wrapped  round  with  “  clothes.”  Around  this  chief
building  were  smaller  square  store-rooms  on  posts  about  the
height  of  a  man;  in  these  were  preserved  the  objects  used  at
the  slaughter  of  a  sacrifice;  axes,  knives,  etc.  Separated  from
these  was  another  little  store-room  filled  with  bones.8

The  sacrifices  of  the  Ostiaks  and  Voguls,  which  may  be
either  annual  or  occasional,  do  not  materially  differ  from  the
corresponding  uses  of  the  Samoyeds.  According  to  the  oldest
sources,  the  mouths  of  the  images  were  besmeared  with  blood
and  fat,  and  the  hides  of  the  animals,  with  horns  and  hoofs
attached,  hung  up  in  trees.  The  use  of  fire  as  a  means  of
transmitting  the  offerings,  met  with  also  among  the  Ostiak
Samoyeds,  is  most  probably  of  later  origin.  Like  these  last
mentioned,  the  more  Eastern  Ostiaks  have  the  custom  of  occa¬
sionally  offering  up  so-called  bloodless  sacrifices,  that  is  to
say,  sacrifices  in  which  the  animal  is  not  killed,  its  “  soul  ”
only  being  made  over  to  the  god.  Even  children  may  thus
be  consecrated  to  some  spirit;  the  child  thus  consecrated  has
to  fulfil  certain  duties  during  his  lifetime,  as,  for  example,
to  marry  a  wife,  or  a  husband,  from  the  direction  of  the  com¬
pass  in  which  the  spirit  dwells.9

The  worshipping  of  heroes  among  the  Siryans,  at  the  pres¬
ent  time  totally  forgotten  by  them,  is  described  in  the  Life  of
St.  Stephen  (d.  1396)  in  the  following  words:  “  In  Perm
many  kinds  of  idols  were  to  be  found :  some  large,  some  small,
others  again,  of  medium  size;  some  were  famous  and  very
fine,  others  were  legion;  a  part  were  worshipped  only  by
few  and  were  shown  little  honour,  but  others  again  were  wor¬
shipped  by  people  dwelling  far  and  wide.  They  have  certain
idols  to  whom  they  travel  long  distances,  bringing  them  gifts"
}
