All  blacksmiths  are  said  to  be  under\nthe  protection  of  these  stars.38\n\nThe  Mongols,  who  also  call  this  constellation  “the  seven\nold  men  ”  or  “  the  seven  Burkhans,”  sacrificed  milk  and  kumiss\nand  even  devoted  some  domestic  animals  to  it.39\n\nVery  widespread  is  a  tale  in  which  the  “  seven  old  men  ”\nor  the  “  seven  Khans  ”  as  they  are  also  called,  are  accused  of\ntheft.  The  Mongols  tell  that  “  the  seven  Burkhans  ”  stole  a\nstar  from  the  Pleiades,  which  numbered  seven  before  but  are\nnow  only  six.  This  little  stolen  star  (Alcor)  is  to  be  seen  close\nto  the  central  star  of  the  arch  of  the  Great  Bear.  With  the\nMongols  it  has  developed  into  the  god  of  thieves,  to  whom\nthese  always  call  on  their  predatory  excursions  to  give  luck\nin  their  wickedness.40  It  is  in  order  to  be  revenged  on  the\nGreat  Bear,  so  say  the  Altai  Tatars,  that  the  Pleiades  pursue\nthe  “  seven  Khans  ”  although  they  never  overtake  them.41\nThe  Kirghis  also  call  the  Great  Bear  “  the  seven  thieves,”  and\naccuse  them  of  having  stolen  one  of  the  two  daughters  of  the\nPleiades.42  In  Northern  Caucasia  there  is  a  tale  of  how  a\ncertain  Khan  left  his  child  in  the  keeping  of  “  seven  brothers  ”\nand  how  they  were  already  on  their  homeward  journey  when\nthe  Pleiades  attacked  them,  wishing  to  kill  the  child,  but  the\n“  seven  brothers  ”  succeeded  in  saving  it.43\n\nThe  tales  about  the  M  seven  brothers  ”  and  their  “  little\nsister  ”  who  was  taken  up  into  the  sky,  belong  to  the  same\nseries.  That  the  “  seven  old  men  ”  of  the  Buriats  also  are\noriginally  robbers  of  a  star-maiden  appears  from  the  following\nstory,  which  has  been  recorded  among  them.  There  was  once\nupon  a  time  a  poor  man  who  received  the  gift  of  understand¬\ning  the  speech  of  birds. On  hearing  the  method  agreed\nupon  by  the  ravens,  he  at  once  hurried  to  the  Khan  and  healed\n\nhis  son.  Greatly  thankful,  the  Khan  presented  him  with  seven\nsteeds.  On  his  homeward  journey  he  met  six  men,  each  of\nwhom  attracted  his  attention  in  a  peculiar  way.  The  first  was\nso  strong  that  he  could  lift  a  mountain  from  the  ground.  The\nsecond  had  so  keen  a  sense  of  hearing  that  he  could  tell  what\nwas  happening  under  the  earth.  The  third  was  an  archer  of\nsuch  power  that  with  his  bow  he  could  bring  down  a  piece  of\nthe  “  heavenly  mountain.”  The  fourth  was  so  clever  with  his\nhands  that  he  easily  transplanted  the  feathers  from  one  kind\nof  bird  to  another.  The  fifth  was  able  to  suck  a  whole  river\ninto  his  mouth  and  squirt  it  out  again.  The  sixth  was  so\nnimble  of  foot  that  he  outran  a  wild-goat  on  the  prairie.  These\nheroes  now  joined  the  poor  man  who  understood  the  language\nof  birds.  Then  the  one  who  had  the  keen  sense  of  hearing\nhappened  to  hear  how  a  certain  Khan,  wishing  to  choose  a\nhusband  for  his  daughter,  set  all  the  suitors-elect  three  diffi¬\ncult  conditions  to  fulfill.  The  heroes,  determining  to  try  their\nluck,  went  to  the  Khan  and  asked  him  for  his  daughter’s  hand.\nHaving  easily  fulfilled  the  most  difficult  tasks  they  took  the\nmaiden  with  them.  The  servants  of  the  Khan  pursued  them,\nbut  the  seven  heroes  escaped  with  their  booty.  In  the  end  God\ntook  them  up  into  the  sky  where  they  were  changed  into  the\nGreat  Bear. Ideas  corre¬\nsponding  to  this  are  found  among  other  peoples.\n\nOrion  has  also  many  names  taken  from  objects. For  this  reason  these  stars  are  also  called  u  the\nstraw-thief’s  track.” 68\n\nNames  of  later  origin  are  the  “  pilgrims’  way  to  Mecca  ”  of\nthe  Mohammedan  Tatars,  and  the  “  Burkhans’  road  ”  of  the\nMongols. When  God  (Numi-Torem),  as  the  Voguls\nrelate,  had  created  the  earth,  he  sent  a  six-footed  stag  upon  it.\nAn  ordinary  human  being  could  not  hunt  this  quick-footed\nanimal,  and  so  he  begged  the  Forest  spirit  to  pursue  it.  But\neven  for  this  being,  who  glided  at  a  terrific  rate  on  his  skis,\nit  was  not  easy  to  overtake  his  six-legged  prey.  When  at  last\nhe  succeeded  in  killing  the  animal,  which  was  so  big  that  its\nbody  “  reached  over  thirty  rivers,”  the  Forest  spirit  broke  off\nthe  two  additional  feet,  saying  to  his  father  Numi-Torem:\nu  Change  this  animal  with  the  power  of  thy  word  into  a  fourfooted  beast,  as,  seeing  that  the  work  of  chasing  and  killing  it\nhas  been  difficult  even  for  me,  how  should  an  ordinary  human\nbeing  have  the  strength  necessary  for  it.”  This  hunt  was  re¬\nflected  in  the  sky.  The  stag  became  the  Great  Bear,  in  which\nare  to  be  seen  the  beast’s  head,  its  two  eyes,  its  forefeet  and\n\nhindfeet,  and  in  addition  the  chopped-off  stumps  of  the  other\ntwo  feet.  The  Milky,  Way  is  “  the  ski-track  of  the  Forest\nspirit.”  Even  the  Forest  spirit’s  house  can  be  seen  in  the  sky  in\na  shape  which  the  Voguls  call  “  the  complete  house  of  the\nForest  spirit,”  (i.e.,  the  Pleiades).  In  this  story  also,  the  hero\nwho  attacks  the  Great  Bear  is  from  the  Pleiades.71\n\nThe  Ostiaks  on  the  Irtysh  River  tell  of  a  man  named\nTungk-Pok.  who  once  when  he  was  in  the  sky  undertook  to\nhunt  this  six-footed  stag.  Having  chased  it  across  the  sky  on\nhis  magic  skis  the  hero  overtook  it  at  the  mouth  of  the  Irtysh,\nwhere  the  stag  threw  itself  on  to  the  earth.  The  hunter  did\nnot  succeed  in  killing  it,  but  could  only  cut  off  its  two  hind¬\nmost  feet.  He  therefore  declared:  “  Men  will  become  more\nand  more  small  and  weak,  how  can  they  then  overthrow  a  six¬\nfooted  beast,  which  even  for  me  is  very  difficult?  May  stags\nand  other  animals  from  this  day  onwards  have  only  four\nfeet!  ”  The  stag  continued  its  flight  towards  the  north  until\nthe  hero  again  reached  it  near  Obdorsk.  The  animal  being\nthen  dead-tired,  it  begged  God  to  save  it  from  the  hands  of  the\nhunter.  God  took  pity  on  the  stag  and  changed  it  into  a  great\nstone,  but,  as  a  memento  of  this  heavenly  chase,  the  Ostiaks\nsee  in  the  Milky  Way  two  parallel  ski-tracks  (“the  ski-track\nof  Tungk-Pok  ”  or  “  the  way  of  Tungk-Pok  ”)  and  in  the\nGreat  Bear  a  “  stag.”\n\nThe  Ostiaks  of  Vasyugan  call  this  hunter  “  the  son  of  the\ngod  of  Heaven.”  72\n\n•  THE  SIGNS  OF  A  TWELVE-DIVISIONED  PERIOD\n\nIn  connection  with  fancies  relating  to  the  stars  it  may  be\nmentioned  that  the  peoples  of  Central  Asia  divide  time  into\nperiods  of  twelve,  usually  calling  each  of  these  units  of  time\nby  the  following  animal  names:  mouse,  cow,  tiger,  hare,\ndragon,  snake,  horse,  sheep,  monkey,  cock,  dog  and  sow.73\nImages  of  these  animals  in  relief  can  often  be  seen  decorating"

Other  objects,  also  decorated  with\nthe  same  images,  for  reckoning  time  can  be  seen  here,  most\nof  which  have  been  brought\nfrom  China  where,  as  in  other\nparts  of  East  Asia,  this  method\nof  keeping  account  of  time  still\nprevails.  From  the  Chinese\npictures  it  will  be  seen  that  the\nanimal-images  there  are  the\nsame  as  those  of  the  Mongols.\n\nOnly  the  sign  of  the  mouse  is\ncalled  a  rat  by  the  Chinese,  and\nthat  of  the  hare  a  rabbit.  Al¬\nthough  these  animal  signs  are  Figmainly  the  same  with  the  dif¬\nferent  peoples  of  Central  Asia,  their  order  varies  somewhat.\nThus  the  Eastern  Soyots  are  said  to  reckon  the  years  in  the\nfollowing  order  —  dragon,  tiger,  cow,  sow,  monkey,  mouse,\ndog,  frog,  snake,  cock,  horse  and  hare.74\n\nThe  Buriats,  who  begin  their  twelve-year  and  twelve-month\nperiods  with  the  mouse,  say  that  they  really  ought  to  begin  with\nthe  camel,  but  that  the  camel  has  lost  this  honour.  Light  is\nthrown  on  the  subject  by  the  following  tale.  The  camel  and\nthe  mouse  quarrelled  over  which  of  them  should  rule  over  the\nfirst  year  of  a  period  or  the  first  month  of  a  year.  In  the  end\nthey  decided  to  solve  the  dispute  in  such  a  way  that  the  one\nwho  first  saw  the  rays  of  the  rising  sun  should  call  the  year  or\nmonth  in  question  by  his  name.  The  camel  took  his  stand\nlooking  towards  the  east,  but  the  mouse  climbed  on  his  hump\nand  from  there  watched  the  west.  At  dawn  the  camel’s  eye\nhad  not  yet  caught  the  sun  when  the  mouse  had  already  seen\nthe  reflection  of  its  rays  on  the  western  mountains.  For  this\nreason  the  first  year  and  also  the  first  month  of  the  year  are\n\ncalled  after  the  mouse.  From  this  tale  the  Buriats  have  a\nproverb:  “  In  believing  himself  great  the  camel  lost  a  year.”  75\nSigns  of  animals  representing  a  period  of  time  divisible  by\ntwelve  are  already  to  be  found  side  by  side  with  the  signs  of\nthe  Zodiac  on  the  marble  tablets  of  the  ancient  Egyptians,\nfound  in  the  beginning  of  the  last  century.  A  period  of  twelve\nhours,  which  were  represented  by  animal  figures  of  the  same\ndescription,  was  called  Dodekaoros  by  the  ancient  Greeks.\nThese  pictures,  which  to  some  extent  resemble  the  time-marks\nof  the  Mongols,  are  mentioned  in  the  following  order:  cat,\ndog,  snake,  crab,  ass,  lion,  goat,  ox,  hawk,  monkey,  ibis  and\ncrocodile.  There  can  be  no  doubt  that  these  time-marks,  which,\nlike  the  twelve-divisioned  period  itself,  seem  to  have  spread\ninto  East  Asia  from  the  west,  are  closely  connected  with  the\ncorresponding  ideas  of  these  civilized  peoples.  Later  Greek\ntexts  call  this  method  of  reckoning  time  “Chaldean,”  which\npoints  to  Babylonian  astrology.  The  signs  of  the  twelvedivisioned  period  are  thus  most  probably  explained  by  the\ntwelve  signs  of  the  Zodiac."

The\nForest  Tungus  speak  of  it  as  such  and  explain  that  the  rustle  of\nthis  mighty  bird’s  wings  is  heard  on  the\nearth,  when  it  flies,  as  the  terrific  rumbling\nof  thunder. The  Eastern  Samoyeds  liken  the\nThunder  bird  to  a  duck,  whose  sneezing  is  the  cause  of  rain.\nIt  is  also  imagined  as  the  Iron  bird,  probably  on  account  of  the\ndin  it  can  create.2  The  Yurak  Samoyeds  of  Northern  Russia,\nwho  make  themselves  an  image  of  thunder  in  the  form  of  a\ngoose,  fancy,  like  the  Tungus,  that  the  Thunder  bird  attends\n\ngus  Thunder-bird\n\nand  protects  the  soul  of  the  shaman. It  is  also\ntold  that  a  certain  Tengeri  rides  on  the  back  of  this  monster,\nchasing  a  striped  or  flying  squirrel.7  The  Tengeri  desires  to\nwreak  vengeance  on  the  squirrel,  which,  while  in  Heaven,  tore\nout  the  eye  of  God’s  youngest  son.   "passage_text": "THUNDER\n\nAltaic  one,  but,  as  its  geographical  area  already  denotes,  comes\nfrom  China.  As  we  know,  the  Chinese  and,  following  their\nexample,  the  Japanese,  imagined  the  Thunder  god  to  have  the\nshape  of  a  peculiar  dragon,  which  is  represented  in  their  art\nin  many  different  ways.\n\nBoth  the  above  mentioned  conceptions,  the  bird  and  the\nwinged  dragon,  are  evidently  born  of  the  swift  movement  of  a\nthunder-storm  and  especially  of  the  sudden  flash  of  the  light¬\nning.  Even  where  human  features  are  attributed  to  the\nThunder  god,  he  is  often  regarded  as  a  being  with  wings.  The\nOstiaks  of  Demyanka  call  him  “  the  Winged  old  man.”  10\n\nAmong  the  Buriats  a  number  of  tales  have  been  found\nrelating  how  some  human  hero  becomes  transformed  into  a\nThunder  god  by  dressing  himself  in  winged  garments.  One\nof  these  tales  tells  of  a  clever  archer  who  came  to  heaven  alive.\nOn  the  earth  he  had  had  a  wife  and  three  sons  with  whom  he\nlived  happily  until  he  became  old.  One  day  he  told  his  sons\nthat  his  days  were  numbered  and  asked  them  to  prepare  him\na  garment  and  saddle  a  horse.  After  wishing  good-bye  to\nhis  family  he  mounted  the  horse  and  departed.  Coming  to\nthe  meeting  of  three  roads  he  chose  the  middle  one,  which  led\nto  the  sky.  There  he  arrived  at  an  empty  house  where  he  was\nsoon  joined  by  four  young  men.  These  feasted  the  old  man\nand  asked  him  to  remain  there  as  guardian  of  that  heavenly\nabode  5  at  the  same  time  they  forbade  him  to  open  a  chest  which\nstood  in  the  room  or  to  put  on  a  winged  garment  hanging  on\nthe  wall.  When  he  was  alone,  however,  the  man  became  so\ncurious  that  he  once  opened  the  mystic  chest  and  saw  there\nstrange,  different-coloured  stones  shaped  like  arrow-points.\nHappening  at  the  same  time  to  turn  his  eyes  to  the  earth,\nwhere  at  that  moment  a  person  was  stealing  vegetables  from  his\nneighbour’s  garden,  he  became  so  angry  that  he  threw  a  red\nstone  at  the  thief.  A  little  later  the  four  masters  of  the  house\nreturned  home  and  scolded  the  old  man  for  having  set  a  whole\nvillage  on  fire  because  of  one  wicked  man.  Still  later  on,\n\nthe  old  man  conceived  a  desire  to  try  on  the  winged  clothes.\nWhen  he  had  dressed  himself  in  them  he  acquired  a  magic\npower  of  flying  and  thus  he  became  the  god  of  Thunder.11\n\nThere  is  another  version  of  the  same  tale  in  a  slightly  dif¬\nferent  form.  A  man  who  had  lost  his  way  while  wandering  in\ngreat  forests  came  to  a  place  where  a  flight  of  stairs  led  up  from\nthe  earth  to  the  sky.  Ascending  the  stairs  he  arrived  at  a  fine\nhouse  glittering  and  shimmering  with  gold  and  silver,  where\nthe  old  god  of  Heaven,  Esege-Malan-Tengeri,  was  sitting.\nHearing  how  the  man  had  come  to  Heaven,  God  was  delighted\nand  begged  him  to  be  his  servant,  the  man  consenting  to  his\nrequest.  One  day  God  urged  him  to  look  down  and  see  how\npeople  were  living  on  the  earth.  On  doing  so,  he  saw  a  man\nleading  a  sheep  stolen  from  another’s  flock,  and  he  became  so\nangry  that  he  seized  one  of  the  stones  which  God  kept  in  a\nchest  and  threw  it  on  the  earth.  Instantly,  God  sent  him  down\nafter  his  stone,  so  that  he  could  see  it  fall  on  the  earth  as  a\ngreat  flash  of  lightning  that  slew  the  thief.  From  that  day  he\nremained  with  the  god  of  Heaven  and  served  him  as  the\nThunderer.12\n\nNotwithstanding  all  these  tales,  which  evidently  belong  to\na  world-wide  group  of  myths,  the  Buriats  have  no  clearlydefined,  anthropomorphic  god  of  Thunder.  They  often  call\nthe  rumble  of  thunder  “  the  song  of  heaven.”  13  As  they  have\nnow,  as  mentioned  earlier,  a  great  number  of  different  Tengeris,  they  cannot  tell  which  of  them  is  at  the  precise  time  the\nThunderer.  Therefore,  when  necessary,  they  consult  a  magi¬\ncian,  sometimes  even  nine  shamans,  who  endeavour  to  find  out\nwhich  god,  one  belonging  to  the  eastern  or  one  belonging  to  the\nwestern  group,  is  the  raiser  of  the  particular  storm.  One  of\nthe  mightiest  Thunder  gods  is  Asan-Sagan-Tengeri,  who  fights\nevil  spirits  with  his  fiery  arrow.14\n\nThe  Yakuts,  on  the  contrary,  have  quite  a  distinct  Thunder\ngod  whom  they  call  Ulu-Tojon  (“  Great  Lord  ”)  or  Syga-\nTojon  (“  Lord  with  the  axe  ”).  Frequently  he  is  only  named"

“  the  Thunderer.”  According  to  one  source  “  the  Lord  with
the  axe”  lives  in  the  eighth  heaven.  Other  sources  speak
separately  of  the  gods  of  Thunder  and  of  Lightning.  In  such
cases  the  Yakuts  call  the  Thunderer  “  Bold  Screamer  ”  and  the
Lightning-maker  “  the  Lord  with  the  axe.”  Both  are  sup¬
posed  to  pursue  demons  and  evil  spirits.  In  order  to  rid
their  homes  of  the  evil  spirits  which  endeavour  to  hide
themselves  there  when  a  thunder-storm  threatens,  the
Yakuts  smoke  them  out  by  burning  pieces  of  a  tree  struck
by  lightning,  crying  at  the  same  time:  “The  Bold  Screamer
shrieked,  the  Lord  with  the  axe  moved!  Away,  away!  ”  They
then  throw  the  bits  of  wood  far  out  on  the  meadow.  Thunder-
*  bolts,  which  the  people  believe  they  find  in  the  earth,  are
treasured  in  the  houses  as  important  talismans  against  light¬
ning.15  The  Goldes  call  old  stone  weapons  found  in  the
ground  “  thunder-axes.”  16

The  Yakut  “Lord  with  the  axe,”  who  pursues  demons,  is
most  probably,  like  the  corresponding  figures  in  European
myths,  derived  from  the  ancient  civilized  peoples  of  Asia.

Of  another  origin  also  is  the  other  conception  of  the  god
of  Thunder,  met  with  already  among  the  Finns,  according  to
which  the  Thunder  god  is  a  skilful  archer.  The  Altai  Tatars
tell  of  a  mighty  hero  whose  bow  is  the  rainbow  and  whose
arrow  the  lightning.17  In  some  Ostiak  districts  the  rainbow  is
explained  to  be  the  Thunder  god’s  bow  and  ancient  stone
weapons  found  in  the  ground  his  arrows,  which  he  shoots  in
order  to  kill  the  Forest  spirit  hiding  in  the  trees.18

Generally  the  peoples  of  the  Altaic  race  do  not  speak  of
the  rainbow  as  the  Thunder  god’s  weapon,  nor  do  they  call
it  the  thunder-bow.  Very  common  is  the  fancy  that  the
rainbow  is  a  kind  of  being  that  drinks  water.  The  Tatars
have  probably  transmitted  this  idea  to  the  Yenisei  Ostiaks,
who  call  the  rainbow:  “The  thunder  drinks  water.” 19
What  this  animated  water-drinker,  as  the  Votiaks  also  call  it,
really  is,  does  not  appear  from  the  beliefs  of  the  Turco-Tatar

peoples.  On  the  other  hand  the  East  European  peoples,  ac¬
cording  to  whom  the  rainbow  sucks  water  from  seas,  lakes  and
rivers,  sprinkling  it  anew  on  the  earth  as  rain,  imagine  it  to
be  a  kind  of  giant  snake.  The  Esthonians  say  that  it  has  the
head  of  an  ox,  which  it  lowers  down  to  a  river,  emptying  it
of  water.20  Could  this  be  the  Vrtra  or  Ahi  (“  snake  ”)  of  the
V eday  from  whose  power  the  Thunder  god  Indra  releases  the
waters?

The  Yakuts  believe  that  the  rainbow  can  also  raise  people
from  the  ground.  A  tale  relates  how  it  once  lifted  up  a  girl
in  the  District  of  Verchoyansk  and  set  her  down  again  near
Irkutsk.21

Both  the  Yakuts  and  Buriats  call  the  rainbow  also  “  the
urine  of  the  she-fox.” 22  The  southern  Tatar  tribes  have
several  names  for  it,  such  as  M  rainbelt,”  “  the  half-bow  of  the
pot,”  “God’s  sword”  (Caucasus).  The  Kirghis  name,  “  the
old  woman’s  sheep-halter,”  is  explained  by  the  following  tale:
A  certain  man  had  two  wives  who  were  always  quarrelling.
The  mother-in-law  cursed  the  older,  who  had  three  sons,  so
that  she  fled  to  the  heavens  with  her  sons  and  her  cattle,  and
now  tethers  her  sheep  to  the  rainbow.23

The  conception  of  the  rainbow  as  the  weapon  of  the  Thunder
god  seems  thus  to  be  quite  local  to  Middle  and  Northern  Asia,
where  it  occurs  sporadically.  Another  tale  written  down  some¬
where  in  the  district  of  the  Altai  belongs  to  a  still  more  limited
area.  It  tells  of  a  camel  moving  in  the  sky  with  three  persons
on  its  back.  The  first  beats  a  drum,  whence  the  rumbling  of
thunder,  the  second  waves  a  scarf,  whence  the  lightning,  the
third  pulls  at  the  reins,  causing  water  to  run  from  the  camel’s
mouth,  whence  the  rain.24  In  other  places  it  is  said  that  a  great
shaman  beats  a  drum  in  the  sky  when  it  thunders.  The  latter
opinion,  though  only  occasionally  met  with,  belongs  naturally
to  Siberia,  the  land  of  shamanism.

winding  streak  of  light  across  the  sky,  to  be  a  fiery  snake  fall¬
ing  down  from  Heaven.25  The  same  idea  has  been  earlier  met
with  in  a  Finnish  poem  on  the  origin  of  fire.

The  most  northerly  peoples  of  Siberia,  with  the  exception  of
The  Yakuts,  do  not  sacrifice  to  the  Thunder  god.  Some,  e.g.,
the  Yenisei  Ostiaks,  bid  him  during  a  storm  pass  by  quietly
without  raising  a  tempest.  Records  of  Thunder  worship  are
found  more  among  other  Siberian  peoples.  Old  Chinese
chronicles  relate  that  the  Northern  Uigurs  fear  the  thunder,
and  cry  out  and  shoot  towards  the  sky  at  every  crash.  They
then  leave  the  place  and  separate.  The  following  spring  they
assemble  again  at  the  spot  where  the  lightning  struck  and
slaughter  a  ram  there.  A  certain  Persian  historian  mentions
that  the  Mongolians  were  greatly  afraid  of  thunder  and  poured
milk  and  kumiss  on  the  ground,  begging  it  not  to  hurt  their
dwellings  or  their  cattle.  It  has  been  a  custom  with  the  Tatars
of  the  Altai  to  assemble  village  by  village  on  high  mountains,
when  the  first  roll  of  thunder  is  heard  in  spring,  and  to  sprinkle
milk  towards  the  four  points  of  the  sky.26

Special  attention  is  awakened  by  the  thunder  when  it  hap¬
pens  to  kill  a  human  being  or  a  domestic  animal.  Such  victims
of  the  lightning  are  regarded  as  sacred  and  so  too  is  the  spot
where  the  lightning  has  struck.  According  to  the  Buriats,
people  and  animals  slain  by  lightning  must  always  be  buried
in  the  air  upon  a  platform  built  on  four  posts.  If  the  light¬
ning  strikes  a  house,  the  house  must  at  once  be  removed  to
another  place,  or  certain  rites,  called  a  the  raising,”  have  to  be
observed,  the  intention  of  which  is  the  sending  of  the  thunder¬
bolt  back  into  the  sky.  Unless  this  be  done  danger  is  be¬
lieved  to  threaten.  These  rites,  which  must  take  place  on  the
third  day  after  the  thunder-storm,  are  conducted  by  a  magician
and  his  eight  assistants,  who  ride  on  horseback  three  times
round  the  dwelling  in  question,  stopping  before  the  door  at
every  round.  The  magician  has  a  branch  of  a  silver-fir  in
his  hand,  the  others  a  drinking-cup.  While  the  magician  re-

peats  a  prayer  his  assistants  sprinkle  liquid  from  their  cups.
The  most  important  of  these  rites  seems  to  be  the  raising  of  a
felt  carpet  spread  before  the  tent,  on  which  some  article  re¬
sembling  or  intended  to  represent  a  thunderbolt  has  been  laid.'
“  The  raising,”  from  which  the  ritual  gets  its  name,  is  per¬
formed  by  the  eight  assistants.  Finally,  molten  tin  is  dropped
into  a  liquid  to  test  by  the  shapes  thus  obtained  whether  the
raising  has  been  successful.  If  the  tin,  on  falling  into  a  basin
containing  wine  or  milk,  forms  into  a  single  lump,  the  sign
is  favourable.27

Exceedingly  strange  is  the  fancy  of  the  Buriats  that  the
Tengeris  who  are  mentioned  as  the  senders  of  thunderbolts
sometimes  pour  down  from  the  sky  urak  (the  “  first-milk,”
differing  in  colour  from  other  milk  given  by  a  cow  after
calving).  Although  many  such  Tengeris  are  mentioned,  e.g.,
Khan-Budal-Tengeri,  Urak-Sagan-Tengeri,  Kharan-Budal-
Tengeri  ( budaly  u  to  let  down  ”),  of  which  the  last  mentioned
is  fancied  to  belong  to  the  black,  i.e.,  the  eastern  Tengeris,  it
is  probable  that  all  these  names  originally  meant  one  and  the
same  being.  According  to  tales,  the  urak  dropped  down  from
the  sky  is  a  thick  yellowish-white  liquid.  The  person  who  re¬
ceives  some  of  this  a  first  milk  ”  during  a  thunder-storm  is
deemed  very  fortunate  and  is  believed  to  remain  rich  for  ever.
It  is,  however,  an  extremely  rare  event  for  a  person  to  receive
urak.  When  a  Buriat  perceives  that  he  has  been  the  recipient

and  examines  from  which  Tengeri  the  urak  has  come.  The

FIRE

TT  THERE  did  fire  first  appear  to  me,  what  is  its  purpose
V  V  and  its  power,  who  has  given  it  birth  ?  ”  So  cries  in  a
Yakut  tale  a  hero,  supposed  to  be  the  ancestor  of  this  tribe,
arriving  at  last  at  the  conclusion  that  fire  is  the  son  of  Yryn-
Ai-Tojon  who  sits  on  a  milk-white  throne  to  which  three  flights
of  silver  stairs  lead  up.1  The  belief  that  the  first  fire  came
down  from  heaven  is  very  common  among  the  peoples  of  the
Altaic  race.

Tales  gathered  from  different  peoples  show  the  origin  of
this  belief.  The  Tungus  told  me  that  the  Thunder  bird
brought  down  fire  from  the  sky  to  earth.  A  fire  caused  by
lightning  is  considered  sacred  by  them  and  they  dare  not  put
out  a  forest-fire  which  has  been  lighted  from  Heaven.  Among
the  Yakuts  also  the  fancy  is  most  common  that  the  Thunder
god  Ulu-Tojon  gave  people  the  first  fire.2  The  Buriats  call
the  god  of  Fire,  who  was  also  the  first  sender  of  fire,  Galta-
Ulan-Tengeri  j  he  is  further  the  god  of  heat  and  drought,  who
“  dries  up  the  growing  grass  to  the  roots  and  the  running
rivers  with  their  springs,”  and  the  sender  of  the  lightning,
who  sets  on  fire  all  that  he  strikes.3  The  Altai  Tatars  declare
that  mankind  originally  lived  on  vegetables  and  fruits  and
therefore  neither  needed  fire  nor  missed  it,  but  with  the
change  in  their  manner  of  nourishing  themselves  fire  became
necessary  for  the  preparing  of  food.  It  was  then  that  Ulgen
took  two  stones,  a  white  one  and  a  black  one,  and  struck  them
together  so  that  the  spark  which  flew  from  the  sky  to  the  earth
set  fire  to  the  dry  grass.  From  this  man  learned  to  strike
fire.4  Through  the  mouth  of  the  Buriat  shaman,  fire  declares

itself  to  be  “  the  middle  son  of  the  day-sky,  the  youngest  son
of  the  night-sky.”  6

Certain  other  North  Siberian  peoples  explain  the  origin  of
fire  in  the  same  way.  The  Ostiaks  on  the  Yenisei  give  a  more
detailed  account  of  how  their  ancestors  received  fire  from
lightning.  The  lightning  kindled  a  tree,  and  some  great
shaman  taught  the  people  to  make  use  of  the  fire.  At  first  a
great  fire  was  kept  burning,  from  which  everyone  could  borrow
a  flame.  Later  on,  fire-steel  and  tinder  were  placed  beside  it,
and  fire  was  thus  transferred  to  these  objects.6

In  some  tales  about  the  origin  of  fire  there  figures  also  an
inventor  of  fire,  often  an  animal.  In  Buriat  tales  this  wise
animal  is  the  porcupine,  which  has  also  in  other  ways  already
figured  as  an  inventor.  In  the  beginning,  it  is  told,  neither
gods  nor  men  could  make  fire,  with  one  exception  —  the  Porcu¬
pine,  which  was  then  a  human  being.  One  day  a  crowd  had
gathered  round  the  Porcupine  to  hear  the  secret  of  fire-making.
But  the  young  maidens,  seeing  the  strange  shape  of  Porcupine,
began  to  laugh,  and  this  angered  him  so  much  that  he  decided
to  tell  his  secret  only  to  his  own  wife,  and  even  to  her  only
against  a  promise  of  silence.  But  the  hawk,  whom  the  gods
had  sent  out  to  steal  his  secret,  happened  to  hear  Porcupine
explaining  to  his  wife  where  flintstone  was  to  be  found  and
how  steel  could  be  made,  with  which  two  articles  it  was  easy
to  strike  fire,  and  the  hawk  told  the  secret  to  the  gods.  From
these  men  learned  the  art  of  making  fire.  Later,  the  descen¬
dants  of  Porcupine  became  porcupines.7

In  the  tales  of  the  Altai  Tatars  the  frog  advises  Ulgen,  who
is  in  perplexity  as  to  where  men  could  get  the  necessities  for
striking  fire,  that  “  the  mountains  contain  stones  and  the  birch
tinder.”  8  The  Mongols  say:  “  Iron  is  the  father  of  fire  and
stone  its  mother.”  9  The  above  tales  give  thus  two  different
explanations:  fire  has  come  down  from  heaven  with  the  light¬
ning,  or  its  spark  has  sprung  from  a  stone.  Both  fancies  are
also  met  with  in  Finnish  poems  on  the  origin  of  fire.

FIRE

45i

In  Mongolian  prayers,  in  which  the  birth  of  fire  is  related  in
many  different  ways,  it  is  said  that  fire  came  from  a  tree  or
that  it  was  born  when  in  ancient  times  Heaven  and  Earth
separated.10

Whether  fires  of  different  origin  have  been  considered  to  be
of  unequal  value  does  not  appear  from  the  sources  at  hand.
Besides  fire  caused  by  lightning,  which  is  esteemed  holier  than
other  fires,  wood-fire  or  friction-fire  has  played  an  important
part  in  the  expelling  of  diseases.  The  Yakuts  are  said  to  have
a  custom,  during  an  epidemic,  of  making  a  fire  by  rubbing  two
pieces  of  dry  wood  together,  this  sort  of  fire  being  supposed
to  have  special  protecting  powers.  The  people,  however,  de¬
clare  that  they  have  learned  this  custom  from  the  Russians,
with  whom  epidemic  diseases  are  also  supposed  to  have  come
into  their  country.11  The  Tatars  of  Eastern  Russia  and  the
Chuvash  also  use  friction-fire  as  a  kind  of  purifying  remedy
during  certain  plagues  either  among  people  or  cattle,  and  even
at  other  times  in  the  hot  summer.  On  some  previously  fixed
day  the  old  fire  in  every  home  is  put  out  and  a  great  bonfire
is  lighted  by  friction  outside  the  village.  Over  this  the  people
spring  in  order  to  purify  themselves  and  drive  their  cattle
through  it.  Thus  cleansed,  each  peasant  carries  a  brand  of
“  new  fire  ”  home.12"

  "passage_text": "One  might  suppose  this  custom,  known  also  to  the  Finno-\nUgric  peoples  of  the  Volga,  to  have  been  learned  from  the\nRussians,  as  the  Yakuts  declare.  But  it  appears  from  old\nsources  that  certain  Turco-Tatar  peoples  already  in  ancient\ntimes  used  fire  as  a  magic  purifier.  Byzantine  Chronicles  tell\nthat  when  the  messengers  of  the  Emperor  Justinian  arrived  at\nthe  court  of  the  Turkish  Great  Khan  at  the  springs  of  the\nIrtysh  river,  the  Khan  could  not  receive  them  until  they  had\npassed  between  two  fires.  The  Tatars  still  observed  this  cus¬\ntom  at  the  time  when  the  Russians  paid  taxes  to  them.  All\npeople,  animals,  or  objects  that  in  some  way,  e.g.,  by  touching\nsome  dead  body,  had  become  unclean,  were  thus  purified.13\n\nWhatever  the  origin  of  these  customs  may  have  been,  the\nmystic,  and  more  especially  the  heavenly  birth  of  fire,  its\nwonderful  power  and  the  part  which  it  plays  in  the  domestic\nlife  of  the  most  primitive  peoples,  resulted  in  the  fact  that\nfire  in  general  is  esteemed  holy.  Many  of  the  peoples  of\nCentral  and  Northern  Asia  have  indeed  worshipped  fire.\n\nWhen  worshipping  the  fire  burning  on  the  hearth  the  Mon¬\ngols  call  it  “  Mother  fire.”  According  to  their  ideas  the\nhearth  is  the  sanctuary  of  the  home  and  may  on  no  account\nbe  desecrated.  The  Altaic  tribes,  the  Kirghis,  the  Yakuts  and\nother  Turco-Tatar  peoples  also  worshipped  fire.  The  idea\nthat  fire  must  be  kept  pure  and  adored  as  a  deity  is  common\nto  all  these  and  even  to  other  North  Siberian  peoples.\nNothing  unclean  or  evil-smelling  may  be  thrown  into  it,  and\nnothing  which  could  weaken  its  power  or  dim  its  brightness.\nFor  this  reason  it  is  wrong  to  spit  into  the  fire  or  to  extinguish\nit  with  water.  It  is  also  inadvisable  to  step  over  it  unneces¬\nsarily  or  to  hurt  it  with  any  sharp  weapon.  Plano  Carpini\ntells  how  the  Mongolians  deemed  it  a  sin  to  hew  wood  in  the\nvicinity  of  a  fire,  or  to  take  meat  with  a  knife  from  a  pot\nunder  which  a  fire  was  burning;  still  more  to  put  the  knife\ninto  the  fire.  The  Yakuts  believe  that  the  fire,  which  “  takes\nas  a  gift  the  pine  forest,  consumes  the  damp  wilderness,  and\nspends  the  night  in  dry  trees,”  understands  speech  and  that  it\nis  therefore  not  well  to  scold  or  speak  ill  of  it.14\n\nFire  is  believed  to  need  nourishment  as  well  as  tender  care.\nThe  pious  master  and  mistress  feed  the  fire  on  the  hearth\nevery  time  they  begin  a  meal.  The  first  morsels  of  food,  the\nfirst  spoonful  of  soup,  the  first  cup  of  drink  belong  to  the\nFire  god.  Especially,  at  family  festivals  must  the  fire  on  the\nhearth  be  remembered.  A  fire-sacrifice  is  a  special  part  of\nthe  wedding  rites  with  most  peoples  of  the  Altaic  race.15  The\nChuvash  bride  brings  ashes  or  a  fragment  of  stone  from  her\nparents’  hearth  to  her  new  home,  this  custom  doubtless  express¬\ning  the  thought  that  the  fire  on  the  hearth  is  to  go  in  heritage\n\n'"

In  worshipping  the  fire  in  their  new  home,  a  young  Mongol
couple  sacrifice  to  it  some  yellow  butter  and  a  yellow-headed
sheep.  Yellow  as  well  as  red,  in  sacrifices  to  the  Fire  god,  is
intended  to  imitate  the  hue  of  the  fire  itself.  The  best  sacri¬

degree  explains  the  beliefs  of  the  Mongols.  It  begins  with
the  following  words:  a  Mother  Ut  (Turco-Tatar  word,
“  fire  ”),  Mistress  of  the  fire,  descended  from  the  elms  on
the  tops  of  the  Khangai-Khan  and  the  Burkhatu-Khan  moun¬
tains.  Thou,  who  wast  born  when  Heaven  and  Earth  parted,
who  earnest  forth  from  the  foot-prints  of  Mother  Otygen
(“  Mother  earth  ”),  thou  creation  of  Tengeri-Khan.  Mother
Ut,  thy  father  is  the  hard  steel,  thy  mother  the  flint,  thy
ancestors  the  elm-trees.  Thy  brightness  reaches  the  heavens
and  spreads  over  the  earth.  Fire,  struck  by  the  Heavendweller,  nursed  by  the  Mistress  Uluken.  Goddess  Ut,  we
offer  thee  yellow  butter  and  a  yellow-headed  white  sheep.
Thine  are  this  brave  boy  and  the  beautiful  bride,  the  slender
daughter.  To  thee,  Mother  Ut,  who  art  always  looking  up¬
ward,  we  offer  cups  full  of  wine  and  handfuls  of  fat.  Give
luck  to  the  son  of  the  ruler  (the  bridegroom)  and  the  daugh¬
ter  of  the  ruler  (the  bride)  and  all  the  wedding-folk.  For  this
we  pray.”  18

If  fire  is  treated  in  an  improper  manner  or  left  without  food
it  is  believed  to  take  vengeance  by  sending  a  kind  of  skindisease.  In  the  worst  case  it  burns  the  whole  building.

There  is  no  doubting  the  fact  that  the  peoples  of  the  Altaic
race  worship  fire  in  itself.  u  Mother  ”  and  other  such  words
are  only  names  for  the  fire  itself.  Because  of  its  numerous
flames  the  Altaic  shaman  calls  it  the  “  Thirty-headed  mother,
the  Forty-headed  virgin-mother.”  19  In  the  prayers  of  the

Chuvash  there  appears  beside  the  “  Mother  fire  ”  a  “  Father
fire.”  The  Yakuts  and  the  Buriats  also  worship  both  a  mascu¬
line  and  a  feminine  Fire  god.  The  former  name  them  “  Old
Man  Ulakhany  and  Mistress  Sabaga,”  the  latter  “  Lord  Sakhadai  and  Mistress  Sakhala.”  Poetic  denominations  are  fur¬
ther  “  the  White-bearded  Lord  ”  and  “  White-haired  Lady  ”
of  the  Yakuts.20

Most  Central  and  North  Asian  peoples  speak  in  addition  of
the  Ruler  or  Master  of  fire,  who,  according  to  the  Yakuts,
“  lives  right  in  the  flames.”  21  What  they  imagine  him  to  be
like  appears  from  their  legends  which  tell  that  the  master  of
fire  “  eats  raw  wood,”  that  he  has  “  an  ashen  bed  ”  where  “  the
pillow  is  a  glowing  coal  and  the  coverlet  fine  ashes  ”  and  that
“  the  smoke  is  his  breath.”  22  They  believe,  however,  that  the
Master  of  fire  can  extricate  himself  from  the  fire  and  appear
in  human  shape.  The  Yakuts  say  that  in  a  home  where  he
is  often  remembered  with  sacrifices,  the  Master  of  fire  is  fat
and  thriving,  but  the  Fire  god  of  a  mean  and  parsimonious
household  is  thin  and  withered.23  A  Buriat  legend  relates  how
a  man  who  had  the  power  of  seeing  gods  and  understanding
their  speech  once  encountered  two  Masters  of  fire.  One  of
them,  though  the  god  of  a  poor  house,  was  well  fed  and
dressed,  but  the  other,  the  Fire  master  of  a  well-to-do  house,
looked  very  poor  and  wretched.  The  latter  complained  of
having  to  live  without  food  in  the  power  of  a  mean  master
and  mistress  who  at  times  even  pierced  his  eyes  by  poking  the
fire  with  sharp  irons.  Because  of  this  he  threatened  to  punish
his  master,  and  very  soon  the  grand  house  of  the  rich  man
was  burnt  down  to  the  ground.24

Such  tales,  in  which  the  Fire  gods  of  different  homes  con¬
verse  together  and  tell  each  other  of  their  life,  are  quite  com¬
mon.  In  the  tales  of  the  Ugrian  Ostiaks  every  hearth  has  its
own  “  Fire  maid,”  her  outward  appearance  being  said  to  show
how  the  fire  has  been  treated  in  that  home.25  Doubtless,  these
tales,  some  of  which  have  been  recorded  even  in  Eastern

The\nTungus  of  the  primeval  forests  of  North  Siberia  are  the  most\nbackward  in  this  respect. We  are  therefore  led  to  think  that\nthe  mighty  and  much  adored  Fire  god  of  the  other  peoples\nrelated  to  the  Turks  has  developed  under  foreign  influence  and\nif  we  further  remember  that  the  Indo-Iranian  peoples  from\nancient  times  have  been  zealous  fire-worshippers  and  that  their\nbeliefs  and  customs  coincide  exactly  with  those  of  the  Central\nAsian  tribes,  we  cannot  be  unaware  from  whom  the  peoples\nof  the  Altaic  race  have,  at  least  in  its  more  developed  form,\ninherited  their  fire-w&rship.  Seeing  that  the  Mongols,  who  in\ntheir  own  language  call  the  Fire  god  Galai-Khan  (“  Ruler  of\nthe  fire  ”),  or,  like  their  kinsfolk  the  Buriats,  Gali-Edzin\n(“  Master  of  the  fire  ”),  use  in  their  prayers  the  Turco-Tatar\nname  for  fire,  Ut,  we  can  agree  with  Banzarov  in  his  supposi¬\ntion  that  the  Mongols  learned  to  worship  fire  from  the  Iranians\nthrough  the  Turkish  tribes.29  This  Iranian  influence  can  also\nbe  traced  in  the  fire-worship  of  the  Finno-Ugrians  in  their  idea\nof  fire  as  a  mediator  of  sacrifices,  which  conception  does  not\nseem  originally  to  have  been  general  among  the  Ugrians  or  the\npeoples  of  the  Altaic  race.  Even  at  the  present  day,  side  by\nside  with  the  later  sacrifices  by  fire  we  find  the  older  custom,\nknown  almost  solely  among  the  Northern  peoples,  of  giving\nsacrifices  to  the  gods  untouched."

Following  the  points  of  the  com¬\npass,  the  Central  Asian  peoples  speak  of  four  winds,  which\narise  at  the  “  four  corners  of  the  earth.” 1  A  stranger  idea\nis  that  the  mountains  are  the  home  of  the  wind.  The  Yakuts\nsay  the  winds  “  sleep  ”  on  the  mountains,  whence  they  can  be\ncalled  when  needed  by.  whistling.2  The  Yakuts  and  the\nLamutes  are  said  to  have  avoided  loud  conversation  when  pass¬\ning  by  a  high  mountain,  in  order  that  the  “  Master  ”  of  the\nmountain  might  not  become  incensed  and  send  a  storm  to\nhinder  their  journey.3  The  Goldes  believe  the  winds  to  come\nfrom  caves  in  the  mountains,  where  the  Wind  spirit  holds  them\ncaptive.  A  shaman  can  persuade  this  spirit  either  to  open\nthese  chasms,  or  keep  them  closed,  according  to  whether  wind\nis  needed  or  not.4  The  Mongols  call  storms  “  running-days,”\nas  they  believe  the  Mountain  spirit  runs  from  mountain  to\nmountain  during  these  times.6\n\nElsewhere  than  in  Siberia,  this  belief  is  met  with  in  moun¬\ntainous  districts,  having  probably  its  origin  in  observations  made\nfrom  nature. By\nZada  they  mean  a  short,  intermittent  wind,  occurring  several\ntimes  on  the  same  day.  Often,  it  brings  with  it  rain  or  snow.\nGenerally,  the  Zada  blows  in  the  spring  and  the  autumn.\nZada-weather  may  be  brought  about  by  men  with  the  help  of\na  certain  root,  the  Buriats  believing  that  if  one  of  these  roots\nis  pulled  or  dug  up  out  of  the  ground,  the  weather  will  begin\nto  change  rapidly.  Certain  hunters,  to  whom  this  magic\nmethod  is  known,  make  Zada  assist  them  in  their  hunting.\nCertain  birds,  also,  such  as  hawks  and  swans,  are  said  to  know\nthe  properties  of  the  said  root  and  to  conjure  forth  a  so-called\n“  bird-Zada  ”  when  migrating  southward  in  the  autumn.\nSimilarly,  some  of  the  bigger  inhabitants  of  the  forest,  notably\nthe  deer  and  the  fawn,  use  this  means  for  their  own  benefit\n(a  deer-Zada  ”).  It  may  also  be  brought  about  by  the  help\nof  a  special  red  stone,  called  “  Zadan-ulan-shulun  ”  by  the\nBuriats.  Further,  Zada  is  sometimes  born  when  a  thunderbolt\nfalls  into  the  water,  when  nine  days  of  this  wind  follow.8\n\nThis  peculiar  belief,  met  with  also  among  the  Kalmucks\nand  the  Turkomans,  has  spread  to  the  Yakuts.  They  say  that\namong  the  entrails  of  an  animal  a  stone  is  sometimes  found,\nwhich  possesses  the  magic  power,  if  taken  into  the  yard  on  a\ncalm  summer  day,  of  awakening  a  cold  and  severe  wind.\nThese  stones  the  Yakuts  call  Sata  (=Buriat  Zada).9\n\n\\\n\n■-‘V"

THE  ALTAIC  peoples  early  regarded  the  earth  as  being
an  animated,  conscious  and  comprehending  being.  Even
now  the  Central  Asian  peoples  are  afraid  of  being  punished
if  they  offend  the  earth.  According  to  the  Soyots  the  digging
or  the  wounding  of  the  earth  with  sharp  instruments  is  a  great
sin.1  The  Altai  Tatars  declare  the  pulling  up  of  plants  out
of  the  earth  to  be  as  improper  as  the  pulling  out  of  the  hair  or
beard  of  a  human  being  would  be.2  With  ideas  such  as  these,
it  is  not  to  be  wondered  at  that  the  nomads  did  not  look  with
a  favourable  eye  on  the  pioneers  of  agriculture.  The  agri¬
culturist  Cain,  according  to  the  Semites,  was  also  less  pleasing
to  God  than  the  nomad  Abel.  Similar  ideas  were  held,  fur¬
ther,  by  the  American  Indians  when  the  first  whites  penetrated
into  their  territory.

As  the  producer  of  vegetation,  etc.,  the  earth  was  regarded
as  a  female  being.  As  the  sky,  which  renders  the  earth  fruit¬
ful,  was  called  a  the  Father,”  the  earth,  which  gives  birth,  was
called  “  Mother.”  Already  in  the  Orkhon  stone  inscriptions
it  is  written:  “  The  sky  above  is  our  father,  the  earth  beneath
is  our  mother,  man  is  the  child  of  both.”  In  the  ancient  tales
of  the  Mongols,  the  “  Blue  sky  ”  and  the  “  Brown  earth  ”  are
two  of  the  chief  deities.3  The  Yakuts  believe  that  the  “  Earth
mother,”  also  called  u  Mistress  ”  (An-Darkhan-Khotun  or
An-Alai-Khotun)  acts  both  as  the  producer  of  vegetation  and
as  the  birth-giver  of  children.4  The  Tungus  lay  to  the  merit
of  the  earth,  as  Georgi  points  out,  “  all  that  it  brings  forth.”  6
The  Mongols  say  that  the  sky  gives  life  to  beings,  but  that  the
earth  gives  them  their  form.6  Thus  the  Earth  mother  becomes

also  the  deity  of  child-birth.  As  is  well  known,  the  ancient
peoples  of  Asia  had  this  same  idea.

Concerning  sacrifices  to  the  earth  there  exist  very  old  re¬

and  Tukiu  peoples  sacrificed  to  the  earth.7  Marco  Polo  tells
us  that  the  chief  object  of  Mongolian  worship  was  the  Earth
god  Natigai,  to  whom  milk,  kumiss  and  tea  were  sacrificed.
When  sacrificing,  the  people  prayed  to  this  deity  for  fruitful¬
ness.  The  name  Natigai  mentioned  by  Marco  Polo  is  prob¬
ably  a  corrupted  form  of  the  name  Otukan,  which  appears  in
the  Orkhon  inscriptions  as  meaning  the  country  of  the  old
Turks,  worshipped  by  them  as  a  special  deity.8

CHAPTER  XVIII

THE  “MASTERS”  OF  NATURE

CONNECTED  with  the  animating  of  natural  objects  and
phenomena  among  the  Altaic  race,  there  is  a  conception
that  a  “  soul,”  corresponding  to  the  soul  of  man,  lies  hidden
within  them,  the  name  given  to  this  being  the  same  as  that  for
the  human  soul.  Thus,  the  Altai  Tatars  use  the  word  kut,
which  appears  in  many  Turco-Tatar  languages,  as  signifying
the  soul  of  both  human  beings  and  natural  objects.  Just  as
the  kut  of  the  former  leaves  its  dwelling  for  one  reason  or  an¬
other,  causing  decline  and  sickness,  so  the  earth,  a  tree,  etc.,
wither  when  their  kut  leaves  them.  When  expressing  the  fact
that  a  field  has  lost  its  fertility,  the  people  say:  “  The  ground
has  lost  its  kut”  ( jer  kudun  fardy.)  Similarly,  the  kut  of  a
dwelling-place  may  depart,  taking  with  it  the  feeling  of  home¬
liness.  In  cases  like  this  last,  kut  is  often  translated  as  mean¬
ing  “  happiness,”  “  health,”  “  homeliness,”  etc.1  A  word  with
a  similar  signification  in  the  Turco-Tatar  language  is  stir
(“appearance,”  “beauty,”  “comfort,”  “power,”  “soul”),
used  when  speaking  of  the  human  soul,  the  haunting  spirit  of
the  dead,  the  health  of  cattle,  the  power  of  an  army,  the
nourishing  properties  of  bread,  etc.  Thus,  for  example,  it  is
said  that  “  when  an  army  loses  its  stir,  it  cannot  defeat  its
enemy.”  When  food  has  lost  its  nourishing  power,  it  is  said
that  “  its  stir  has  departed.”  A  soul  of  this  description  is  be¬
lieved  to  animate  and  to  govern  all  the  phenomena  of  nature
and  its  parts,  and  thus  a  conception  arises  that  these  invisible
souls,  to  use  the  words  of  M.  A.  Castren,  are  “  in  respect  of
all  visible  nature,  in  a  position  of  power  resembling  that  of  a
master  towards  his  property.”  2

That  the  metaphor  “  Master  ”  used  by  Castren  is  correct,  is
best  proved  by,  the  names  of  like  signification  given  by  the
peoples  of  the  Altaic  race  to  the  invisible  Nature  gods.
“  Master,”  “  Lord,”  or  “  Ruler  ”  is  expressed  in  the  different
Tatar  dialects  by  the  words  Ea  or  Oja,  in  Chuvash  Hoza,
Yakut  Itshi  and  Buriat  Edzhi.  An  invisible  Ruler  of  this
description  is  to  be  found  in  the  sky  and  its  phenomena,  the
stars,  fire,  land  and  forest,  trees  and  grass,  rivers  and  lakes,
mountains  and  rocks,  the  different  animals,  and  even  in  objects
made  by  man,  buildings,  weapons,  tools,  vessels,  etc.  Espe¬
cially  in  sharp  or  “diving  ”  weapons,  with  which  it  is  easy  to
harm  oneself,  such  as  knives  or  axes,  do  the  Yakuts  see  a  Ruler
(Itshi),  and  similarly  in  objects  capable  of  motion,  such  as  a
spinning-wheel,  or  of  noise,  such  as  a  magic  drum  or  a  musical
instrument.  The  Yakuts  even  speak  of  a  Ruler  in  the  bundle
of  birch-branches  with  which  they  beat  themselves  in  their
baths.3  The  trade  of  blacksmith  is  held  in  great  respect  by
both  Yakuts  and  Buriats,  and  a  Ruler  is  believed  to  dwell  in
all  the  tools  needed  for  this  work.  Troscanskiy  points  out
that  each  blacksmith’s  tool  not  bought  from  the  Russians  has
its  Itshi:  the  anvil  and  striking-hammer  have  theirs  in  common,
the  tongs  and  the  forge  have  each  their  own,  but  the  “  Head-
Itshi  ”  is  in  the  bellows.4  Pripuzov  speaks  of  a  special  tutelary
genius  of  blacksmiths,  called  Kudai-Bakshy  by  the  Yakuts,  and
whose  dwelling-place  is  in  the  underworld.  The  smiths
slaughter  a  brown  cow  in  its  honour  and  anoint  themselves  and
their  tools  with  the  animal’s  blood,  but  the  heart  and  the  liver
they  roast  in  the  forge  and  place  them  on  the  anvil,  where
they  are  beaten  until  nothing  remains  of  them.6

The  Buriats  of  the  Balagan  District  worship  a  deity  of
blacksmiths  called  Boshintoi,  with  nine  sons  and  one  daugh¬
ter,  who  are  said  to  have  taught  the  blacksmith’s  craft  to  men.
In  sacrificing  to  these,  the  smiths  pour  kumiss  and  other  sacri¬
ficial  liquids  on  to  the  glowing  forge.  A  lamb  is  also  some¬
times  slaughtered  to  them.  Iron  images  are  made  of  the

THE  “MASTERS”  OF  NATURE  465

aforesaid  sons  and  the  daughter,  each  with  some  blacksmith’s
tool  in  its  hand,  a  hammer,  tongs,  an  anvil,  bellows,  charcoal,
etc. ;  these  are  called  the  corresponding  “  Masters  ”  of  these
objects.6

The  Master  of  a  musical  instrument  (Khuri  Edzhin)  is  said
by  the  Buriats  to  teach  people  to  become  skilful  musicians.
The  neophyte  has  to  go  out  on  a  moonless  night  to  the  junction
of  three  roads  and  there  sit  down  on  the  skull  of  a  horse  fitted
with  silken  reins.  At  midnight  the  skull  is  said  to  try  to
unseat  its  rider.  Should  the  latter  fall  he  loses  his  life,  but
if,  being  on  his  guard,  he  remains  seated  and  continues  to  play,
he  becomes  a  very  skilful  player.7"

How  close  the  connection  between  these  Masters  and\ntheir  visible  incarnations  has  actually  been,  appears  from  the\nhabit  of  making  images  of  the  Masters  of  the  sun  and  moon\nin  the  shape  of  these  heavenly  bodies.  The  Masters  of  ani¬\nmals  appear  to  men  in  the  shape  of  the  respective  animals.\nThe  Tungus  make  an  image  of  the  reindeer  to  represent  the\nReindeer’s  Master,  and  similarly  certain  North-East  Siberian\ntribes  make  an  image  of  a  fish  to  represent  the  Fish  Master.\nThe  Buriats  speak  of  a  Master-tree,  which  is  recognized  by\nthe  fact  that  its  pith  is  blood-red;  the  tree  is  thus  the  body  of\nthe  Master  dwelling  in  it,  from  which,  as  from  a  human  body,\nthe  blood  can  run.8  This  conception  of  Masters  animating\nnature  is  not  confined  only  to  the  Altaic  race,  but  the  same\nbelief  is  met  with  among  other  Siberian  peoples,  the  Yukagirs,\nthe  Chukchee,  etc.9\n\nThe  anthropomorphism  of  certain  Masters,  such  as  those\nof  dwelling-places,  forests  and  water  would  seem  to  have  been\nhelped  by  the  spirits  of  the  dead,  who  are  said  to  dwell  in\nthese  places.  Often  the  dead  can  be  seen  to  have  become\n\ndirectly  assimilated  into  these  Masters.  Thus  the  Master  of\nthe  Yakut  dwelling-place  (Balagan  Itshita)  sometimes  appears\nin  the  shape  of  former  dwellers  in  the  place.  Middendorff\nsays  that  the  oldest  inhabitant  becomes  after  his  death  the\nMaster  of  a  home.10  The  ancient  Finns  had  the  same  belief.\nThe  Masters  of  forests  and  water  are  also  said  by  the  people\nto  have  originated  in  the  spirits  of  those  lost  or  drowned\nthere.  Buriat  tales  relate  how  a  hunter  was  once  lost  in  the\nforest,  dying  finally  there  of  hunger,  and  how  this  unfor¬\ntunate  man  became  the  Forest  Master.11  Similar  tales  are\ntold  of  the  origin  of  the  Water  Master.  These  tales  make\nclear  why  the  Masters  of  forests  and  water  seek  the  company\nof  men,  and  in  tales  aspire  to  marriage  and  other  ties  with\nthem. THE  “  MASTERS  ”  OF  NATURE

have  two  sons,  one  living  in  the  depths  of  the  primeval  forests
and  giving  valuable  game  to  the  hunter,  such  as  sable  foxes,
blue  foxes,  etc.,  the  other  dwelling  on  heaths  and  giving  brown
foxes,  squirrels,  and  other  animals  of  smaller  value.14

Many  North  Siberian  tribes,  for  whom  hunting  is  an  im¬
portant  means  of  subsistence,  have  a  habit,  at  the  beginning
of  the  autumn  hunting  season,  of  sacrificing  a  part  of  the  first
“  bag  ”  to  the  Forest  Master.  The  Yakuts  are  even  said  to
have  sacrificed  black  bulls  to  Bajanai.  In  sacrificing,  the
Tungus,  the  Yakuts,  and  other  northern  peoples  make  an
image  of  the  Forest  Master,  either  by  carving  human  features
on  the  trunk  of  a  living  tree  or  by  shaping  a  billet  of  wood
roughly  into  a  human-like  shape.  The  mouth  of  the  image
is  smeared  with  the  blood  of  the  sacrifice.  At  each  sacrifice,
a  new  image  is  made.lu

Comparing  the  Yakut  Forest  Master  with  the  corresponding
Russian  spirit,  Serosevskiy  points  out  that  beliefs  brought  by
the  Russians  have  become  connected  with  the  former.  Ac¬
cording  to  his  view,  the  Yakuts  did  not  originally  possess  a
single  spirit,  comprising  all  forests,  but  each  forest  and  thicket,
each  separate  tree  even,  had  its  own  Master.16  It  is  also
related  of  the  Buriats,  that  they  do  not  beg  for  game  from
one  general  Forest  spirit,  but  separately,  from  each  local
Forest  Master.

Among  the  European  Tatars  and  Chuvashes  the  Forest
spirit  has  already  received  a  strictly  defined  appearance,  which
proves  a  more  developed,  more  stable  plane  of  thought.  Here
the  Forest  Master,  corresponding  to  Russian  spirits,  is  chiefly
an  evil  being,  which  is  seldom  worshipped.  In  this  respect
it  differs  from  the  Forest  spirits  of  the  most  northern  primeval
forests  of  Siberia.

The  evil  Shurale  of  the  Volga  Tatars,  which  can  .increase  or
diminish  its  height,  has  exceedingly  large  nipples  on  its
breasts,  and  kills  its  victims  by  tickling  them,  we  have  already
met  with  among  the  Volga  Finns.17

A  corresponding  evil  Forest  spirit  is  the  Chuvash  Obyda,
which  wanders  in  the  forest  as  a  human  being,  but  naked,  long¬
haired,  with  large  nipples,  and  with  feet  turned  in  the  wrong
direction.  Having  caused  a  man  to  lose  his  way,  it  tickles  or
dances  its  victim  to  death.  The  poor  animal  on  whose  back
Obyda  seats  himself  begins  to  run  backward.  According  to
folk-tales  this  spirit  itself  wanders  backwards.  The  evil  Forest
spirit  is  also  called  the  “  Half-human  ”  (Ar-sori)  by  the
Chuvash.18  Possibly  this  name  signifies  a  being  known  also
to  the  Votiaks,  which  has  only  half  of  a  human  body,  viz.,  one
eye,  one  arm,  and  one  leg.  The  Yakuts  speak  also  of  an  evil
being  with  the  same  name,  declaring  it  to  live  in  an  icy  mound
with  a  door-opening  at  the  top.19

Worse  than  Shurale  is  the  Tatar  Albasta,  which  they  believe
to  dwell  in  desert  spaces,  bogs  and  chasms.  This  also  is  human
in  shape  but  takes  on  the  form  of  many  objects  belonging  to
the  forests  or  fields.  It  is  said  to  kill  people  by  suffocating
them.20  The  Kirghis  imagine  Albasta  as  a  great  woman,  with
a  large  head,  and  breasts  reaching  to  the  knee.  She  has  long
and  sharp  nails  on  her  fingers.  The  Kirghis  believe  her  to
attack  chiefly  women  who  are  enceinte,  killing  her  victims  by
suffocation.  They  relate  tales  of  how  a  certain  Kirghis  once
saw  her  rinsing  in  a  brook  the  lungs  of  a  woman,  whom  she

lead  travellers  astray.  The  Mongols  say  that  the  Steppe

In  dreams  it  wanders\nunfettered  by  material  means,  visits  distant  places,  strange\nraces,  passes  through  locked  doors,  and  even  keeps  company\nwith  deceased  companions.  The  Buriats  say  that  what  the\nsoul  has  seen  or  heard  during  its  journeys,  remains  in  its\nmemory,  so  that  a  person,  when  the  soul  has  returned  and\nawakened  its  owner,  can  relate  to  others  the  experiences  of  his\nsoul.  Dreams  are  thus  believed  to  be  actual  truths,  and  for\nthis  reason  are  regarded  as  important.4  But  the  wandering,\nreleased  soul  is  also  an  actual  and  in  some  degree  material\nbeing,  which,  e.g.,  may  be  both  visible  and  audible  to  others.\nBesides  its  human  form  the  soul  of  a  sleeper  can  also  take  on\nthe  form  of  some  animal.  The  Yakuts  say  that  it  wanders\nin  space  as  a  little  bird  or  butterfly.  In  a  Buriat  tale  the  soul\nissued  from  the  mouth  of  a  sleeper  in  the  form  of  a  bee  or  a\nwasp.  Such  soul-animals  must  be  left  strictly  in  peace.5\n\nLike  dreams,  sickness  is  caused  also  by  the  temporary  absence\nof  the  soul  from  the  body.  But  during  sickness,  the  soul  is\nbelieved  to  have  been  driven  out  of  the  body  against  its  will.\n\nOften  a  malicious  spirit,  for  some  reason  or  other,  generally\nto  obtain  a  sacrifice,  carries  off  the  soul.  This  may  happen  in\ndifferent  circumstances,  and  the  soul  is  exposed  to  this  danger,\nespecially  during  its  nocturnal  journeys.  In  the  stillness  and\ndarkness  of  the  night  all  evil  spirits  are  in  motion  and  on  the\nhunt  for  souls.  To  obtain  help,  the  soul  has  to  seek  its\ndeceased  friends  or  other  protecting  spirits.  Thoughtful  souls\ncan  also  help  themselves  by  skilfully  hiding,  e.g.,  in  the  fur  of\nanimals,  in  leafy  trees,  or  in  other  objects.  Should  a  poor\nsoul  be  pursued  too  long  it  loses  itself  in  deep  forests  or  other\nplaces  strange  to  it,  so  that  it  can  no  longer  find  its  way  home.\nWhen  a  soul  is  seized  by  an  evil  spirit,  one  can  sometimes  hear\nits  weeping  and  cries.6\n\nAnother  very  common  belief  is  that  the  soul,  against  its\nwill,  may  be  driven  by  a  shock  from  the  body.  The  Buriats\nbelieve  that  the  homeless  soul  then  remains  for  some  time  at\nthe  place  where  this  misfortune  happens.  Unless  attention  is\ngiven  at  once  to  this  accident,  the  soul  begins  to  wander  about\nand  flies  further  and  further  away,  with  the  result  that  the\nvictim  becomes  more  and  more  seriously  ill  and  in  the  end  dies.\nThe  souls  of  little  children  can  easily  be  driven  away  in  this\nmanner  if  they  are  frightened. Should  one  succeed  in  winning\nthe  soul  back  again  by  special  ceremonies,  the  sick  one  becomes\nwell  again.  Often,  however,  the  soul  may  disappear  without\nits  owner  being  aware  of  the  fact,  and  when  he  or  she  grad¬\nually  begins  to  feel  apathetic,  weak,  and  in  a  decline,  it  is\ntoo  late  to  find  the  soul  again. malicious  and  cunning  spirits.8

A  further  means  of  driving  a  soul  from  its  home,  said  to  be
used  by  the  spirits,  is  a  tickling  of  the  nose,  which  induces
sneezing.  This  appears  from  the  following  Buriat  tale,  which
in  many  other  respects  also  throws  light  on  the  beliefs  of  the
Mongols  regarding  souls.

Once,  a  man  who  had  the  power  of  seeing  spirits  and  talking
with  them  went  on  a  journey.  Meeting  three  spirits  on  the
way  he  went  on  in  their  company.  As  they  journeyed  he
ascertained  that  these  spirits  had  formed  wicked  plans,  intend¬
ing  to  steal  away  the  soul  of  a  rich  man’s  son.  The  man  tried
to  worm  himself  into  the  spirits’  favour  by  promising  to  help
in  the  capture  of  the  soul,  and  thus  obtained  an  opportunity
of  accompanying  them.  This  man,  who  wished  to  play  the
part  of  a  spirit,  could  not,  however,  but  awaken  the  attention
of  the  spirits.  When  they  had  travelled  awhile  together,  the
spirits  asked  in  astonishment:  “  Why  dost  thou  walk  so  that  the
grass  falls  down  and  the  dry  leaves  rustle  under  thy  steps?  ”
The  man  replied  cunningly  that  he  had  died  so  recently  that
he  had  not  yet  learned  to  walk  silently  and  without  leaving  a
track  as  a  spirit  should.  The  spirits  believed  this.  When
they  arrived  at  the  rich  man’s  house,  one  of  the  spirits  placed

itself  at  the  door,  the  other  at  the  chimney,  the  third  went  to
the  unlucky,  son,  and  by  producing  an  irritation  in  his  nose,
caused  him  to  sneeze  violently.  During  the  sneeze  the  son’s
soul  jumped  out  of  his  body  and  tried  to  escape  by  the  door,
but  the  spirit  watching  there  seized  it  at  once  and  held  it  tight,
although  the  soul  wept  bitterly.  The  spirits  then  took  the
captured  soul  away  with  them.  On  the  way  back,  the  man
who  had  joined  the  spirits  asked  them  if  they  had  anything  in
the  world  to  fear.  The  spirits  answered  that  they  were  very
much  afraid  of  thistles  and  thorns.  “  But  what  art  thou
afraid  of?  ”  asked  the  spirits.  “  I,”  said  the  man,  “  am  most
afraid  of  fat  meat.”  The  spirits,  unaware  that  the  man  in¬
tended  to  deceive  them,  travelled  further  and  further.  On
the  way  the  man  begged  to  be  allowed  to  help  by  carrying  the
soul,  which  was  also  granted.  But  just  then  they  happened
to  come  to  a  place  where  thorny  bushes  and  thistles  grew.
The  man  jumped  with  the  soul  in  his  arms  among  the  prickly
bushes,  where  the  spirits  were  afraid  to  come.  Remembering
that  the  man  had  expressed  his  dread  for  fat  meat,  they  began
to  throw  pieces  of  meat  among  the  bushes  to  drive  him  out.
But  the  man,  who  was  very  fond  of  meat,  ate  them  without
danger  to  himself,  on  seeing  which,  the  spirits  realized  that

hurried  back  to  the  rich  man’s  house,  taking  the  soul  with  him
so  that  the  son  recovered.9

Sickness  may  also  be  caused  by  the  soul  injuring  itself  in

bodily  pain  is  often  closely  connected  with  damage  to  the  soul

limp;  should  the  soul  catch  cold,  its  owner  begins  to  shiver,
etc.,  etc.  Similar  ideas  are  met  with  among  the  Tungus,  and
are  reflected  in  the  general  belief  that  everything  done  to  the
image  of  a  person  affects  the  person  himself.  The  word
“  soul  n  originally  meant  both  shadow  and  image.10

dead  dwell,  and  where  in  the  place  of  the  sun  and  moon,  only

reflection  of  the  Yenisei  District.  The  underground  Yenisei
is  said  however  to  flow  in  the  opposite  direction.

The  above  seven  grottoes  are  obviously  closely  connected
with  the  seven  or  nine  underground  storeys,  which  according
to  the  Altai  Tatars  and  others  are  situated  horizontally  under
the  “  middle  place  ”  or  the  earth  and  correspond  to  a  similar
number  of  planes  of  Heaven  above.9  The  Central  Asian
people  generally  regard  the  underworld  as  populated  by  evil
beings,  ruled  over  by  the  stern  Erlik-Khan,  who  is  said  to  sit
on  his  black  throne,  surrounded  by  a  court  consisting  of  evil
spirits.  At  the  command  of  their  lord  these  spirits  often  make
excursions,  more  especially  in  the  night-time,  to  the  world  of
the  living,  where  they  seize  some  poor  soul  and  carry  it  off
with  them  to  their  home.  Extremely  common  is  also  the  idea
that  this  ruler  over  the  dead  has  power  only  over  those  who
were  wicked  in  this  life.  Those  mortals  again,  who  have  done
more  good  than  evil,  are  taken  after  death  to  the  heavenly
dwelling-places.10  The  path  to  both  the  underground  dwell¬
ings  and  those  above  is  believed  to  go  through  a  hole  in  the
middle  of  each  plane,  and  according  to  this  idea  the  Ostiaks
call  the  seven-storeyed  sky  “  seven-holed,”  11  the  Chukchee  ex¬
plaining  that  each  hole  is  perpendicularly  under  the  North
Star.12  As  the  hole  leading  to  the  underworld,  which  is  often
used  by  the  shaman,  is,  of  course,  also  in  the  centre  of  the
earth,  one  may  often  see  among  his  magic  things  a  disc  repre¬
senting  the  earth,  in  the  midst  of  which  is  a  round  hole.  In
travelling  to  the  heavens,  the  Altai  shamans  use  also  a  worldtree  furnished  with  divisions,  the  Dolgans  explaining  that  the

pay  visits  to  one  another,  drink  spirits  and  get  intoxicated.15

which  live  there  in  families  and,  like  the  people  of  the  earth,
exist  by  fishing  and  hunting.  Often,  however,  the  game  they
seek  is  human  souls,  which  they  carry  with  them  to  some  storey
of  the  sky,  whence  only  a  clever  shaman  can  save  them.16

How  far  these  ideas  of  Heaven  as  the  dwelling-place  of  the
dead  have  originated  among  the  above  peoples,  is  hard  to

or  descend  underground.  According  to  the  Chukchee  the

The  most  original  views  do  not  regard  the  realm  of  the  dead

sins  committed  during  life.  Such  Altaic  peoples  as  have  come
under  the  influence  of  alien  and  more  highly  developed  teach¬
ings,  form  exceptions  in  this  respect.

knives  while  drunk.  The  inhabitants  of  the  seventh  room
brought  on  their  punishments  by  teasing  mad  dogs  in  life  and
being  bitten  by  them.  In  the  eighth  room  were  married
people  who  had  quarrelled  through  their  lives  and  looked  only

thrown  into  a  dark  pit,  where  it  is  tormented  by,  terrible  cold,

It  was  then  that  I  began  to\nshamanize,  recovering  immediately.  Even  now,  if  I  refrain\nfrom  shamanizing  for  a  long  time,  I  become  indisposed  and\n\nfall  ill.”  The  spirit,  which  appears  to  the  chosen,  is  said  to\nbe  the  soul  of  a  dead  shaman,  and  is  called  Amagat  by  the\nYakuts. member  of  a  family  or  clan  that  has  earlier  contained  shamans
can  become  a  shaman.  The  calling  goes  thus  in  inheritance.
But  individuals  with  shamanic  talents  do  not  appear  in  every
generation.  The  Tungus  at  the  Yenisei  explained  to  the
author,  that  if  a  shaman  is  buried  in  the  earth  and  not  on  an
erection  in  the  air,  the  “  loom  ”  ( Cavia  lumma ,  a  soul-bird  of
the  shaman)  of  the  deceased  will  return  no  more  to  his  family.
Often  the  “  loom  ”  appears  first  after  a  longer  period.  It  is
held  that  this  “  loom,”  the  reappearance  of  which  in  the  family
is  regarded  as  a  great  honour,  is  the  wandering  soul  of  the
deceased  shaman.  When  the  cc  loom  ”  has  appeared  to  anyone,
that  is  to  say,  when  shamanic  gifts  become  apparent  in  any
individual,  a  wooden  image  is  made  of  the  bird  and  a  reindeer
sacrificed  to  it.  This  “  loom  ”  becomes  the  protective  spirit  of
the  new  shaman.  Here  we  meet  with  a  conception,  peculiar  to
shamanism,  that  besides  the  ordinary  souls  common  to  all  men,
the  shaman  possesses  a  special  shaman-soul,  lacking  to  others.
From  the  beliefs  connected  with  death  it  appears  that  this
shaman-soul  is  immortal  in  a  much  higher  degree  than  other
souls.  For  this  reason,  special  ceremonies  are  necessary  at  the
burial  of  a  shaman.  Not  even  a  chief,  however  many  herds
of  reindeer  he  possesses,  can  compare  in  matters  of  religion
with  the  poorest  shaman,  who,  on  account  of  his  a  loom  ”  is
honoured  and  feared  already  during  his  life,  but  still  more
after  his  death.

The  Yakuts  sometimes  call  the  shaman-soul  sur>  which  in
other  Turkish  languages  signifies  soul  in  general.  Its  seat  is
said  to  be  in  the  head  of  the  shaman.  It  is  related  in  a  tale,
how  a  great  shaman  received  his  head  “  in  the  Heaven  of

Manariks  ”  ( maridrik ,  “  nervy,”  “  insane  ”5  mandril  y  u  to  lose
one’s  sense”).4  According  to  the  Buriats,  a  person  who  has
been  scared  out  of  his  wits  by  violent  thunder  receives  a  special
shamanic  talent.5  The  Yakuts  say  such  persons  have  received
stir  from  Ulu-Tojon,  the  god  of  thunder.6

Besides  male  shamans,  female  shamans  are  also  met  with,
though  these  can  in  no  way  be  compared  with  the  male  in
power  and  importance.  Generally,  they  are  called  also  by  a
different  name  from  the  male  shamans  (Yakut,  Altai-Tatar,
Buriat,  Mongol,  “  udagan,”  “  utagan,”  etc.).  There  have
been,  however,  especially  among  the  Buriats,  many  famous
female  shamans,  worshipped  after  their  death  by  their  rela¬
tives.  Each  place,  each  family,  and  each  tribe  has,  according
to  the  Buriats,  its  individual  Zajans  or  protective  spirits  of
deceased  shamans,  both  male  and  female,  who  after  death
were  buried  on  adjoining  heights,  where  their  images  ( ongon )
were  also  placed.  At  times  even  ordinary  Buriat  men  or
women  become  Zajans  after  death,  and  special  ceremonies  are
gone  through  in  their  honour  j  but  these  are  said  to  become
Zajans  “  by  the  power  of  their  shamanic  origin  and  the  pro¬
tective  powers  springing  therefrom  for  the  survivors.”  7

It  is  extremely  important  for  each  person  to  remember  his
shamanic  origin,  called  Utkha  by  the  Buriats.  Each  family,
or  clan,  has  its  own  Utkha,  which  imposes  special  duties  on  its
members.  It  is  said  of  the  family  Sartul,  which  dwells  east
of  the  Baikal,  “  that  they  do  not  devour  the  blood  of  animals,

shaman  animals.”  An  animal  or  a  bird,  regarded  as  pro¬

their  opinion,  each  shaman  has  his  own  protectors,  some  a
snake,  some  a  vulture,  some  a  frog,  etc.8

Closely  connected  with  the  family  Utkha  are  also  the  house¬
hold  spirits  or  household  Ongons.  These  household  spirits,
worshipped  by  the  members  of  the  family  and  preserved  in  the

tent,  generally  consist  of  a  sheepskin  on  which  tinplate  figures
of  human  beings  and  other  things  are  fastened,  or  these  figures
may  also  be  painted  on  the  sheepskin  or  on  a  cloth.  These
Ongons  are  inherited  with  the  tales  and  traditions  attached  to
them.  Among  the  Buriats  of  the  Khangin  clan  one  may  see
an  Ongon,  called  Borto,  in  nearly  every  dwelling,  and  of  this
it  is  said  that  the  forefather  of  the  clan,  Khorton,  a  great
shaman,  had  borne  it  on  his  back  from  Mongolia.  Prayers

Sen-Serel  bird  (sen,  a  Siberian  swan),  Utkha  of  the  Serel  Mon¬

  "passage_text": "Animals,  and  especially  birds,  which  play  some  part  in\nshamanic  beliefs,  may  not  be  killed  or  even  molested,  other¬\nwise  sickness  or  some  other  misfortune  will  result.  Among\nthe  Tungus,  as  among  many  other  North  Siberian  peoples,\ncertain  birds,  water-birds  in  particular,  such  as  the  loom,  sea¬\ngull,  swan,  crane,  etc.,  are  sacred.  One  may  not  even  point\na  finger  at  them.  Further,  one  tries  to  avoid  mentioning  their\nnames.  A  Buriat  tale  tells  how  a  swan,  whose  nest  had  been\ndamaged,  flew  with  a  burning  brand  in  its  beak  and  dropped\nit  on  a  house,  so  that  the  whole  village  was  burnt  up.  Among\nthe  Yakuts  and  Buriats,  the  eagle  is  treated  with  extraordinary\nrespect  and  dread.  The  Yakuts  say  that  it  is  not  a  sign  of\ngood  luck  if  an  eagle  flies  over  a  village.  The  Buriats  round\nthe  Baikal  call  the  eagle  “  Olkhon  island’s  master  ”  or  “  the\nson  of  the  god  living  on  Olkhon  island.”  Often  the  great\nshamanic  powers  of  the  eagle  are  praised,  some  myths  calling\nit  “  the  first  shaman.”  There  are  countless  tales  of  misfor¬\ntunes  which  befell  people  who  ill-treated  this  bird.  A  man\nonce  saw  how  an  eagle  plucked  at  the  carcase  of  his  cow,  which\nhad  been  killed  on  the  steppes  by  a  wolf.  The  man  became\nangry  and  started  to  drive  away  the  bird  with  a  bough.  Shortly\nafterwards  he  became  seriously  ill,  and  received  the  knowledge\nin  a  dream  that  his  illness  had  been  caused  by  his  treatment\nof  the  eagle.  The  Buriats  throw  milk  or  kumiss  into  the  air\n\n♦\n\neach  time  a  swan  or  an  eagle  flies  over  their  village.10  If  a\nYakut  finds  a  dead  eagle  or  the  skeleton  of  one,  he  regards  it\nas  his  duty  to  bury  the  bird  on  a  special  erection  of  wood,  or\nin  a  tree,  in  the  manner  in  which  human  beings,  particularly\nshamans,  were  earlier  buried.  While  doing  this,  he  utters\nthe  following  words:  “Lift  up  thyself,  fly  to  thy  birthplace,\ncome  not  down  on  the  earth.  Thy  bones  of  copper  I  have\nplaced  on  the  grave-erection,  thy  bones  of  silver  have  I  lifted\nup.”  11  With  similar  respect  do  the  Tungus  also  treat  shaman\nanimals.\n\nIt  is  not  always  easy  to  define  the  difference  between  shaman\nanimals  and  such  as  are  regarded  as  the  forefather  or  mother\nof  a  clan  or  a  people.  The  myths  of  the  Altaic  peoples  tell\nalso  of  the  latter.  Among  the  Buriats  tales  have  been  recorded\nof  three  swans  which  once  came  down  from  the  sky  to  bathe\nin  a  lake.  They  took  off  their  swan-garments  and  became\nchanged  into  three  fair  women.  A  hunter,  who  had  hidden\nhimself  on  the  shore,  took  one  of  these  swan-garments  and\nhid  it.  When  the  swan-women  had  bathed  for  a  time,  they\nhurried  to  the  shore  to  clothe  themselves  again,  and  when  the\nothers  were  ready  to  fly  away  the  one  who  had  lost  her  gar¬\nment  had  to  remain  behind  on  the  earth.  The  hunter  mar¬\nried  her  later  and  she  bore  him  eleven  sons  and  six  daughters.\nOnce,  after  a  long  time,  the  wife  remembered  her  former\ngarment  and  inquired  of  her  husband  where  he  had  left  it.\nThe  man  was  so  certain  that  she  would  not  now  leave  him  and\nher  children  that  he  decided  to  return  the  wonderful  garment\nto  her.  With  his  consent,  the  woman  then  put  it  on  to  see\nhow  she  would  look  in  it.  But  no  sooner  had  she  got  the\nswan-garment  on,  than  she  flew  up  through  the  smoke-hole\nand,  floating  high  above  her  home,  shouted  to  those  left  be¬\nhind:  “Ye  are  earthly  beings  and  remain  on  the  earth,  I  am\nfrom  Heaven  and  fly  back  to  my  home.”  She  added:  “  Each\nspring  and  autumn,  when  the  swans  fly  northward  and  return,\nye  must  carry  out  certain  ceremonies  in  my  honour.”  She  then\n\nblessed  her  children,  hoping  that  they  would  live  happily  on\nthe  earth,  and  disappeared  in  the  sky.  It  is  further  related\nhow  one  of  the  swan-woman’s  daughters  tried  to  hinder  her\nmother  from  flying  by  grasping  her  feet,  which,  as  the  daugh¬\nter  had  dirty  hands,  became  black  and  have  remained  so  to\nthis  day.12"
