  "passage_text": "Tales  related  to  the  above,  are  met  with  also  in  Europe,
having  probably  come  there  from  Asia,  but  it  should  be  noted
that  among  the  Buriats,  certain  ceremonies  are  connected  with
this  belief.  Generally  speaking,  tales  of  the  supernatural
origin  of  certain  tribes  and  clans  are  not  scarce  among  the
Altaic  peoples.  According  to  the  notes  made  by  Potanin  in
the  Altai  territory  the  forefather  of  the  Bersit  clan  was  a  wolf,
which  lived  in  the  forest  near  a  lake  together  with  a  deer
( Cervus  elaphus ).  Of  these  a  son  was  born  who  became  the
ancestor  of  the  said  clan.13  Regarding  the  origin  of  the  Mon¬
gols  there  are  several  myths.  In  some  it  is  related  that  their
ancestor  was  a  dog,  or  that  he  was  given  birth  to  by  a  tree  and
nourished  by  a  dog.  It  is  also  related  how  two  Khans  warred
together  and  destroyed  all  the  people  until  only  one  woman
was  left.  This  last  woman  met  with  a  bull  by  whom  she  had
two  children.  From  these  the  whole  race  of  the  Mongols  was
born.  A  variant  of  this  tale  describes  how  a  woman  gave
birth  to  the  son  of  a  bull,  the  child  walking  on  all  fours.
When  the  forefeet  had  been  cut  off  this  ancestor  of  the  Mon¬
gols  began  to  live  like  a  human  being,  and  ate  meat  in  the
place  of  grass.14  The  Kirghis  believe  themselves  to  be  de¬
rived  from  a  wild  boar,  and  for  this  reason  do  not  eat  pork.
According  to  one  tale  Jenghiz  Khan’s  son  lived  at  Gobi  to¬
gether  with  a  wild  boar,  the  latter  bearing  him  several  sons.
Thus  arose  a  great  people,  i.e.,  the  Kirghis.15

Several  myths  have  been  recorded  among  the  Buriats  re¬
garding  their  ancestor  Bukha-Nojon  (“  Bull  Lord  ”).  South
of  the  Baikal  lived  a  king,  Taizhi-Khan,  who  had  a  mottled
bull.  This,  an  exceptionally  large  and  powerful  animal,  once

said  in  its  pride:  “Whoever  in  the  world  dares  to  measure
his  strength  against  mine,  may  come  and  try.”  Then  Bukha-
Nojon  was  changed  to  a  blue-grey  bull  and  went  to  the  king¬
dom  of  Taizhi-Khan  to  wrestle  with  the  mottled  bull.  Dur¬
ing  the  day-time  he  wrestled  as  a  bull,  but  in  the  night  he
kept  company  as  a  fair  youth  with  Taizhi-Khan Js  daughter.
After  a  time  the  latter  became  enceinte  and  told  Bukha-Nojon
that  she  would  soon  give  birth  to  a  child.  Then  Bukha-
Nojon  ripped  the  child  from  her  stomach  and  cast  it  with  his
horns  over  the  Baikal.  After  he  had  vanquished  the  mottled
bull,  Bukha-Nojon  swam  over  the  lake,  found  the  child  on
the  shore  and  began  to  nourish  it.  A  shaman  woman  found
the  child  later  sucking  at  a  blue-grey  bull,  adopted  it  and
called  it  Bulagat.  This  Bulagat,  who  had  two  sons,  the  an¬
cestors  of  two  clans,  Khori  and  Buriat,  of  which  the  shamans
sing  that  they  are  derived  from  “  the  resting-place  of  the
blue-grey  bull,”  found  a  playmate  on  the  shore  of  the  Baikal,
Ekerit,  also  an  ancestor,  of  whom  it  is  said  that  “  the  burbot
( Lota  lota )  was  his  father,  the  shore  his  mother.” 16

According  to  another  myth,  the  forefathers  of  the  Buriats
came  down  from  Heaven  and  were  nourished  by  a  wild  boar.
It  is  further  related  that  Khurmusta’s  daughter,  who  became
enceinte  from  some  unknown  cause,  came  down  to  the  earth  in
the  form  of  a  goat  and  gave  birth  to  two  sons  and  a  daughter.17

What  appear  to  be  relics  of  totemism  were  found  in  Siberia
among  the  Yakuts  in  the  eighteenth  century.  Strahlenberg
says :  “  Otherwise,  each  family  regards  a  particular  creature
as  sacred,  such  as  the  swan,  the  goose,  the  raven,  etc.,  and  such
animals  as  are  held  sacred  by  a  family  are  not  eaten  among
its  members,  though  others  are  free  to  do  so.”  18  Similarly,  in
an  appendix  “  Concerning  the  Yakuts,”  which  is  said  to  be  taken
from  “  two  old  manuscripts  ”  and  which  appeared  in  a  Russian
book  published  in  1844,  A  Journey  to  Yakutsk ,  each  clan  has
its  own  particular  protector  or  mediator,  represented  by  an
image  of  a  stallion  with  white  lips,  a  raven,  a  swan,  etc.

These  animals  were  never  used  as  food.19  According  to  a
third  source  such  animals  are  the  eagle  and  the  crane.20

Probably;  the  family-names  derived  from  the  animal  king¬
dom  and  the  ownership-marks  of  certain  North  Siberian
peoples  denoting  animals,  are  connected  with  these  totemistic
ideas.  But  during  the  centuries  and  thousands  of  years  of
their  use,  the  original  significance  of  these  matters  has  faded
from  the  consciousness  of  the  people.

Certain  investigators  have  attempted  to  trace  the  rise  of
totemism  from  an  old  custom,  known  over  nearly  the  whole
world,  of  giving  names  taken  from  nature  to  children,  often
from  the  animal  kingdom.  The  most  northern  peoples  of
Siberia  give  their  children  even  today  names  taken  from  some
object  which,  at  the  moment  when  the  soul  was  believed  to
have  taken  possession  of  the  child,  awakened  the  interest  of
the  mother  or  those  around  her.  The  Yenisei  Ostiaks  give
their  children  the  name  of  the  object  “on  which  the  shadow
( ulvei )  of  the  child  fell  first.”  21"
}

  "passage_text": "GEOGRAPHICAL POSITION OF THE FINNS 5\n\ndivisions of the Finns: the Vepsas or Northern Cudes, the\nVotes (Vatjalaiset) or Southern Cudes, and the Esthonians\n(Virolaiset). The Northern Cudes occupy the north-west of\nthe Bielozersk and the west of the Tikhvinsk districts, all\nthe upper basin of the Ojat, and eastwards into Vitegorsk.\nSjogren estimated their number at fully 21,000, though\nformerly they were more numerous. From documentary\nand other evidence there is reason to believe, that, in the\neleventh century, Finns, known to the Russian chronicler\nas Em, Yem, lived on the east side of Lake Onega, where\nabundant traces of their presence have been left in local\nnames. There is written testimony to the effect that as late\nas the middle of the thirteenth century Cudes (Vepsas) and\nKarelians lived on the north-east of Lake Kubinsk, in the\ngovernment of Vologda. And in the middle of the fourteenth century a Russian monk, who founded a monastery\nat the south-east corner of Lake Onega, mentions that\nCudes and Lapps lived in the vicinity of the lake.?\n\nIt is generally believed that the Vepsas, from their\nname and geographical position, represent the Ves of the\nRussian chronicle, a people that dwelt near Lake Bielozero.\nThis seems probable enough, but since the time of Fraehn’s\nedition of Ibn Fozlan they are also identified with the\nVisu of Arab travellers of the tenth and eleventh centuries.\nFraehn, however, was misled by the similarity of the names\nVes, Visu (Isu, Isui). Ibn Fozlan merely says that the\nVisu lived at a distance of three months’ journey from\nBolgari, but Abu el Kassim, who visited Bolgari later,\nrelates that he had been informed by the king of the\nBolgars that a people called Visu lived at a distance of\nthree months’ journey to the orth of his country, and that\n\n1 Sjgren, pp. 469, 292, 507, 509.\n\nwith them the night in summer did not last even an hour\nHe adds that the Visu are adjacent to the country of the\nYura (Ugra, Ugrians), which is bounded by the Sea ot\nDarkness.! The only possible route to the north from\nBolgani lay up the Kama, the Kolva, the ViSerka, through\nLake Cusovoe to the head of the Vogulka, where a short\nportage (volok) of about four and a half miles brings the\ntraveller to the Voldsnitsa, a navigable tributary of the\nPetéra. Descending the river, he would at length reach\nthe Usa, about lat. 66° N. As at lat. 66° 19’ the night at\nthe summer solstice is just about an hour long, the position\nof the Usa suits to a nicety the position of the Isu or\nVisu, according to the indications of Abu el Kassim. It\nmay also be observed that up the Usa lies the regular route\nto Obdorsk, at the mouth of the Ob, then in the hands\nof the Yura or Ugrians of whom he makes mention. In\nall probability, then, the Isu or Visu were the same as the\nPetérans of Nestor and early Russian chroniclers, and are\nnow represented by the Zirians.\n\nThe Votes are now restricted to about thirty parishes in\nthe north-west of Ingria. They are first mentioned by\nNestor in 1069, and probably occupied the whole of Ingna\ntill partly dispossessed by Karelians from Finland and by\nRussians from the south. The Esthonians call themselves\n‘Country people’ (ma més, ma rakvas), and are found in\nEsthonia (Vivo) and the north of Livland nearly as far\nsouth as the river Salis, as well as in the islands of Dago\nand Oesel. The old Finnish inhabitants of West Livland\nand North Kurland have been almost entirely absorbed by\nthe Letts, and their language is almost extinct, save along a\nnarrow fringe of coast between Domesness and Lyserort.\n\n1 Abou el Cassim, pp. 8r, 82."
}

  "passage_text": "GEOGRAPHICAL POSITION OF THE FINNS 7\n\nGEOGRAPHICAL POSITION OF THE EASTERN FINNS.\n\nFrom a linguistic point of view the Mordvins (Mordod)\nstand nearest to the Western Finns. Though now in a\nhighly dispersed condition they occupy a considerable area\nin the governments of Nizegorod, Kazdn, Tambov, Penza,\nSimbirsk, and Sardtov on the west side of the Volga, and\nof Ufa and Orenburg on the east side. They are divided\ninto two great divisions, the Mok&a and the Erza, who\npredominate numerically. The latter occupy the south\npart of Nizegorod and Simbirsk, and extend into the governments of Tambov and Penza. They also constitute the\nprincipal contingent of the Mordvin population in the\nsteppes beyond the Volga in the governments of Samara,\nUfa, and Orenburg. The country on the west side of the\nVolga, where the Mordvins dwell, is still partly covered\nwith huge forests, largely composed of deciduous trees, such\nas the oak, lime, maple, ash, etc.; and as late as the\nseventeenth century elks were hunted in the forest and\nbeavers tenanted the streams.!\n\nFrom an examination of the place-names Professor\nSmimov has arrived at the conclusion that the original\nterritory of the Mordvins was bounded on the north by the\nVolga, on the west by the Oka, the MokSa, and the Tsna,\non the east by the Sura, while southwards they once\noccupied the governments of Orél, Kursk, and Vordénez.?\nUnder the form ‘Mordens’ the Mordvin name first\nappears about the middle of the sixth century in a catalogue,\ngiven by Jordanes, of the peoples subjugated by Ermanaric,\nking of the Goths, about two hundred years earlier.\nThough their geographical position is in no way defined, it\n\n4 Smirnov, (4) pp. 117, 118. 3 Jbsd. (4) p. 15; (x) p. 12.\n\nseems likely that at any rate as early as the fourth century\nthe Mordvins lived west of the Volga, though perhaps a\nlittle further south than at present. A proof that they\nhave long been settled in the vicinity of the Volga is the\nfact that they call it the Rav, evidently the same as the\nRha of Ptolemy.\n\nThe Ceremis call themselves Mari, ‘people.’ According\nto Zolotnitski the word Ceremis is from the Turkish\nCirmes, ‘warlike,’ which corresponds formally with the\nCuva’ Syarmis, the term this people applies to the Ceremis.\nThis name, under the form Tsarmis, is believed to occur\nfor the first time in a letter addressed by Joseph, prince of\nthe Khozars, to the vezir of the Khalif Abdurrahman 11. in\nthe year 960. No details, however, are given; they are\nmerely mentioned in a list of tributary peoples living\nalong the Volga! For the most part they live on the\nleft or low bank of the Volga, with the Vetluga as their\nwestern boundary; along the Volga they extend nearly to\nKazan, then northwards to the Vidtka in the neighbourhood of Urzum, and thence westwards to the Vetluga.\nThe Hill Ceremis, so called from living on the high or right\nbank of the Volga, are confined to the south-west corner\nof the government of Kazan. Besides these there are\nsmall isolated groups on the Kama in the districts of\nElabuga and Sarapul; also in the government of Perm, as\nwell as on the Biélaya and its tributaries. Altogether they\nare believed to number over 242,000 souls. Their name\nfor the Volga is the Yul.\n\nProfessor Smirnov, basing himself on the chronicle of\nNestor, places the original seat of the Ceremis on the Okd,\nand brings them as far southwards as Spask (Riazan), and\n\n1 Semenov, p. 1."
}

Within this area he finds a number of\nplace-names ending in -mar, ‘people,’ -nur, ‘field,’ -iner,\n-ener, ‘tavine, river,’ and Aust, which he ascribes to this\npeople. From this position he supposes they were\ngradually pushed north by the Mordvins, who lay immediately to the south of them; for an examination of the\nplace-names shows that the Ceremis formerly covered\nalmost the whole of the existing government of Kostroma\nnorth of the Volga at a time when their eastern boundary\nwas the Vetluga. In the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries\nsome of the Geremis probably still lived in the northern\npart of the government of Kostroma, but from the fourteenth century they began to be dislodged by the in-\ncoming Russians. The new country finally settled by the\nis was not a desert. Before their arrival all larger\nrivers had received names which are not Ceremisian.?\n\nThe Votiaks, who call themselves Ud-murt, or Urt-murt,\noccupy a large tract of county east of the Vidtka, in\nthe upper basin of the river Ceptsa as far west as the\nKosa, and a large portion of the south-east corner of the\ngovernment of Vidtka. They speak a language\nmutually intelligible, and both call themselves Xoms.\nBut Permian is more strictly applied to those settled on\nthe right bank of the Upper Kama, in the districts of\nCérdin and Solikamsk, called Great Perm collectively,\nbut by the natives Kom-mu, or ‘land of the Komi.’\nZirlans are met with at various points on the upper course\nof the Vitegda, with its tributaries as far west as Ust-Vim,\nformerly known as Old Perm ; in a north-westerly direction\non the upper course of the Mezen and its tributary the\nVaSka ; also on the [Sma and the Petéra as far north as\nUst-I8ma. On the west side\nthere are copper-bearing beds of sedimentary origin, and\nsometimes the metal is found in a native state. In insignificant quantities oxide of tin with galena is also found\nthere, but there is no tin or silver in the Urals. Iron is\nworked near Murom and in the neighbourhood of Petrozavodsk, on the west side of Lake Onega.\n\nTHE PHYSICAL AND MENTAL CHARACTERISTICS\nOF THE FINNS.\n\nHaving briefly described in general outlines the geographical distribution of the East and West Finns now\nand in the past, so far as it can be inferred from placenames, we have now to pass on to their physical and\nmental characteristics.\n\nProfessor Retsius defines the Tavastland or Hame type\nas follows :—\n\n‘In physique it is strong, solid, broad-shouldered ; in\ngeneral, thickset and plump, with coarse limbs ; of medium\nheight, though individuals are found above and below the\naverage.\n\n‘The flesh is firm, generally without disposition to fat\nor to leanness ; the muscular system is strong.\n\nI B\n\n‘The skin is white, but often greyish inclining to olive\ngrey; it is rarely as clear and pure with a transparent rosy\nhue as among blonde Teutons (Scandinavians and English).\n\n‘The head is usually large, short and broad (brachycephalous), but not particularly high, often rather square\nwith well-developed ‘udera parietalia.\n\n‘The face is large, long, but above all comparatively\nbroad both in the frontal region and still more so in those\nof the zygomatic arch and the jaws; the lower jaw is\nstrongly developed.\n\n‘The nose is small, rather wide, obtuse, or more often\nwith a small point, just a little refroussé; the nostrils are\nrather wide. The eyebrows\nare feebly developed and light.\n\n‘The expression is rather morose and little sympathetic.\n\n‘The hair on the crown is blonde, oftener flaxen, otherwise ash-grey ; in women it is often yellow or yellowish-red\nat the tips, straight, never curly, and very silky. He is suspicious and does not appear to be\nexempt from jealousy or vindictiveness; he cherishes a\ngrudge for a long time, and postpones his revenge till the\npropitious moment arrives; hence grave, premeditated\ncrimes are not altogether uncommon. In a high degree\nhe is a fatalist; he is content with very little, enduring\nsuffering and privation with admirable fortitude and\npatience. Though slow by nature he is very assiduous at\nhis work, and with inborn tenacity never gives in so long\nas he sees a possibility of gaining his point. He is inclined\nto assist a neighbour, and is hospitable when civilly treated.\nTaken all in all he is an honest fellow. He is absolutely\nfaithful, even if not lavish in his expressions of tenderness\nand goodwill, preferring to translate them into deeds rather\nthan into words and demonstrations; in general he never\nexpresses himself in the superlative, or in a positive and\nperemptory manner, but with diplomatic prudence and\nreserve. As regards his other psychical qualities he is not\nhasty, but sure in his judgment ; he goes to the root of the\nmatter slowly but thoroughly. He is neither musical nor\npoetical, at least he is not creative in these directions, and\nhe is seldom heard to sing.\n\n‘Thus in spite of its sterling merits the Hame type does\nnot as a rule possess an exterior either beautiful or attractive ; at least one seldom meets persons that answer to\nour ideas of beauty. This remark applies not only to men,\nbut also to women ; the latter have generally less angular and\nmore rounded features, but beauties are extremely rare ; at\n\nleast we have not found a single woman that merited this\nname among the thousands that we have seen. If then\nthis Hame race is not distinguished by external beauty, it\npossesses at any rate, owing to its physical and moral\nsolidity, its tenacity and meditative nature, the traits of\ncharacter that make it a strong race that can hold its own\nin the struggle for existence. It is also on the whole\nfertile ; from the point of view of sexual morality it is not,\nhowever, commendable, but rather the contrary.\n\n‘The Karelian type is distinguished as follows :—\n\n‘The physique is less strong than that of the Hame; it\nis less broad-shouldered, less thickset and plump, with less\npowerful limbs, but more slender, and the proportions more\ncomely. As a rule it exceeds the average height, and often\npresents individuals of considerable stature.\n\n‘The flesh is tolerably firm, with little disposition to fat,\nrather to leanness.\n\n‘The colour of the skin is darker brunette, or rather ashgrey.\n\n‘The head is not large, but in proportion, rather short\n(brachycephalous), but less so than the Hame type. The\nlength of the neck is proportionate.\n\n‘The face is in length proportionate, generally with a\nrelatively small breadth both in the frontal and zygomatic\nregions and in the maxillary parts; these, however, are\nrather strongly developed, chiefly in height, especially the\nlower jaw.\n\n‘The nose is long, straight, proportionate, and pointed.\n\n‘The mouth is well proportioned.\n\n‘In the eyes the apertures are in good proportion, and\nnever or very seldom oblique. The iris is dark-grey blue.\n\n‘ The eyebrows are dark, strongly developed, often slightly\nbushy.\n\nria, ‘ad"

movements. Without displaying any grace of movement,
the MokSan girls and women exhibit in their gait, speech,
and gestures a remarkable self-confident strength and
energy. The excellent physique of the Mordvins, their
stature, and the healthy colour of the skin, which distinguishes them sharply from the Ceremis, Votiaks, and
Permians, is the result of having lived for centuries in
a fertile region where food is abundant.1 At the last
census they numbered rather less than 800,000 souls.

It has been supposed by some that the Erza Mordvins, by
others that the Biarmians, are referred to by various Arab
travellers and writers of the tenth century. They mention
nearly in the same words that the Rus were divided into three
tribes. The first lived nearer to Bolgar, and its king had his
seat at Kuyaba (v. Kutaba, Karbaya), a town larger than
Bolgar ; the second were called Slawiya, or Salawiya ; and the
third were the Arthaniya, the king of which dwelt at Artha
(v. Arta, Arba, Abarka, Abarma). This latter people killed
any foreigners that entered their country, but did a good trade
with Kiev, the Khozars, and Bolgars, the exports being the fur
of the black sable, the black fox, and lead. Dorn and Fraehn
read Artha, Arthaniya as Erza, Ertsa, and identified the people
with the Erza Mordvins, who, if they had black sables, had
certainly no lead to export. Chwolson thought the name of
the third tribe should be read Barmaniya, and identified it
with the Biarmians of Scandinavian legend; Mr. Snellman,
the latest Finnish writer on the early history of the Finns since
the beginning of the present era, is inclined to agree with him.
But apart from the fact that by Rus we generally have to
understand Swedes and Northmen, not Finns, there are other
notices of the Arthaniya which show that they dwelt far to the
South, at no great distance from the coast of the Black Sea.
Istakhri vaguely states that Artha lay between the Khozars

1 Smirnov, (4) pp. 115, 121.

and Great Bulgaria, which bounds Rum to the north.’ Idrisi
is more explicit, though some of his geographical statements
are hard to reconcile, and his place-names still more difficult to
identify. Starting from Trebizond, he describes what seems to
be a coasting journey round the east end of the Black Sea as
far as the large town of Matrika, or Matrakha, by which
Tmutarakhan, or Old Taman, is intended. Nevertheless it is
said to be situated on the river Sakir, which branched off from
the Athil (the Volga), the chief affluent of which passed near
Athil, a town near the Caspian. One day’s sail, or 100 miles
before reaching Matrika, he places the considerable town of
Matluka or White Comania. Its situation weuld therefore be
near the port of Novorossisk. He then mentions four towns in
Comania: Kirah, Narus, Nui, and Kiniow or Kiniu, and their
relative positions may be given diagramatically as follows :—

Before proceeding further, we must hear what Idrisi has to
say of the Rus. ‘Kokania,’ he says, ‘is inhabited by the Turks
known as Rusa. They are divided into three hordes, one of
which is called Beraws, and its king resided at Kokania; the
second is called Slawia, and its king resided at Slava, a town
on the top of a hill; the third is the Arthania, and its king
lived at Arthan, a pretty town built on an abrupt hill between
Slawa and Kokania, that is to say, four days (100 m.) from
each. Musulman merchants went to Kokania, but it was
reported that any stranger entering Arthania was infallibly put
to death. One of their exports was lead.’ Referring back to
the diagram, we have to imagine Artha as situated 100 miles
from Slava, though the direction is not mentioned, and 100
miles beyond this was Kokania. Further on, Kokania is stated
to be about twenty stations from Bolgar, though I do not know
what this distance implies. With regard to Nai, the most
westerly point, in mentioning some of the towns on the
Danabros or Dniepr, Idrisi states that from Kaw (Kiev?) to
Nai, ‘a town of Comania,’ was six days’ journey, apparently in
a southerly direction, as he describes the places in a descending
order. Though the position of the Arthaniya cannot be
exactly laid down from the indications given by Idrisi, it could
not have been far removed from the coast, and lay somewhere
in Comania, in the steppe between the Dniepr and the Don,
or not far from it, so that the idea that these people were
Biarmians or Erza Mordvins is without foundation. The next
witness is Ibn Batuta, who made a land journey from Astrakhan to Constantinople. He mentions that at one day’s
journey from Ukak are the Hills of the Russians, who are
Christians with red hair and blue eyes, an ugly and perfidious
people. They possessed silver mines, and from their country
were brought ingots of silver called sum, som, each weighing
five ounces. He gives the position of Ukak as ten days’
journey from Sardi (near Tsarev, and east of Tsarftsin), and
ten days from Sudak on the east coast of the Crimea. Colonel

appears late, and is usually blonde. The colour of the
iris varies from blue to dark chestnut, but is more often
yellowish grey and chestnut. The eyes are usually small,
and sometimes a little oblique. In character the Ecremis
are mild and of a good disposition ; the Russians praise
their honesty ; but they are poor and dirty, shy, mistrustful,
extremely obstinate, and endowed with a slow, limited
intellect.1_ Dr. Papai observed that their skin is white, and
in uncovered places bronzed. Their hair is dark, and very
dark tones predominate, though lighter ones often occur.
The eyes are generally dark, though medium and lighter
tones are common, and among women predominant.?

There is a marked difference between the Hill Ceremis
and those on the left bank of the Volga, the former being
taller and stronger. Yet the type of face on the whole is
the same, and in both we find prominent cheek-bones, with
the same admixture of dark- and light-haired persons with
dark or light skins. The difference of physique between
the two groups is entirely due to physical causes. The
Ceremis on the left bank live among huge swamps and
boundless forests, drink bad water, suffer from insufficient
and improper food, and are consequently subject to fevers,
lung disorders, goitre, and premature old age.®

From the resemblance between the names M/é7i and
Méria, as well as from their geographical position, it is
generally believed that the latter people, whose name is
now extinct, were of the same stock as the Ceremis.
About the end of the eleventh century they are mentioned
by Nestor as paying tribute to Novgorod, and having their
centres at Lake Rostov and Lake KleStino. But their

1 Sommier, (2) pp. 245-250, 238.
2 PApai, p. 264. 3 Smirnov, (x) pp. 84, 85.

territory embraced a far larger area, and included at least
the whole of the governments of Vladimir, Yaroslav, and
the western part of Kostroma. Their old position, therefore, lay between the Ceremis and Mordvins to the east,
and the Finns to the west or north-west. The earliest
mention of them is in the catalogue of names given by
Jordanes in the middle of the sixth century, where, under
the name of Merens, they are placed immediately before
the ‘ Mordens.’

THe VOoTIAKS.

The Votiaks number about 276,000 persons. According
to Dr. Buch their muscular system is only moderately
developed, and their muscular force is small, though of
course there are exceptions, and strong-built men are not
uncommon. The trunk compared with the legs is longer
than among Europeans. The skin is white, though in |
about twenty per cent. of instances it is brown; it is
smooth and comparatively hairless on the body and the
extremities. As regards colour, the hair of the head is
of various shades of brown, but is sometimes reddish
or yellow, very rarely black. The growth of the beard is
scanty, and in colour usually reddish. The eyes, which
are of average size, are generally blue, but also brown, grey,
and occasionally green. The face is oval ; the forehead low
and narrow; the mouth of average size, with lips not
unduly thick; the nose is usually straight and not very
wide. Sometimes the younger women are not bad-looking,
but the older ones are hideous. In general, the Votiaks are
said to bear a great resemblance to the Esthonians.

In character they are described as extremely peaceful,
very industrious and hard-working. Amongst themselves

CHARACTERISTICS OF THE FINNS = 29

they hardly ever come to blows, even in their cups. They
are of a very retiring disposition, and keep themselves as
much as possible apart from the other stranger nations that
surround them, such as, Tatars, Bagkirs, Ceremis, etc., but
especially from the Russians. On the whole, they struck
Dr. Buch as being a dull, heavy people, for they take a
long time to answer a very simple question. On feast-days
the men drink to excess, but the women, though far from
being teetotalers, manage to keep sober.! The low
stature and feeble frame of the Votiak lies in close
connection with his physical surroundings. It has been
observed that inhabitants of low marshy ground are everywhere of lower stature than those living on high ground.
The contrast already noticed between the Hill Ceremis and
those on low ground is found between the Votiaks in the
Viatka government and those in the government of Ufa.
When the latter migrated into the fertile black soil of the
BaSkirs, they became physically regenerated and in no
way inferior in appearance to their Russian and Baskir

and Lettish skulls, such as those, for instance, in Table IV.,
are also mesocephalous. For the present it is an open

question whether the Livs are a mixed Letto-Finnish people
or not.!

Assuming with Professor Virchow that the brachycephals
of the lower series were Finns at a neolithic stage of
civilisation, though the vertical and orbital indices of the
males are lower than might be expected, it does not follow
that they were the first settlers in what is now Livland.
It would seem they were not permanently living on the
shore of the lake, and one of the skulls of the series
appears to have belonged to a sub-dolichocephalous old
woman of Lettish type. Whether a captive or not, after
death she was treated with respect. She was buried with
a curious carved bone ornament on her breast, arrow-heads
at her head and feet, and her body was laid in the same
direction as a genuine member of the tribe. It is impossible to fix a precise date to the shell-mound at Rinne-
kaln, but it was rather late in the neolithic period, as the
presence of sheep and of two breeds of oxen sufficiently
show. It is also later than the stations at Kunda in
Esthonia, of which we shall have to speak in another
chapter.

By a brief study of the archeology of Finland and the
north centre of Russia, we may form an idea when man
first came into these northern climes, and make more or

civilisation, as well as the quarter of the compass from
which he proceeded. The north of Russia must have been
habitable for a long time before man thought it worth while
to try his fortunes in the wintry land, for traces of the
mammoth have been found in almost every part of

west. Yet no handiwork of man is found associated

it is likely that Finns have ever resided. It is true

implements of palzolithic type with tusks of the mammoth
at Kara¢drovo, near Mirom, but the antiquity of the flint
implements has been disputed, and the presence of sherds
of pottery clearly relegates the find to the neolithic period.
The history of man in the north and centre of Russia
begins with the neolithic age, when he had learnt to grind
and polish his stone implements, though he often neglected
to do so. _ As illustrations of archzological objects would

be somewhat out of place in a work of this sort, I have

referred, whenever possible, to the well-known and very
useful atlas of Mr. J. R. Aspelin, Antiguités du nord finnoougrien, under the shorter form of Asp. No.

Finland is a crowbar-shaped tool, a foot or two long,

From the illustrations given by Inostrantsev, it is not
very easy to say how far the Ladogan objects agree with
those found in Finland, though the chisels, with straight
short sides, and some of the gouges, seem tolerably similar
in both regions, as well as the hacking instrument mentioned above. Some of the carved work is specially deserv-
ing of notice, as it may be supposed to possess a distinct
ethnological value. One piece, Fig. 1, represents what is
supposed to be the silhouette of a seal, carved in bone,
with short strokes upon the surface to represent the fur.
The eye is formed by a hole of suspension, and the plaque
may have been worn as an amulet to bring luck to the
bearer. The next, Fig. 2, is the muzzle of a dog or a bear
carved at the end of a bone-scraper; the illustration, unfortunately, is not very distinct, but is interesting as the
precursor of the stone picks with animal heads. Fig. 3
was compared by Inostrantsev to the handle of a dagger,
but it was afterwards recognised by Dr. Tischler as ‘the
figure of a man, without a shadow of a doubt.’ He considered these Ladogan carvings as belonging to the same
category as the sculptured figures in bone and amber from
East Prussia and Galicia, and regarded them as the beginning of plastic art in the north and east of Europe.’ If
this view is correct, it militates against the theory that the
Ladogans were not a European people in the ordinary
usage of the word; but I see very little likeness between
the amber carving of East Prussia and the bone carving
of Ladoga. The main likeness lies in this, that the human
figures in both regions have a hole of suspension under
each armpit, though the Prussian examples have sometimes
another pair of holes on the level of the wrist, but never

1 Tischler, p. 116,

is the head rendered as it is in the Ladogan figure. The
carving of the human figures and of two horses’ heads in
amber is coarse, rude work, clumsy in the last degree,
without a shadow of skill or taste in design or execution.
The art and technique of the Cracow figure is on a par
with that of East Prussia. The firm, clear outlines of the
Ladogan carving, the careful handling of the fur on the
seal, and the general symmetry of Fig. 3, point to qualities
that the amber-cutters never possessed. That Fig. 3 is
intended for a human figure seems to me doubtful, for if
the double row of vertical dots is taken to represent the
separation of the arms and legs, how are the diagonals that
connect these, and the vertical line through the centre of
the neck, to be explained ?

The pottery was coarse, thick, uneven in thickness, and
the clay was often mixed with pounded granite or musselshells. The size of the vessels was considerable, for the
largest must have had a diameter of 224 inches at the
top and the smallest 13 inches, but the idea of attaching
a handle to a clay pot had not yet occurred. Only about
ten per cent. of the sherds were ornamented, which probably means that the lower part of the vessel was left
undecorated. The ornamentation consisted of single and
double rows of holes, arranged horizontally ; of diagonal
rows of punch-marks; of parallel grooves; and of combinations of these elements. We have already seen that
the Ladogan pottery has a great resemblance to that of
Finland.

No date can be assigned to the Ladogan station, though
It is certainly very ancient, and is prior to the introduction
of perforated axes and hammers.

THE NEOLITHIC AGE IN FINLAND | 65

THE STATION OF KOLOMTsI.

More than one hundred miles to the south, at Kolomtsi,
on the right bank of the Volkhov where it issues from Lake
Ilmen, Mr. Peredolsky found abundant traces of prehistoric
man. Though he considers the station to belong to the
palzolithic age, there is no doubt it is neolithic. Several
crushed and broken skulls were found, eight of which he
was able to restore, with the result that seven proved to be
dolichocephalous and one brachycephalous. Unfortunately
no details are given. The bed of dark earth in which the
crania lay was about 5 feet thick, and rested partly on a
glacial deposit, partly on blue clay. This bed was itself
covered by a stratum of brick-clay about 64 feet thick, and
above it came layers of sand and vegetable earth from
3 to 4 inches thick. In his opinion the remains of man
and his industry present an evident resemblance to what
was found at the Ladogan station. They were evidently
of the same primitive tribe, and their crania show features
of likeness with those from the Xurgans of Novgorod, and
generally of Western and Southern Russia. But here again
details are wanting. Like the Ladogans, they had a taste
for carving. One piece of bone was carved into the head
of a bird; another represented the head of a man witha
pointed chin, a very long nose, and a head-dress in shape
like a fez. The clay of the pottery was mixed with gravel,
bits of quartz, and broken shells, and was often ornamented. One design is the same as on a Ladogan sherd ;
another is found on sherds from Lake Onega. The bottom
of the pots was either round or flat. The implements consisted of knives, scrapers, flat wedge-shaped axes, hammers,
straight and concave saws, arrow-heads of various types

I E

with and without a tang, and awls of flint; axes, chisels,
arrow-heads, and whetstones of schist; lance- and arrowheads, awls, harpoons, hooks, gouges, and small axes of
bone. Small pieces of cornelian, jade, agate, etc., with
traces of having been used by man, must have been brought
from a distance. Perforated teeth of the bear, lynx, and
other carnivore were worn as ornaments or amulets.!

FINDS IN OLONETs."

As flint is found on the east side of Lake\nOnega the arrow-heads were made of that miineral.\n\nThese weapons are very abundant, and of various types,\nvery generally lancet- or almond-shaped ; they show various\ndegrees of skill from very coarse to very fine workmanship.\nThe knives and scrapers are also of flint. there was nothing on the surface to betray their presence below. No trace of human handiwork was to be

Three crania, two of them very imperfect, were measured

Kazan, where again the great difference between sepulchral

used the clay was mixed with gravel, broken shells, and

in thickness ; the top was always wide, and the lip seems
sometimes to have turned a little inwards or was slightly
everted. No ears or handles were attached, for these
means of lifting or suspending were replaced by holes
through which a cord was run, but this only in the case of
the larger vessels. When finished, the bow! was burnt,

oval, lancet-shaped, rhomboidal, and tanged: a few were
triangular, or with a notch at the base. Out of about thirty
flint saws one was semicircular.

animals chipped out of a piece of flint. I reproduce four

It might be\ntaken for the skin of an animal, such as a beaver, dried\nand stretched. What the other represents I cannot even\nhazard a guess, though it is doubtless an animal form.\nThe Voldésovans also carved in bone. Mr. Kudriavtsev\nhas in his collection the head of a swan in full relief, carved\nat the end of a long bone, the rest of which was left\nuntouched. Another piece represents the head of a duck ;\na third a very small fish with a small hole of suspension\nthrough the tail. As it is difficult to believe that neolithic\nman in a low state of civilisation, when it is not certain\nthat even the dog was domesticated, should take the\ntrouble to hew out of flint and bone representations of\nmen and animals merely to satisfy his artistic and creative\ninstincts and faculties, some other reason must be sought\nfor. It is more consonant with the extreme laziness of\nuncivilised man to sappose that he had a practical object\nin view, that the human and animal figures served as\nhousehold gods or as personal amulets to secure luck when\nfishing or hunting.\n\nBone implements, such as awls of bird- or fish-bone, harpoons barbed on one side only, axes, knives, fish-hooks—\nthough some of these were of flint made in two parts and\ntied together—and perforated teeth, were very numerous,\nthough bone arrow-heads were rare. Besides fish-hooks\nthey must also have had nets, as the impression of one has\nbeen found on a sherd of pottery. The commonest animal\nbones found were those of the martin, fox, hare, wild boar,\nand beaver ; less common were the remains of the badger,\nwolf, bear, elk, wild ox, otter, reindeer, and dog. In fact,\n\n1 Uvarov, vol. ii. Pl. 14 C D.\n\nTHE NEOLITHIC AGE IN FINLAND _ 73\n\ncanine bones were only found once, and then as an entire\nskeleton that resembled the smaller Ladogan dog. This\nmakes it doubtful whether the dog was domesticated at all.!\n\nA good many miles down the Oka from Murom is the\nstation of Plekhanov Bor. The people lived largely on\nmussels ; in fact, no animal bones were found there at all.\nBut the identity of the ceramic ornament with that at\nVoldésovo shows that people of the same tribe lived at both\nplaces synchronously.”"
}

The decoration is endlessly\nvaried, very complicated at times, and consists of different\ncombinations of linear ornament. It is generally placed\nbelow the rim, and never covers the whole height of the\nvessel ; the inner surface is seldom decorated. A curious\nbut very rare method of adornment was to impress the\nclay with a small spiral shell, probably that of a snail, and\nthus form horizontal bands of spiral depressions, separated\nby horizontal lines of small dots. This novel mode of\ndecoration is also found on neolithic sherds from Le&vina,\na mile and a half above the junction of the Cusovaya with\nthe Kama.? The cord ornament was also used as at\nLeSvina and beyond the Urals. No handles were used,\nbut sometimes a vessel could be suspended by means of\ntwo large round holes placed opposite each other. The\nbottom was always flat, and, with one exception, never\nrounded.   "passage_text": "GENERAL CONCLUSIONS.\n\nThe results, then, ofa survey of the archzology of Northern\nand North Central Russia from the Gulf of Finland to the\nfoot of the Ural chain may be summed up as follows.\nAlong the lower course of the Oka dwelt a people whose\npottery, sculpture, and methods of art connect them with\ntribes inhabiting what is now the government of Oldnets,\nthe west coast of the White Sea, part of Finland, the course\n\n1 Aspelin, (3) p. 6; Grewingk, (4) pp. 92-96.\n\nTHE NEOLITHIC AGE IN FINLAND 85\n\nof the Volkhov, the north coast of Esthonia, and Lake\nBurtneek in Livland. But though the civilisation of this\nhuge region is practically the same, it covers a great space\nin time. It is difficult for us, who live in an age of new\ndiscoveries of the most extraordinary kind, and of great\nsocial changes, to realise that bodies of men can live\ncentury after century, millennium after millennium, without any sensible change in their mode of life. But it is so.\nUncultivated human nature is so constituted that having\nonce accommodated itself to circumstances, and shaken\ndown into a groove, it is content to rub on as best it can,\nand to pass on the heritage of life to another generation\nwithout further thought. Isolated as the tribes were that\ninhabited Central Russia, empires might and did rise and\nfall without their knowledge; nations might and did pass\nalong the great natural highway of the steppe that fringes\nthe Black Sea, but no echo of the event reached the\nsolitudes of Central Russia. It is not surprising, then, that\nwe must believe that a long interval existed between the\nfirst settlement of Voldsovo and the temporary station at\nLake Burtneek, just as a great space of time must be\nimagined between the former and the stations on the\nVolga below Kazdn. In the south-west of Finland we\nseem to have a Scandinavian people that could hardly\nhave arrived later than 1500 B.c., a period when bronze\nwas already known in ‘Scandinavia and Central Europe.\nThe Ladogan station may be quite as ancient, while\nthe settlements on the Oka have all the appearance of\nbeing considerably older. About s00 B.C. is perhaps not\ntoo early to set the animal-headed picks of Oldénets and\nMezen. As perforated stone implements seem unknown\nat Rinnekaln this station is older than that date; while the\n\nstation at Kunda is still older than the last, but less ancient\nthan that on the south shore of Lake Ladoga. The\nstations on the Volga, and certainly some in the Upper\nvalley of the Kama, are very much later than that at\nVolésovo. The Volgan pottery differs from that found on\nthe Oka and further west ; it seems to have more affnity\nwith the ceramic products of the Kama valley, and the\npeople of the Volga may have been somewhat different\nfrom those on the Oka and to the west of it. It is not\nunlikely that the domestic animals came from the steppe to\nthe north and north-east of the Caspian, and with them\nwould naturally come the owners, who might belong to\ndifferent, though not absolutely alien, tribes. Though the\ncivilisation and arts of the fishers and hunters on the Oka,\nas well as to the north and to the west of it, were at such a\nlow stage that they were almost the same everywhere, the\naborigines were not all of the same stock: some were\nlong-headed, others short-headed.   "passage_text": "THE BRONZE AGE IN FINLAND 87\n\nTHe Bronze AGE IN FINLAND.\n\nThe belief that a Scandinavian population existed in the\nsouth-west of Finland in neolithic times is strengthened by\nfinding objects of the Bronze Age in that part of the\ncountry, though they are few in number. With the\nexception of two useful omaments, all of them are weapons,\nconsisting of five swords, seven daggers, one lance-head,\ntwo knives, six palstaves, eight socketed celts, two spectacle\nfibulz, all of bronze, and one large copper arrow-head. As\nall are quite Swedish in character, and no moulds have been\nfound, they must have been imported from Sweden. The only\napparent exceptions are three swords of Central European\ntype, but as these types are also known in Sweden, the\nweapons were probably brought to Finland by way of\nScandinavia. Nearly all the objects came from the southwest corner of Finland, including the Aland Islands ; from\nnear the lower course of the river Kumo; from the lower\ncourse of the river Kyro in the district of Vasa; or\nbetween Viborg and the west coast of Lake Ladoga. All\nwere found south of lat. 64° N., save the large copper\narrow-head, which was picked up as far north as about\nlat. 69°30° N., only about a couple of dozen miles south\nof the Varanger Fjord. Nearly a third of these bronzes\nwere found in cairn graves. Using the classification of Mr.\nO. Montelius, twelve of the weapons belong to his second\nperiod (1450-1250 B.c.); one socketed celt to the third\nperiod (1250-1050); four socketed celts to the fourth period\n(1050-850); and the remainder, including the spectacle\nfibulz, to the fifth period (850-650). It is evident, then,\nthat there existed an intermittent communication between\n\nFinland and Sweden for several centuries, and it is to be\nnoted that all the weapons of the second period, with one\nexception, came from the Aland Islands or from the\nextreme south-west angle of the country, from what is\ncalled Proper Finland. But these importations are not\nthe only reasons for believing the south-west of Finland to\nhave been settled by a Scandinavian people. Hundreds\nof cairn graves are found in a broad belt along the coast\nof the gulfs of Bothnia and Finland, in the islands of the\nsouthern and south-western coast, and in the Aland Islands.\nIn smaller numbers they occur along the shores of lakes\nin the interior. The correspondence in external form, and\npartly in the internal structure, of these cairn graves in\nFinland and Sweden, especially in Uppland, is very striking. The cairns are found singly, in groups, or in a long\nrow; they vary in size and height, the diameter ranging\nfrom 20 feet to 81 feet, and the height from 3 feet to 10 feet.\nIn internal structure there are also differences. Many\nare disposed round a tall upright central stone, quite the\nsame as in Uppland, Sweden, where the arrangement is\ncharacteristic of the Bronze Age. But eastwards, in that part of\nthe valley of the Kama which forms the southern boundary\nof the government of Vidtka, the case is otherwise. Near\nthe old mouth of the Toima, where it fell into the Kama\na little below the town of Eldbuga, is the cemetery of\nAndnino, the approximate date of which is placed by Mr.\nAspelin in the fourth century B.c. Here objects both of\nbronze and iron are found together, and, what is most\nimportant, with hardly an exception the types of the iron\nweapons and instruments are simply continuations of the\nolder bronze forms. As we have seen above, the cemetery\nseems to overlie or, at any rate, to be in very close juxtaposition with, a still older neolithic settlement. Externally\nthe site presented the appearance of an irregularly-shaped\nridge of no great height or size, lying east and west, and\nwithout any indication that there were graves below;\nthough the surface seems to have been strewn with flat\nslabs, on some of which human figures and inscriptions\nwere carved. With four exceptions all had been laid with\nthe head to the south, and only six were inhumed, while\nthe others had undergone incomplete cremation. Traces\nof the action of fire on some of the objects showed that\nthe deceased had been cremated with his clothes, weapons,\nand ornaments upon him. By the side of the male skeletons\nwas placed a knife and a bronze socketed celt or a spearhead, on the breast arrow-heads; with women were de-\nposited necklaces, beads, and other ornaments. Some had\nI G\n\nbronze, others iron weapons, and the knife was usually at\nthe left side, while the celt lay near the right hand. In the\npoorer graves only a knife and some clay vessels were\nfound. In 1881 excavations were resumed, when an untouched sepulchre was opened containing ten skeletons,\nby the side of which were objects of stone, bronze, iron,\nand even silver, but no detailed account of the find has\nas yet been published.! The burialplace found here was ina low natural mound, running east\nand west, about 4o yards long, 12 yards wide, and close\nto the high-road from Reval to Narva. On removing the\nupper layer of soil were disclosed three areas, marked off by\nlarge blocks of granite. The easterly compartment was\noblong, the central one was of irregular form, but approximated a narrow oblong figure, and was the smaller of the\nthree ; the westerly area was also of irregular form, the\nnorth side being considerably longer than the south side,\nso that the long sides, running north and south, were not\nparallel. The eastern compartment measured 19 feet\n6 inches long by 9 feet 9 inches wide, and all three were\npaved with blocks of stone. Between the three compartments were borders of gravel about 3 feet 3 inches wide,\ncontaining no sepulchral remains.\n\nIn the western and central compartments the dead were\nburied at no great depth, almost without any accompanying ornaments, sometimes singly, sometimes piled one on\nthe top of the other. Over them was laid a pavement of\nlarge stones. In the eastern and probably later area there\nwere no skeletons, but between the stones of the pavement\nornaments and numerous bones and teeth of young and\nold were scattered in confusion. Most of these had not\nbeen cremated, though a few burnt bones were found\namong them. In the case of two skeletons in the western\nand central compartments it was possible to observe that\nthey had been laid with the head to the south and the feet\nto the north, and that one of them, a robust man of\nabout thirty years of age, only measured 4 feet 104 inches\nin height. The skulls, unfortunately, were all crushed.!\n\n1 Hausmann, (1) pp. 3-7.\n\nThe cemetery of Tiirsel, about sixteen miles west of\nNarva, and less than a mile from the coast, lies by the\nside of the highway from Narva to Reval. It consisted of\nan oval stone heap, lying east and west, about 50 feet\nlong by 20 feet wide and 3 feet high, overgrown with\nturf. The area over which the mound was raised seems\nfirst to have been paved with stones, for between them\nwere found cremated human remains, as well as the ornaments and other objects they had used when alive. The\noutline of the cemetery appears to have been marked\nby a row of stones, and two rows of stones running north\nand south divided it into compartments.! From an\narcheological point of view the finds from the two contiguous cemeteries of Tiirpsal and Kuckers are closely\nrelated, though also distinguished by well-marked differences; so too those of Tiirsel and Malla. The most\ninteresting fact connected with Kuckers and Tiirpsal is the\ngeographical distribution of some of the fibulze found there.\nMost of them are absent from contemporary grave-finds in\nLivland and Kurland, are hardly known in Sweden, but\nwere common in the Roman provinces north of the Alps\nin the first century, are plentiful in the island of Bornholm,\nand not infrequent in West Prussia. Again, one fibula from\nTiirpsal is not known elsewhere in the Baltic Provinces,\nnor apparently in East Prussia, but analogies are to be\nfound for it at Darzau in Hannover. So too object No. 6\nin Table VIII.,? a bangle of thick bronze wire, thicker in\nthe middle, terminating in round knobs, ranging as far\nsouth as Auzeem in Livland, only recurs at Rondsen, near\nGraudentz in West Prussia, in a grave of the second century. transition from a stone to an iron age. Of course it is
possible that future exploration may introduce us to graves

evidence as yet goes the change seems to have been made
by totally discarding the old order and plunging headlong
into the new civilisation with all the fervour of new converts. The presence of the tooth of a sheep and a pig at

the fibulz, apart from a shred or two of cloth from Malla,

Between\nthese lay many bones, most of them showing marks of\nfire. But here there were few objects of the older time; all\nthe other numerous ornaments, etc., belonged to the newer\nperiod. This cemetery is of great interest, as it is the\nlatest known of its class. Close beside this cemetery lay\nanother, belonging entirely to the later period (700-1200\nA.D.), in which one or more bodies were laid uncremated\nin a shallow grave over which a mound was raised. One\nmale skeleton lay with the head to the north and the feet\nto the south, another was orientated from west to east.!\nTwo skulls from this cemetery have already been spoken\nof at p. 47, and shown to be far removed from the\nFinnish type. Comparing the description given above of the cairn graves in Finland, that\nlasted through the Bronze into the Iron Age, and were\nconstructed by a Scandinavian people, with the description\nof the compartment graves at Tiirpsal and Tiirsel in\nEsthonia, we find little in common, and many important\ndifferences. But the structure of the graves in North\nLivland does not seem to differ much from those in\nEsthonia, and the method prevalent in Livland can be\ntraced as far south as Ronneburg to the east and Auzeem\nto the west. A line drawn between these two places is\nonly about twenty miles south of the boundary between\nthe Esthonians and the Letts about the year 1250. An\ninspection, too, of Table VIII. shows there was considerably\nmore intercourse between Esthonia and Livland north of\nthis line than between the northern and southern halves\nof the latter province. Unfortunately little or nothing\nseems to be known of the mode of sepulchre south of this\nline till we reach Kurland, though the single kist grave at\nAuzeem points to a very different type from that which\nexists in the northern half of Livland. Though contemporary, the mound graves with inhumation in Kurland are\nevidently of a very different character from the compartment graves in Esthonia and the northern half of Livland.\nWe seem then to be in the presence of two distinct\npeoples, that divided the Baltic Provinces nearly equally\nbetween them. And what is more, they seem tranquilly\nto have remained there from the beginning of the Christian\nera till the present time. In Kurland, too, there are transition\nfinds that seem to attest that no alteration had taken place\nin the native population. With regard to this province,\nand perhaps the south of Livland, it seems highly probable\nthat the population was of Letto-Lithuanian stock, as is\nnow the case. With regard to the northern half of the\nProvinces, the population was probably Finnish—at any\nrate in part. Though this view is entirely opposed to\nthat held by Finnish historians and archeologists of the\nhighest repute, it does not seem to me impossible, when\nwe remember that, if Dr. Virchow is correct, there were\nFinns at Rinnekaln, though only temporarily, in the\nneolithic age, at a time to which we have found reason to\nassign a date earlier than 500 B.c. The main objection\nto this theory is that nothing attributable to the earlier\nIron Age has been found east of the Narva, though Finns\nwere probably living near the head of the Gulf of Finland\nall the time. But it may be there was an uninhabited\ntract for a considerable distance east of the Narva, which\nprevented trade articles from being distributed in that\ndirection. RUSSIA 123\n\nplaced near the idol as an I.0.U., and destroyed when\nthe vow is fulfilled.1 Why these promises to pay, if such\nthey were, were not destroyed at Gliadénova, can be\nexplained by supposing that the vows were often made\nbefore going on a dangerous journey or raid, and that\nmany of those that had made vows lost their lives and\nwere thus unable to fulfil their promise.\n\nMost of the metallic objects enumerated or described\nabove are of local manufacture, but now it becomes\nnecessary to notice briefly a series of silver vessels and\ncoins, all of which were imported from a great distance\nduring the fifth, sixth, and seventh centuries, and are found\nsolely in the government of Perm. The silver vessels,\nsome sixty in number, consisting of large dishes, bowls,\newers, chargers, etc., are for the most part specimens of\nPersian art during the Sassanide dynasty. A very few\nare of late Greek or of Greco-Roman work, somewhat\nearlier than the Persian. The former can be dated in\nsome measure by the Sassanide coins struck in the reigns\nof seven kings from Yezdegerd I. (397-417) to Chosroes 11.\n(590-628), the last of the dynasty. Though it is unknown\nin what spot most of the vessels were found, in some\ninstances the places are ascertained, and it is well to\nenumerate them, as it is an important point of history to\ndetermine, if possible, the routes by which they were\nbrought within reach of the natives of the province.\nBeginning from the south, silver coins have been found\nnear Sestakova in the district of Krasnouffmsk; silver\nvessels near Kliiti in the above district; silver vessels\nand coins near Vereino in the sub-district of Cusovsk\non the Cusovaya; coins near Kovina, sub-district of Ust\n\n1 Munkdcsi, (1) p. 68.\n\nGdreva in the district of Perm; coins from the subdistrict of Sludsk in the district of Perm; coins from the\nsub-district of Filatovsk in the district of Perm; a silver\ndish from the sub-district of RoZdestvensk in the district\nof Solikamsk; silver vessels from the sub-district of\nKuvinsk in the above district ; coins from the sub-district\nof Koéebsk in the district of Cerdin; coins near Glazov\nin the government of Viadtka, a district that was formerly\noccupied by Cudes. The commerce that brought these\nprecious commodities from Persia to Perm was interrupted\nfor a time by the fall of the Sassanide dynasty, but was\nafterwards resumed by the victorious Arabs, and lasted for\nfour centuries longer. This last fact is only mentioned\nbecause if the Arab trade-route can be ascertained the\nolder Persian route was probably the same. Mr. Teplotkhov, from whom I have taken the information with regard\nto the finds of Sassanide treasures in the province of Perm,\nconsiders it probable that in the ninth and tenth centuries\nthe merchandise of the Arabs was chiefly transported by\nwater across the Caspian and up the Volga, but that in\nthe eighth century, when this route was partly in the hands\nof the Khozars, they most likely used a road that actually\nexisted to the east of the Caspian. and affirmed it was impossible Ptolemy could have located

to understand Lapps or Finns, it may certainly be granted
that they never permanently lived near the right bank of
the Vistula, and this position does not quite tally with that
assigned to them by Tacitus. His Peucini inhabited the
region north of the Carpathians, what is now Galicia ; north
of them were plundering Venedi, who may be placed in
Volhynia, and north of them were the Fenni, in what is
now the government of Minsk. Both authorities place the
latter people in the same latitude, or nearly so, but Ptolemy
sets them about two degrees further west. Although it is
difficult to believe that any Western Finns ever resided
permanently so far to the west and south as the government of Minsk, and although their civilisation in the
second century A.D. was very different from that portrayed
by Tacitus, it is not impossible to suppose that they made
hunting or predatory excursions in that direction. To
judge from the practice of modern Zirians and Samoyedes,
a hunting or trading expedition to a place several hundred
miles distant from their headquarters is no great matter ;
and the former, even in winter, travel very lightly attired,
with no more property than can be placed on a light sledge
and dragged along by its owner. At certain seasons, when
wild fowl were in abundance, the Pinsk marshes may have

Although the Kurs are mentioned earlier than the Letts
in Kurland, it does not follow that they were the older
inhabitants. There is ground for believing them to be
intruders. Both in Kurland and Livland, to judge from
the evidence of place-names, the Finns only occupied a

the map gradually diminish in number as we recede from

CHAPTER IV
THE PREHISTORIC CIVILISATION OF THE FINNS

Havinc reviewed some of the craniological, archxological,
and historical facts that bear more or less directly on the
Finns, we have now to turn to comparative ethnography
and philology for any help they may afford towards
enabling us to form a slight picture of their prehistoric
condition. Theoretically the prehistoric past may be
divided into two divisions, hereafter to be mentioned as
the first and second periods. To the first belong words
that are common to the Ugrian and the various Finnish
groups ; these originated in Asia, when Finns and Ugrians
seem to have lived in close contact, for the physical and
craniological differences between the Finns and Ugrians
are too great to allow us to suppose they are descended
from a common stock. But they were neighbours, living
under conditions of life precisely similar. Though we
have to believe that once the remotest ancestors of the
Finnish peoples lived in Asia, it is, I think, impossible to
trace them there; the inference is made purely on linguistic grounds. In the craniological chapter we have
found that the crania at Voldésovo, and at the Ladogan
station seem to have analogies with existing Eastern
Finnish skulls. So there is ground for assuming that

the earliest neolithic inhabitants of Central Russia were

ancestors of Finns that had somehow reached Europe
and settled on the Oka. Having done so, it is difficult
to imagine any external cause that could oblige them to
leave it. For though they had nomadic instincts, like
all other nomads they did not roam at large, but over
a certain more or less defined district, which they regarded
as their own. They were so isolated from the rest of the
world that no direct outside pressure could be brought to
bear upon them. The only influences that could touch
them and induce some of them to move were of an internal
nature: the natural increase of population, famine, pestilence. Of these the most efficient factor would be the first ;
to a people living only on fish, shell-fish, and wild animals,
famine of a very severe kind would probably be of rare
occurrence ; but when too many members of a clan died
at one time the remainder would very likely abandon the
locality, at any rate for a time, and migrate elsewhither.
I assume, therefore, for the present—the reasons can best
be brought forward at the end of this chapter,—that at
the end of the first period the undivided Finns had
entered Europe, bringing with them, of course, various
simple notions embodied in the language they had
acquired in Asia; and that the earliest neolithic settlements in the Volga region of Central Russia belong to
this time. As the settlements on Lake Ladoga and the
Upper Volkhov are later than those on the Oké, the movement of the Finns was evidently westward, and the finds
at Fatidnovo and Galit seem to show that, even on European soil, Finns and Ugrians lived at no great distance
from each other for part of the second period.

The second period embraces the time between the first
settlements in Europe and the first contact with an Iranian

civilisation, which may have taken place from four hundred
to six hundred years before the present era. It covers a
long lapse of time, and may be divided into an earlier and
later half. The first half is characterised by a series of
words common to all, or nearly all, the East and West

split into different linguistic groups, though various fractions of the united body may have lived at very consider-
able distances apart. The second half is marked by words

only be guessed at. So it would be wrong to maintain

  "passage_text": "common wild animals among the Eastern and Western
Finns. But nevertheless on the whole the new words of
the second period must be taken to mean increase of experience, modification of the ancient mode of life, and a
slight forward development of the different groups made
independently of each other during the latter half of it.
They are also to be considered as older than the first
contact with an Iranian or European civilisation. But of
many genuine words confined to the West Finns alone we
cannot always be quite sure whether they came into use
before or after this event in the history of their civilisation.

The late Professor Ablayist.has.already drawn us a picture
of the prehistoric civilisation of the Finns that has often
been referred to, but now I propose to supplement it in
some respects by drawing upon the existing customs and
beliefs of the Eastern Finns, and laying more emphasis on
the psychological element. But in doing so it must be
borne in mind that they too are more or less civilised, for
the most part Christianised, and living under conditions
very different from those of their prehistoric ancestors.
From about the eighth to the thirteenth century they were
exposed to the civilising influence of Bolgars and Turks,
who have left many traces of their superior civilisation and
higher religion in a series of loan words. All that is known
of their sacrificial rites, their ‘divinities, their ideas about
the phenomena of nature, cannot therefore be accepted
without considerable reduction and allowance for subsequent growth and accretion. The mere passage from a
hunting and fishing stage to one that is almost purely
agricultural, the change from a nomad to a settled mode
of life, undoubtedly affected the class of gods to whom
they paid especial worship. ‘To a hunting nomad the idea

of a great and benevolent earth-mother that gave forth of
the fruits of the earth in due season, of a beneficent sungod that ripened them, could never occur. Hence all
notice of gods whose being and worship entirely depends
on the practice of agriculture by their worshippers may be
excluded from our survey. The beliefs, customs, and so
forth, of the Ostiaks, Voguls, Samoyedes, and Altaian Turks
are on the whole more likely to tally with those of the
prehistoric Finns than any other people on the globe,
though they too have been subjected to various civilising
influences for which allowance must be made.

THE Gops AND DIVvINITIES.

Had the Finns of the first and second periods any notion
of the supernatural? This question, as it seems to me,
must be answered in the negative. At the first beginning
of humanity on the globe there could have been no such
notion, for before it can be formed at all some idea must
exist of nature and the natural. As an idea, Nature is so
complex that a long time must have elapsed before man
could form the least conception of it. Yet at a very early
period the human mind, working unconsciously, must have
framed categories and separated the phenomena of nature
into those of daily occurrence and those that happen at
longer or shorter intervals. Under the first category would
fall the relative weights of common things, such as stones
and feathers, the fact that if a thing dropped from one’s hand
it fell to the ground, the recurrence of night and day, the
heat of the sun, etc. These being facts of daily experience
excited no astonishment. Under the second category
would come the distinction between a hot and cold or dry

and wet portion of the year; the phases of the moon; the
fact that fish run up rivers at a certain season and return at
another ; that certain animals frequent particular parts of
the country at one time more than other. These and
many other similar observations that they made would
seem to them, no doubt, what we should now call natural ;
that is to say, these phenomena excited no astonishment.
But others of uncertain periodicity, and recurring at long
intervals, such as eclipses, earthquakes, comets, famines,
and the like, would certainly create wonder, sometimes
fear, and might therefore be termed wonders, marvels, or
miracles in the old sense of the word, but not supernatural,
for they had no conception of nature as a starting-point
from which the idea of supernatural could be deduced.
Their gods even, conceived probably as invisible beings
with purely human attributes, the attributes of humanity at
a very slow stage, could in no sense be considered supernatural. Men could also render themselves invisible.
The gods too were so human that they could be forced to
act in accordance with the wishes of their worshippers,
and could likewise be punished. But in course of time,
though not everywhere at the same time, to the worship of
the older gods, that resided chiefly in trees, wells, rivers,
and animals, was added the worship of a higher order of
divinity whose seat was in the sky. This was the result
of the gradual development of a new order of ideas. Just
as a man in need of anything applies first to his friends or
neighbours nearest at hand before turning to a distant
stranger, sO man in the early stages of his history had
recourse, when in danger or trouble, to the helpers that
seemed nearest at hand, that dwelt, as he believed, in the
trees and waters at his very door, rather than to the distant

heaven, to which no human voice could be expected to
reach."

  "passage_text": "At last a change took place in this respect. Some men,
resolving to leave no stone unturned, ventured to seek aid
from the sky-god, who in time would gain a large circle of
worshippers. The intellectual energy and development
of these adherents of the new god would no doubt be
superior to that of the adherents of the older gods. Yet
to them the sky-god was not supernatural, though a step
was taken in that direction; he was now supermundane:
Partly from his elevated position, partly perhaps from
regarding the sun as his eye, the sky-god would in time
acquire the attribute of omniscence; though at first this
would merely be superhuman, not supernatural knowledge ;
it would exceed the knowledge of any one man, but would
only be equal to the sum of knowledge of all men, what
each man knew of his own actions. Again, instead of attributing storms, thunder, lightning, rain, and drought to the
anger of witches, sorcerers, or of the inferior order of gods
that dwelt in trees and stones, these phenomena were now
ascribed to the will of the god in the sky above. This
tended to produce the impression that he was all-powerful
as well as omniscient. Still, with all this, his power was
merely superhuman in the sense that it exceeded the
capacity of any one man or body of men. The idea of
his being a supernatural personage could only arise when
his omnipotence was raised to such a pitch that he became
thought of as the creator of the world, of nature as we
perceive it. As the creator is necessarily greater than the
created, it now for the first time became possible to regard
him as a being transcending nature in every conceivable
way—as supernatural, in fact. The notion ofa supernatural

being or god, wielding supernatural power, must, if this
view is correct, be of late origin. It never could develop
among a people in whose pantheon there was no creator
of the world. If such a people possess a notion of the
supernatural they must have borrowed it.

It cannot be doubted that the prehistoric Finns, when
they stood in the open air and gazed around, were under
the impression that nearly every object in nature was the
habitation of a spirit. This cosmological theory naturally
accounted for the life and movement they perceived around
them ; even inanimate objects, like rocks and stones, required an active cause to account for their presence, for
their difference in size, and for their often strange shapes.
Of course, all spirits were not of equal value or of equal
strength: that would depend in some measure on the size
of their habitation. The spirit of the sky was greater than
an ordinary tree, stone, or house spirit. So a Samoyede
wizard in addressing his familiar spirit says: ‘I cannot
approach Num’ (the god or spirit of the sky), ‘he is too
far away; if I could reach him I should not beseech thee,
but should go myself, but I cannot.’? The Samoyedes
of the government of Tomsk, who are partly Christianised,
fear Num to such an extent that they pronounce his name
with evident trembling, and prefer the use of an epithet
meaning ‘the watcher over reindeer.’ Tiirm, the skygod of the Northern Ostiaks, who only speaks in thunder
and the angry voice of the storm, is an inexorable being
whom no prayers can reach, whom no offerings can propitiate. He is therefore not the object of any worship, and
Ostiaks in need of help must turn to a spirit of lower
degree. Here we see that the physical remoteness of

2 Castrén, (2) i. 207. 9 [bid., (2) ii, 162. 3 /did., (2) i. 30%, 909.

the sky from the earth gave rise to the idea of an inaccessible god. Like the Ostiaks, the Turks of the Altai do
not turn for help to the highest god, but to deities of lower
rank.! Some Votiaks allege another reason for not paying
full honour to Inmar, the god of the sky. He is very good,
‘and so they do not fear him, worshipping him with prayers,
but not with sacrifices. Though, in the above instances,
the sky is conceived mainly as a spirit, the latter was not
quite incorporeal. To the Samoyede the rainbow is ‘Num’s
mantle’; to a Ceremis it is ‘the bow of Jumo’ (sky, god),
the thunderbolt is his stone (/umon ki); to a Vogul the
lightning is ‘the arrow of Tarim.’ Compared with the
Northern Ostiaks, the Voguls have greatly modified their
view of the sky-god Numi Tarim. He is a great hunter,
the bear is his dear daughter, and they pray to him as ‘our
father’ to let down fish and wild animals from above.’ He
is therefore no longer inaccessible to direct entreaty, which
shows a later stage in religious development ; the fear of
using his name has passed away, and the feeling of distance
from him is removed or lessened. The ascription of the
epithet ‘father’ is not, as might be supposed, the result of
Christian influence, for in the heroic poems of the Irti§
Ostiaks, which go back to about the thirteenth or fourteenth
century, a prince who is hard pressed in battle calls to his
god in the following terms: ‘Is it possible the Golden
Light (the Sky-god), my father, has decreed that common
soldiers should take my iridescent scalp?’* Judging from
their poetry, the Tiirim of the Southern Ostiaks on the
IrtiS was very different from the Tiirm of the Northern
Ostiaks described by Castrén. The former is rather a

1 Radloff, ii. 8. 2 Ostrovski, p. 33.
3 Munkacsi, (1) pp. 185, 186.' 4 Patkanov, (1) pp. 48, 49.

ee

mild god ; ‘father’ is his constant epithet, and he dispenses
good solely from his merciful nature and his love for man.
And judging from the epic poetry he does not seem to
have demanded any worship, sacrifice, or prayers. Even
animals in danger cry for help to him, and never in vain.
It would be interesting to know whether this revolution
of ideas with respect to the character of the sky-god was
independent of all foreign influence ; it is difficult to believe
that it could have taken place spontaneously.

Num, like the Turk. fefirs, means ‘sky’ and ‘god,’ and
among the Finns we find the same confluence of two
distinct ideas in a single word."

carry away from each house in the place the old fagot,

left. A new fagot is cut and taken home. The}master
of the house then says: ‘Old one, go away! let another,
a good one, come! Whenever anything happens, preserve
me, do not bring evil!’? But to return to the Votiaks: the
most important family sacrifices are those held in the kuala
which each family possesses, and is the home of the vorsud.
Besides the family Aua/a there is a clan kuala in every
village. If there is more than one clan in a village, an
event of rare occurrence, there is a corresponding number
of additional £ua/as. The clan 4ua/a forms part of the
farm-buildings of the oldest man directly descended from
the ancestor of the clan, but differs in nothing from a
family Auala. Sacrifices in these buildings are held
on fixed and on accidental occasions. The family and
clan sacrifices are held regularly twice a year, at the
beginning of summer, and autumn when the field-work is
over. The offerings consist of bread, groats, beer, spirits,

be explained as the adjective of Biger, ‘a Tatar,’ ‘a Bolgar.’

of a list of Votiak patronymics written down at the end of

derived from the still existing Vorsud names Birga, Z’um’a,
Kib’a, Sudz’a. Some river-names are identical with voriud

these rivers had been adopted as tutelary spirits, and so
became clan names, though other equally plausible reasons

the threshing-floor, the corn-kiln, etc., to whom small

Ugrians and Eastern Finns, we may safely assume that the
prehistoric Finns also had gods of the family and the clan,
who were supposed to be domiciled in quaint-looking
stones, in small stone piles, in fagots of twigs, and in

inhabited and personified every large river. Whether they

seen, all that he could bestow could also be given by the
personal or family god.

A brief mention of some of the beliefs of the Ugrians
and Eastern Finns will help to show what the general
mental attitude of the prehistoric Finns might have been
